pool: US OEM and prime purchases of metal castings from foundries (defense-critical)
title: Tooling Bank: custody and digital twins for every OEM-owned casting pattern, triggered by foundry closures
one_liner: Be the Iron Mountain for casting patterns: take custody of OEM-owned tooling before its foundry closes, scan it into a validated digital pattern, and become contractor of record when the part is re-sourced or printed.
deciding_reason: TAM is bounded by roughly 45 foundry closures a year, foundries store tooling free, OEM tooling platforms exist, and printed sand erodes the need for patterns.

pool: US OEM and prime purchases of metal castings from foundries (defense-critical)
title: Second-Source Factory: sell approved part numbers, not consulting hours
one_liner: A fixed-price factory that turns a sole-sourced or backordered casting into two prime-approved sources, where the approval package and the process data are the product.
deciding_reason: Primes own the approval gate and are hiring in-house; free government substitutes cover DLA parts; no evidence primes will buy a third-party package, which is the idea's own kill test.

pool: US OEM and prime purchases of metal castings from foundries (defense-critical)
title: Tier-Three Credit: lend against the prime's payment and the customer's tooling, not the foundry's balance sheet
one_liner: Multi-tier supply chain finance for defense and aerospace foundries and machine shops, repaid by sweeping the prime's payment so the borrower's weak credit matters little.
deciding_reason: Incumbent supply chain finance and PO lenders already target this gap, the prime-sponsored structure is unproven, and the revenue test needs a roughly $830M book.

pool: US OEM and prime purchases of metal castings from foundries (defense-critical)
title: Foundry BOT: build, staff, operate and transfer foundries for the new buyers who cannot hire the people
one_liner: Fluor plus an operating team for foundries: design, power, permit, commission and run a plant for 3 years, then hand it over, so buyers with money and no casting people get capacity in about 24 months.
deciding_reason: Net fee revenue is small and lumpy, turnkey incumbents exist, and the named buyers are building their own teams.

pool: US OEM and prime purchases of metal castings from foundries (defense-critical)
title: The Non-GE Foundry: customer-funded independent castings capacity for everyone who just lost a neutral supplier
one_liner: A neutral investment and structural casting platform financed by 10-year take-or-pay contracts from the engine, turbine and defense makers who cannot buy a CPP and do not want to depend on a competitor's captive.
deciding_reason: Genuine $100M+ prize, but capital-heavy, incumbents and SpaceX are already spending, the neutral-supplier premise is mostly false, and first parts would arrive after the shortage window.

pool: US OEM and prime purchases of metal castings from foundries (defense-critical)
title: US-Pour: the verified melt-and-pour ledger that turns 'made from US steel' into a 25-to-40-point tariff cut
one_liner: The compliance rail for the April 2026 Section 232 rule that taxes steel derivatives made entirely from US-melted-and-poured steel at 10% instead of 25-50%: heat-level attestations from foundries and mills, audit-ready for CBP.
deciding_reason: Volatile rule, unmeasured and probably tiny qualifying pool, and melt-and-pour reporting is already mandated and built into broker software.

pool: US OEM and prime purchases of metal castings from foundries (defense-critical)
title: Cleaning Room as a Service: we run the foundry's finishing department and bill per casting
one_liner: Take over the department foundries cannot staff: robotic grinding, cut-off and weld-repair cells plus trained operators inside the foundry's building, billed per casting finished with a guaranteed cost ceiling.
deciding_reason: Price exceeds value: foundries self-build cells for about $25k and vendors sell them, so a $250k cell-year managed service has no buyer logic.

pool: US OEM and prime purchases of metal castings from foundries (defense-critical)
title: One Approved Supplier, Two Hundred Foundries: the supplier of record that CT-screens before machining and guarantees good parts
one_liner: A prime-approved supplier of record that buys rough castings from a vetted network, CT-screens them before machining, machines them, and ships finished parts at a guaranteed-good-part price, carrying the yield risk nobody else will.
deciding_reason: CT screening does not work on heavy ferrous castings, buyers can already order machined castings, Hadrian is better funded and integrated, and $100M is pass-through revenue at thin margins.

pool: Gas-turbine fleet services and aftermarket (maintenance, repair, parts, upgrades, LTSAs)
title: Spare-Set Pool: hot-section outages with a guaranteed return-to-service date
one_liner: A neutral pool of pre-inspected, pre-fit hot-gas-path sets (rotor, nozzles, shrouds, combustion hardware) for the common F- and E-class frames. Owners with one to four units rent a set per outage and send their retired set into the pool, under a contract with a return-to-service date and liquidated damages.
deciding_reason: Rotor exchange and hot-gas-path component exchange are already sold by GE, Hanwha, MD&A and EthosEnergy; the remaining lease-with-guarantee gap is thin, capital-heavy and needs 20%+ share of reachable events.

pool: Gas-turbine fleet services and aftermarket (maintenance, repair, parts, upgrades, LTSAs)
title: Hot-Section Core Exchange (LKQ for turbines)
one_liner: Pay owners real money for retired hot-gas-path parts, give every part a serial-level remaining-life record, route them through partner repair shops, and sell warrantied remanufactured parts at 55-70% of OEM price.
deciding_reason: GE and every ISP already run exchange or trade-in programs, owners repair and return their own parts instead of selling cores, and the LKQ flow of scrapped assets does not exist here. Ceiling about $25M.

pool: Gas-turbine fleet services and aftermarket (maintenance, repair, parts, upgrades, LTSAs)
title: Certified Unfired: the grading and escrow layer for stranded turbines and slot reservations (collectibles liquidity stack)
one_liner: A grading standard, escrow and OEM-consent layer so unfired and low-hour turbines, and later slot reservations, trade as a standardized asset: the PSA of turbines. The weakest idea of the 8: revenue is easy, a defensible profit pool is uncertain.
deciding_reason: A handful of deals, OEM refurbishment already provides the 'grade', OEM consent is the key dependency, and the principal version is a cyclical dealer with no moat. Exposed to an AI-capex pullback.

pool: Gas-turbine fleet services and aftermarket (maintenance, repair, parts, upgrades, LTSAs)
title: Outage Bench: a credentialed bench of turbine specialists (expert-labor marketplace plus spot labor)
one_liner: An employer-of-record bench of vetted ex-OEM technical advisors, Level-III inspectors, rotor and controls specialists and precision millwrights, with a published skills passport that insurers, owners and ISPs accept in place of an OEM badge, plus remote senior supervision. Weakest moat of the 8: a staffing business unless the credential becomes a standard.
deciding_reason: A commodity staffing business that the idea itself calls the weakest moat; competitors exist, and the credential that would make it defensible has no evidence of acceptance. Fails the 'path to something that scales' rule.

pool: Gas-turbine fleet services and aftermarket (maintenance, repair, parts, upgrades, LTSAs)
title: Progressive for Turbines: a condition-priced, insurer-backed independent LTSA
one_liner: A fixed-price per-hour maintenance contract for F- and E-class units priced on measured wear and operating history instead of the OEM's averaged equivalent-hours formula, with a pooled spare inventory and a reinsurer-backed parts-cost cap. It skims the best-run units the OEM formula overcharges.
deciding_reason: Only idea whose arithmetic reaches $100M at 3-5% share with an existing budget line and an unproductised pricing/risk wrapper. Weaknesses: ISPs already sell F-class LTSAs, OEM can match price, casting scarcity cuts both ways, ceiling about $70M.

pick.from_title: Progressive for Turbines: a condition-priced, insurer-backed independent LTSA
pick.title: Condition-Priced Turbine Maintenance Contracts: LTSA takeout, hardware-pooled and insurer-wrapped
pick.one_liner: A 10-year per-hour maintenance contract for older-design F- and E-class frames, priced on measured wear instead of OEM fleet-average equivalent hours, backed by a pooled spare-set and core inventory and a reinsurer-backed parts-cost cap, sold through a free LTSA forensic audit.
pick.sharpened_pitch: Open with a free forensic audit of expiring or transactional-rate OEM LTSAs: normalise the equivalent-hours math, true-up, and the title-to-remaining-parts-life clause into a dollar exit value per unit. The takeout is a 10-year per-hour contract on older-design F- and E-class frames (7FA.03, 501F, 7EA, 6B) where aftermarket parts already sell 25-40% below OEM list, priced on borescope, NDE and start/trip history with an annual true-up. Do not build shops or foundries: buy repair and parts from ISPs (Hanwha Power, EthosEnergy, Allied, Sulzer, Chromalloy) under framework agreements, and own the layers they are conflicted on. First, the underwriting model and serial-level remaining-life data. Second, a pooled spare-set and core inventory financed with equipment-finance capital, which is also the hedge against casting scarcity (this folds in the spare-set pool and the core-exchange data feed). Third, a fronted, reinsurer-backed excess-of-loss on parts cost plus an outage-delay guarantee, written through a licensed carrier. Sell to the CFO and VP Generation, with the lender's independent engineer pre-cleared through a published reference framework. Keep the $100M path: 20-25 grid units at $3-4M ($70-85M), plus availability contracts on 300-500 MW of aeroderivative and behind-the-meter fleets at $80-100/kW-yr ($25-40M), plus Canada and Mexico. Raise a risk-capital facility before signing the first fixed-price contract.
pick.payer_and_signer: CFO and VP Generation at co-ops, municipal and joint-action agencies, PE-backed IPPs and industrials sign; the lender's independent engineer gates project-financed units. Budget line: LTSA or transactional maintenance fees of about $2-5M per large unit-year, plus major-outage O&M of $5-12M per hot-section event.
pick.path_to_100m: 25-35 F-class units at $3-4M a year = $75-140M, about 3-5% of a corrected ~600-800 addressable US F-class units (not the 1,100 in the original idea). Realistic 5-7 year trajectory is 15-20 units ($55-70M) plus E-class modular agreements; the last $30M comes from BTM/aeroderivative availability contracts ($80-100/kW-yr x 300-500 MW) and Canada/Mexico. Gross margin 12-18% means $12-18M gross profit at $100M, so value depends on the data and pricing edge, not volume.
pick.competitors_and_edge: Hanwha Power (PSM, https://www.psm.com/services/service-agreements), EthosEnergy, MD&A/PW Power Systems and Wood Group-lineage contracts already sell third-party F-class LTSAs; OEMs offer customizable LTSAs and can match price on the best units; Aon sells parametric forced-outage cover but not maintenance cost. Edge: no one found prices on measured condition with a reinsurer-backed parts-cost cap and pooled hardware; ISPs are parts sellers and cannot credibly underwrite their own contract; OEM averaging makes the best units overpay.
pick.why_now: The 2000-2008 F-class build-out is rolling off LTSAs; OEM bandwidth is consumed by a 116 GW backlog (GE Vernova Q2 2026) and component quotes have stretched from about 4 to 12-16 weeks (PSM); capacity prices cleared at the $325-333/MW-day cap three auctions running. Caveat: PJM's collar is only approved through 2029/30, so the window is 2026-2030.
pick.moat: Serial-level condition and remaining-life data that improves pricing with each unit; counter-positioning (OEMs cannot reprice their book without losing their cross-subsidy); 10-year contract switching costs; pooled inventory scale economics; reinsurer and fronting-carrier relationships.
pick.biggest_open_risk: Whether condition-based pricing yields a real, bankable 10-20% discount after paying aftermarket parts and repair costs, and whether any reinsurer will quote parts-cost excess-of-loss when standard property cover excludes wear and tear; secondarily OEM price-matching on the best units and casting scarcity hitting independents harder than OEMs.
pick.cheapest_next_test: Six weeks, under $25k: run five free LTSA forensic reviews for co-ops and municipal agencies, price each unit on its borescope/NDE and operating history versus the OEM equivalent-hours quote, ask two specialty reinsurers through a broker for an indicative parts-cost excess-of-loss term sheet, and interview three lender independent engineers. Kill if the median measured saving is below about 8% or no reinsurer will quote.

pool: Gas-turbine fleet services and aftermarket (maintenance, repair, parts, upgrades, LTSAs)
title: Hot-Section Repair Factory: automated multi-cycle repair the OEM would rather replace than do
one_liner: Two automated, permitted repair-and-coat shops that make second and third repairs routine on E- and F-class buckets, nozzles and shrouds, selling capacity to owners, ISPs and OEMs drowning in backlog.
deciding_reason: Incumbents are well-capitalized roll-ups with the same capacity problem and the same automation toolkit; automation is not a moat and the metallurgy premise is shaky. Capital-heavy business with thin differentiation.

pool: Gas-turbine fleet services and aftermarket (maintenance, repair, parts, upgrades, LTSAs)
title: Megawatts from existing iron: financed, multi-vendor uprates paid from capacity revenue
one_liner: Packages of inlet cooling, controls and firing-temperature tuning, compressor and steam-path upgrades and supplemental firing, sold with financing and an accredited-MW guarantee. Weakest-evidenced of the 8: the uprate market must grow roughly 3-5x for it to work.
deciding_reason: Market is small (~200 MW per auction), served by OEMs and in-house IPP teams, depends on a capacity price collar that ends after 2029/30, and an accredited-MW guarantee is not controllable. Ceiling about $30M.

pool: Gas-turbine fleet services and aftermarket (maintenance, repair, parts, upgrades, LTSAs)
title: Uptime Wrapper for mixed behind-the-meter data-center gas fleets
one_liner: Cross-OEM operations, maintenance and spares for AI-campus gas fleets built from whatever turbines and engines could be found: one contract, one uptime number for the whole site, with a pooled spare-engine inventory and a remote operations center.
deciding_reason: Demand is real but addressable owners either self-operate or buy power-as-a-service that bundles O&M; OEMs and dealers cover most boxes. A pure wrapper without owned assets is a services niche with ceiling about $35M.

pool: US farmers' spend on equipment repair, maintenance and parts
title: Harvest Pit Crew
one_liner: A per-machine, per-season uptime subscription for custom harvesters and big grain farms: winter inspection, parts caches and roving techs staged along the northbound harvest route, a loaner combine, and a 24-hour-or-credit promise on the older, mixed-brand machines the OEM uptime programs exclude.
deciding_reason: Deere and dealers already run free harvest-run vans and parts trailers; crews self-repair; the buyer pool is a few hundred crews; the fee approaches the crew's whole repair bill. Too small and partly done.

pool: US farmers' spend on equipment repair, maintenance and parts
title: Shared Shop
one_liner: Run the shop for clusters of large farms: embedded lead techs, a shared regional bench and parts cache, maintenance planned around the farm's field calendar, priced per machine per year with an uptime promise and shared savings.
deciding_reason: Revenue is mostly pass-through cost, the buyer must give up its own techs, and dealers already sell on-site contracts. Gross profit at the idea's own ceiling is $15-20M.

pool: US farmers' spend on equipment repair, maintenance and parts
title: Machine Passport
one_liner: The PSA/ACV of farm machinery (collectibles authentication-plus-liquidity pattern): a serial-keyed condition grade and service-and-telemetry history for used tractors, combines and sprayers, sold to lenders, auctions, dealers and buyers, with warranty and financing attached at the sale. It has not happened because the record-holders are single-brand counterparties and only dealer tools could read full machine history until the settlement.
deciding_reason: Lender valuation and inspections already exist, prices are 4-10x the market, and the best-funded peer is tiny. Useful as a feeder dataset for a warranty product, not a $100M business alone.

pool: US farmers' spend on equipment repair, maintenance and parts
title: Tech Bench
one_liner: Travel-nurse-style bench (capex pass-through to a scarce trade): OEM-neutral farm-equipment technicians on 13-week W-2 contracts who follow the planting and harvest waves from state to state, with a short-program training pipeline financed by employers and the new Workforce Pell. It has not happened because ag is small to national staffing firms and technician credentials are brand-specific and dealer-tied.
deciding_reason: Priced 2.5x above market wages, no moat by the idea's own admission, a staffing margin, and existing ag recruiters. Even a good outcome is a $30M staffing business.

pool: US farmers' spend on equipment repair, maintenance and parts
title: Any-Shop Plan
one_liner: Mechanical-breakdown coverage and an uptime promise for out-of-OEM-warranty tractors, combines and sprayers that pays any qualified shop on a preferred price schedule, underwritten from machine data and sold through lenders and used-equipment sales.
deciding_reason: Structurally the most scalable (balance sheet, lender distribution) but crowded, priced at combine rather than blended levels, and the math lands near $25-40M revenue unless attach reaches about 11% of the base.

pool: US farmers' spend on equipment repair, maintenance and parts
title: Standard Shop
one_liner: NAPA AutoCare for farm equipment: certified multi-brand independent shops under one brand, a 12-month or 2,000-hour repair guarantee honored by any member, one parts and credit program, and farmer-facing booking.
deciding_reason: A parts-distribution margin business at heroic wallet share, squeezed by Deere's price cuts and second-tier parts, with a PE-backed multi-state supplier already serving independents.

pool: US farmers' spend on equipment repair, maintenance and parts
title: Core Bank
one_liner: Win the cores and own independent remanufacturing of farm machine components: pay cash for failed engines, hydraulic pumps and motors, final drives, transmissions and electronic modules, remanufacture to OE spec with a warranty, and sell back on exchange.
deciding_reason: Best structure in the set (core stream as moat), but the event math contradicts itself, OEM reman and a PE-backed 42-location rebuilder already hold the core stream, and independent rebuilders compete on price.

pool: US farmers' spend on equipment repair, maintenance and parts
title: Elevator Depots
one_liner: Consigned depots of fast-moving farm parts inside co-ops and ag retailers, delivered by the retailer's own trucks and billed to the farmer's existing retailer account, which settles when grain is delivered; first-party supply includes Deere's new second-tier parts, which Deere says will be sold through 'other places' besides dealers.
deciding_reason: Revenue is gross sales, not net; first-party supply is open to every retailer; dealers and Deere already stock parts on or near the farm. A $20M GMV, single-digit-million net business.

pool: US building-permit plan review and inspection (government and private providers)
title: The Tele-Inspection Factory
one_liner: A licensed, insured private provider whose inspectors sign off from a desk on guided video that tradespeople capture on their own phones, priced per inspection, starting with Florida single-trade finals.
deciding_reason: Already built: Inspected has 100k+ Florida virtual inspections, a Series A, and Broward access since Aug 2025, with under $10M revenue. Low statutory barrier means no moat, and 1.7M inspections is about 28x the leader.

pool: US building-permit plan review and inspection (government and private providers)
title: Inspection-as-a-Service for the Top Homebuilders
one_liner: One master contract that replaces the builder's patchwork of city inspection windows, third-party QA walks and lender looks with a single independent inspection crew per division, funded by the city inspection fees the builder no longer owes.
deciding_reason: Builder-paid private-provider inspections are already 25-35% of inspections in sample Florida counties. Reaching $100M needs about a third of reachable-state homes, and the defect-data premium is a few hundred dollars per home.

pool: US building-permit plan review and inspection (government and private providers)
title: Technical Control plus Latent-Defect Warranty for Attached Housing (an NHBC for the U.S.)
one_liner: Independent staged inspections during construction that unlock an insured 10-year structural warranty, sold to condo and townhome developers who otherwise cannot price or insure defect liability.
deciding_reason: Tiny, legislation-dependent pool: Colorado condo output is in the tens to low hundreds of units, Washington is not a second market, and the incumbent warranty leader earns under $700 per home versus the $2,800 required.

pool: US building-permit plan review and inspection (government and private providers)
title: The Platform Behind Independent Private Providers
one_liner: A licensing, insurance, software and payments platform that lets individually licensed engineers, architects and building code administrators run private-provider practices without running a firm, like an independent broker-dealer for inspectors.
deciding_reason: Gross-to-net kills it: the idea itself calls $450M gross heroic, the employee rule favors hiring firms over platforms, and no evidence independents want a 22% take.

pool: US building-permit plan review and inspection (government and private providers)
title: Fixed-Price Special Inspection and Closeout
one_liner: Replace time-and-materials special inspection and testing on commercial projects with a fixed price per project, remote review, digital evidence and a guaranteed closeout package the building official accepts.
deciding_reason: Share math is plausible but it is a labor business against $1B incumbents who can already quote lump sum; remote review does not remove the on-site technician, and the closeout-date value is an untested insider claim.

pool: US building-permit plan review and inspection (government and private providers)
title: Permit-Clean: Verified Permit Status and Closeout at the Closing Table
one_liner: A rail that tells title agents, lenders and insurers whether a property has open, expired or unpermitted work, and clears it out of the seller's proceeds.
deciding_reason: Unsourced incidence, existing lien-search workflow, aggregator data already for sale, and a statute that eases the problem. The cure work belongs to contractors, so revenue is a thin referral margin on a small pool.

pool: US building-permit plan review and inspection (government and private providers)
title: The Shot-Clock Concession
one_liner: Take over plan review and inspection for large departments that now lose volume and fee revenue when they miss statutory clocks, paid a share of retained fees, with the clock guaranteed.
deciding_reason: The concession model is SAFEbuilt's, built over two decades and 19 acquisitions. The clock guarantee is the only novelty and is untested; procurement is slow and the fee pool shrinks as private-provider volume grows.

pool: US building-permit plan review and inspection (government and private providers)
title: Energize-on-Schedule: Inspection, Commissioning and AHJ Desk for Hyperscaler Build Programs
one_liner: A program-level service that guarantees the inspection, special-inspection, commissioning and certificate-of-occupancy path across a hyperscaler's pipeline, priced against the idle-capital cost it removes.
deciding_reason: Narrow buyer set, funded commissioning roll-ups already exist, and a date guarantee depends on power and AHJs outside the vendor's control. The idea's own path needs 7-13% of a $0.75-1.5B pool.

pool: US purchases of power and distribution transformers (utilities, developers, data centers, industrials)
title: Swap, Don't Buy: AMI-driven redeployment of the installed transformer base
one_liner: Use smart-meter data to find oversized, lightly loaded transformers and move them to sites where load has outgrown the unit, so a utility buys fewer new ones during a 2-year-plus wait; paid a share of the purchases avoided.
deciding_reason: Avoided purchase ($2-3k) is about the cost of the two truck rolls a swap needs, upsizing costs only about $196, and four vendors already sell the analytics. Value per swap is near zero.

pool: US purchases of power and distribution transformers (utilities, developers, data centers, industrials)
title: Cores for Coils: a closed-loop second-life factory for retired distribution transformers
one_liner: Buy utilities' retired and failed transformers on scrap-plus terms, test and strip them, put new coils on good grain-oriented cores, and sell warrantied rebuilt units in 6-10 weeks at about 60-70% of new price.
deciding_reason: Already done by Maddox, RESA and a PE-backed 1,600-person Sunbelt Solomon; DOE says the rebuild market is historically small, labor-limited and its recent uptick is temporary. Only automated winding is a real wedge.

pool: US purchases of power and distribution transformers (utilities, developers, data centers, industrials)
title: Gavi for Transformers: a take-or-pay buyers' consortium that underwrites standard-spec capacity
one_liner: Pool the demand of non-investor-owned utilities and mid-size developers into one binding 3-year take-or-pay on about a dozen standard designs, credit-enhanced by a lender, so manufacturers can finance US capacity and small buyers finally get production slots.
deciding_reason: The best-organized buyers already pool through RESCO/UUS/ERMCO, DOE gives spec standardization away, and a 6-9% distributor margin cannot support a venture-scale company without a financing spread that belongs to CFC/CoBank.

pool: US purchases of power and distribution transformers (utilities, developers, data centers, industrials)
title: TSMC for Transformer Cores: a neutral, automated core-and-coil foundry
one_liner: Build a US plant that cuts and winds cores and builds core-coil assemblies for dozens of independent transformer makers, new entrants and rebuilders, buying GOES from every mill, because the only domestic mill is now also a competitor.
deciding_reason: A neutral core supplier already exists and is doubling (Tempel, Cogent), OEMs keep cores captive, and the one US GOES mill is a competitor with a defense contract. Capital-heavy with pass-through revenue.

pool: US purchases of power and distribution transformers (utilities, developers, data centers, industrials)
title: Time-to-Power Fleet: build-to-stock multi-ratio substation transformers for whoever signs the interconnection first
one_liner: Hold a financed fleet of pre-built, multi-ratio 30-100 MVA substation transformers (US or allied origin) and sell, lease or option them for 8-16 week delivery, because utilities cannot order speculatively and developers cannot carry the order.
deciding_reason: Strongest demand story, but the fleet needs scarce OEM slots, utility spec acceptance is unproven, four funded or PE-backed players already sell stock, leases or modular units, and new capacity lands in 2027-28 against a $0.85B fleet.

pool: US purchases of power and distribution transformers (utilities, developers, data centers, industrials)
title: Time-to-Restore Cover: parametric outage insurance plus spares access for owners nobody covers
one_liner: Sell independent power producers, data centers and industrial plants a contract that pays per day, and delivers a pre-qualified spare and crew, if a named main transformer is down more than N days, filling the gap between 12-24 month insurance indemnity periods and 3-4 year replacement times.
deciding_reason: Revenue is a fraction of a premium pool the idea itself says would need 28-40% share; low failure base rate caps losses; parametric and spare-pool competitors already cover the pieces.

pool: US purchases of power and distribution transformers (utilities, developers, data centers, industrials)
title: Achilles for the Grid: the supplier-paid, accredited trust network under Executive Order 14420
one_liner: Run the accredited qualification network (ownership and sub-tier bill-of-materials tracing, firmware attestation, witness inspection and a warranty/spares wrap) that DOE's pre-qualified-vendor list and lenders' replacement-reserve demands will need, paid by suppliers to be listed and by buyers per purchase.
deciding_reason: Real mandate, but rules are unwritten, DOE may run a free list, Fortress already owns utility vendor-risk with $125M, and the order mainly bites on China-linked gear. Ceiling hinges on DOE choosing accredited assessors.

pool: US purchases of power and distribution transformers (utilities, developers, data centers, industrials)
title: Virtual Transformers: buy capacity from the installed fleet instead of the factory
one_liner: Contract to deliver extra megavolt-amperes at existing substations in months (cooling upgrades, bushing, tap-changer and current-transformer swaps, dynamic ratings, load transfers), priced per MVA unlocked at a fraction of new-unit cost, for utilities and data centers that cannot get a new transformer for 3-4 years.
deciding_reason: No one guarantees MVA, but OEMs, Doble and monitoring vendors sell every component, funded startups compete for the same speed-to-power budget, and $100M needs thousands of uprate jobs a year in a services-heavy model.

pool: US HOA, condo and co-op association assessments and capital repairs
title: Capital Projects Desk: the financeable-package standard for association repairs
one_liner: Turn a liability-driven engineering report into a vote-ready, lender-ready, bid-leveled package and run the project, so boards stop buying repairs from one bid and a PDF.
deciding_reason: Size premise is false: real Phase-2 repair permits average $337k-$496k, not $3M, so Florida managed construction is about $0.25B a year (a 4% fee is about $10M), and owner's-rep firms already sell this service.

pool: US HOA, condo and co-op association assessments and capital repairs
title: Living reserve study: the annual, lender-accepted reserve record (Fannie's three-year clause)
one_liner: Sell an annual, signed, machine-readable reserve record as a subscription, because Fannie reportedly only trusts a study less than three years old as a substitute for the 15% test.
deciding_reason: A direct incumbent already sells the 'living' study, and the premise fails: lenders need a study under three years old, which a normal update satisfies, so annual pricing exceeds the value delivered.

pool: US HOA, condo and co-op association assessments and capital repairs
title: Ledger-underwritten association credit (CondoConta for the US)
one_liner: A non-bank lender-of-record for association repair loans, underwritten from live management-company ledgers and funded by capital markets, with a partner bank keeping the deposits.
deciding_reason: The structural insight (banks lend for deposits) is real, but demand is smaller than assumed, managers' captive desks own the channel, and deposit-funded banks beat a warehouse-funded non-bank on price. Gross revenue plausibly tops out near $35M.

pool: US HOA, condo and co-op association assessments and capital repairs
title: Association treasury: project-funds escrow, draw and instant-pay rail
one_liner: A custody rail for special-assessment and loan proceeds that releases money only against lien waivers and inspector sign-off, earning float and a contractor instant-pay fee.
deciding_reason: A feature, not a company: payments, reserve ladders and draw periods each have an owner (Vantaca Vendor Pay, HOA Invest, association banks), and the $103M path sums thin fees on an inflated flow base.

pool: US HOA, condo and co-op association assessments and capital repairs
title: Fee-only board CFO: conflict-free cost recovery for associations
one_liner: A cost-recovery service that audits insurance, reserve cash, vendors and utilities and is paid a share of verified savings by the association only, because managers, brokers and banks are structurally conflicted.
deciding_reason: The conflict thesis is legitimate and legally supported, but each savings leg has a funded incumbent or captive program, success fees are hard to attribute, and the realistic fee pool is low-tens of millions.

pool: US HOA, condo and co-op association assessments and capital repairs
title: Manager-of-record for small and self-managed associations
one_liner: A licensed management firm that runs about 3x the associations per licensed manager through automation, priced per door-month with an SLA, for the 110-150k associations big managers decline.
deciding_reason: An AI-plus-licensed-manager services roll-up with a funded YC competitor, a cheap profitable software substitute for self-managed boards, and license-bound leverage; the idea itself notes it matches a flagged cliche.

pool: US HOA, condo and co-op association assessments and capital repairs
title: Assessment deferral: pay the association in full, collect from the owner at sale
one_liner: Pay a special assessment to the association on day one and collect from the owner at sale, refinance or death, secured by a junior lien and underwritten on the building.
deciding_reason: Legal path exists but the business needs about $150M of equity for $30-40M of net interest, competes with cheaper association-level loans and public programs, and adversely selects troubled buildings. Ceiling about $25M.

pool: US HOA, condo and co-op association assessments and capital repairs
title: Neutral association data exchange with an indemnified lender desk
one_liner: Managers connect once and get paid; lenders, title agents and insurers buy a verified, living eligibility record per building, and lenders can buy the determination with a repurchase indemnity.
deciding_reason: Best structural fit to the shock, but CondoSafe, InspectHOA, RealPage and free GSE tools already cover it, the per-project wallet is capped, and the indemnity is regulated insurance. A network-standard bet with a ceiling near $20M.

pool: US health plans' and self-funded employers' out-of-network payments through No Surprises Act arbitration (IDR awards)
title: Pre-Op Lock: ancillary network check at prior authorization
one_liner: Catch the 20x-QPA awards weeks before the surgery: at prior authorization, find the out-of-network ancillary vendor a surgeon always uses and lock an in-network rate or reroute the case.
deciding_reason: Vendors earn far more through IDR than any benchmark-linked SCA, so lever 1 fails; neuro volume was overstated 2.4x; Zelis and network teams own the channel. Honest ceiling is a niche analytics/consulting product.

pool: US health plans' and self-funded employers' out-of-network payments through No Surprises Act arbitration (IDR awards)
title: Sponsor Desk: the employer's own IDR control tower
one_liner: Give the employer that actually pays every award a control tower and a written authority grid its TPA must follow, priced flat per member, because contingency representation fails on the math.
deciding_reason: Genuine mandate and no sponsor software, but buyers act through brokers and TPAs who hold the data; reachable lives times $5 gives low tens of millions, not $100M.

pool: US health plans' and self-funded employers' out-of-network payments through No Surprises Act arbitration (IDR awards)
title: Lockstep: employer master agreements with the ten big filers
one_liner: A multi-employer buying coalition that signs rate-card master agreements with the groups filing two-thirds of all disputes, so the plan pays a fair collared price in seven days instead of rolling dice at 404% of QPA 150 days later (PBM-style benefit manager on a pass-through flow).
deciding_reason: Counterparties' alternative (85% win at ~445% of QPA) beats the proposed rate card; ERIC reports offers far above market; no evidence the big filers want a floor-setting coalition deal.

pool: US health plans' and self-funded employers' out-of-network payments through No Surprises Act arbitration (IDR awards)
title: Float: seven-day pay against contract-rate receivables
one_liner: Pay the group in seven days at a known discount, funded against contract-rate claims a plan has agreed to pay and awards from payers that reliably pay, with remittance flowing through a lockbox the funder controls (float and spread on a payment rail; legal-shock claims pool).
deciding_reason: Collateral enforceability just worsened; biggest filers need no financing; the contract-receivable leg depends on dead Lockstep; a lender needs ~$685M capital for $100M revenue.

pool: US health plans' and self-funded employers' out-of-network payments through No Surprises Act arbitration (IDR awards)
title: Cold Open: neutral price opinion and settlement inside open negotiation
one_liner: A confidential, non-binding price opinion plus sealed-bid settlement inside the 30-business-day open-negotiation window, so a payer or sponsor can pay a number 'a neutral said' and a provider gets certainty before either spends the dispute toll.
deciding_reason: Payer-paid negotiation is already done at scale; no evidence a filer winning 85% at ~445% of QPA would accept a neutral's range; portal why-now lands in 2027-28; 15% take-up is heroic.

pool: US health plans' and self-funded employers' out-of-network payments through No Surprises Act arbitration (IDR awards)
title: Guild: group-owned IDR and contracting mutual for independent groups
one_liner: A mutual owned by the independent hospital-based groups, with flat fees, an eligibility warranty and a built-in route into master agreements, aimed at the third of filings that are not from the ten big filers. Weak; flagged.
deciding_reason: Crowded, legally exposed provider-side segment with scaled incumbents; mutual structure adds no scale advantage; $100M needs ~20% of the pool.

pool: US health plans' and self-funded employers' out-of-network payments through No Surprises Act arbitration (IDR awards)
title: Plumb Line: QPA-of-record after TMA III
one_liner: The neutral, court-grade verifier of QPAs and benchmark of record: recompute and audit QPAs, issue a per-dispute evidence packet, and give plan fiduciaries a reasonableness opinion for direct contracts.
deciding_reason: Most regime-robust idea, but the comparable neutral benchmark earns ~$37M, Zelis already ships QPA analytics, and no recompute mandate with a deadline exists yet.

pool: US health plans' and self-funded employers' out-of-network payments through No Surprises Act arbitration (IDR awards)
title: Gavel: an AI-native, ownership-clean certified IDR entity
one_liner: Be the 18th certified IDR entity and the first built for the post-June-2026 regime: five-business-day eligibility, 50-line batches, 3.5M-dispute years and a cap table with no provider or payer money.
deciding_reason: Providers pick the entity and pick provider-favorable ones; a clean, calibrated entity gets only the randomized remainder (~$13M). Certification is not the barrier; selection is.

pool: US building owners' spend on fire and life-safety inspection, testing, maintenance and monitoring (POTS copper cutover)
title: Zero-Down Copper Exit: pay for the cutover out of the phone bill
one_liner: Take over the copper exit for multi-site owners at no upfront cost: find every analog life-safety line from the carrier invoices, replace them with one brand-neutral listed communicator per site, and fund it from the POTS charges that stop, with the new recurring contract financed by RMR lenders.
deciding_reason: Real mandate and budget line, but the owner-side managed program is already sold by MarketSpark, Ooma and Alarm.com; the $100M needs more than the leader's own stated goal.

pool: US building owners' spend on fire and life-safety inspection, testing, maintenance and monitoring (POTS copper cutover)
title: Wire-Center Sweeps: convert every unconverted small system in a retiring footprint, one visit each
one_liner: Treat each retiring wire center like a storm-response territory: build the list of every small commercial life-safety system inside it, convert them in one visit with standard kits, and sell the resulting ITM contracts and monitoring to dealers and roll-ups or keep the RMR.
deciding_reason: Demand arrives in small rural pockets and is already served by the monitoring dealer; cold-canvass CAC for a commodity swap cannot support a $100M path.

pool: US building owners' spend on fire and life-safety inspection, testing, maintenance and monitoring (POTS copper cutover)
title: Second-Opinion Desk: free quote checks that become the owner's neutral fire-and-life-safety program
one_liner: Check any deficiency quote for free against a price book and competing bids, then become the owner's single contract, bidding and records layer for fire and life safety across all sites, paid from the savings.
deciding_reason: A 40-year-old independent incumbent (Telgian) shows the model tops out near $100M of revenue, and the entrant would be thin-margin pass-through.

pool: US building owners' spend on fire and life-safety inspection, testing, maintenance and monitoring (POTS copper cutover)
title: Panel Liberation: zero-down replacement of locked proprietary fire panels
one_liner: Move owners off panels that only one dealer can program onto open-protocol panels with zero-down monthly pricing, hand over the programming files and passwords, and bid out the ITM, paid from the lock-in premium the owner stops paying.
deciding_reason: Lock-in is narrow (mostly Simplex), the work is ordinary bid-out capital construction, and there is no scalable moat.

pool: US building owners' spend on fire and life-safety inspection, testing, maintenance and monitoring (POTS copper cutover)
title: Full-Service Fire Protection: one flat price per square foot a year, repairs included
one_liner: Sell mid-size owners ITM, monitoring and all routine repairs for one flat annual price per square foot, priced from fleet data and backed by contractual liability insurance, which time-and-materials contractors cannot offer without destroying their repair margin.
deciding_reason: Flat-fee comprehensive fire service is already sold (JCI, public full-service specs), and the revenue per building is overstated by 2-3x.

pool: US building owners' spend on fire and life-safety inspection, testing, maintenance and monitoring (POTS copper cutover)
title: Impairment Desk: the first four hours after any fire system goes out of service
one_liner: A 24/7 desk that handles the hours after a fire alarm or sprinkler system is out of service (copper cut, panel fault, valve closed, construction shutoff): mobilize a remote or roving fire watch, notify the AHJ, central station and insurer with a time-stamped record, and dispatch the repair.
deciding_reason: Insurers, dealers and guard firms already own each silo, and the idea's own condition for survival (AHJ log data showing the event count) is unmet.

pool: US building owners' spend on fire and life-safety inspection, testing, maintenance and monitoring (POTS copper cutover)
title: Hyperscale Life-Safety Crew: the scarce-trade play behind the data-center build
one_liner: A specialist prime for data-center fire detection, suppression and integrated systems testing, plus ITM for operating halls, with an in-house apprenticeship academy and prefabrication to relieve the scarce-labor constraint.
deciding_reason: Real demand, but it is an operating contractor business competing with funded primes for the same scarce labor, with no data, software or network moat.

pool: US building owners' spend on fire and life-safety inspection, testing, maintenance and monitoring (POTS copper cutover)
title: Hood-to-Alarm Program for restaurant franchise systems
one_liner: Sell the 20-30 largest restaurant franchisors and purchasing co-ops one program for hood cleaning (NFPA 96), kitchen suppression, extinguishers and alarm and sprinkler ITM, with proof of service for insurers and AHJs.
deciding_reason: The bundling gap is real but the ticket is small, the leader is a $74M system, and filing and compliance records already run through Brycer.

pool: 340B Drug Pricing Program covered-entity purchases (the spread and the rebate transition)
title: Retro-Flag: post-adjudication 340B correction rail for state Medicaid
one_liner: Take the 340B status that administrators assign days after a script is filled, push it back into the state Medicaid or MCO claim, reprice at acquisition cost, and invoice manufacturer rebates only on units that qualify, paid out of the rebates recaptured.
deciding_reason: Real gap on the state side, but the pool is small, politically contested by hospitals, locked behind Gainwell, and one simple state ban removes the need for a vendor.

pool: 340B Drug Pricing Program covered-entity purchases (the spread and the rebate transition)
title: Route Desk: per-unit 340B / MFP / non-340B router for health systems
one_liner: A decision engine on the hospital's virtual inventory that assigns each administration and fill to 340B, MFP or non-340B, paid a share of the margin it preserves; the first tool for the three policies that cap 340B value at once.
deciding_reason: Real shock and a CFO budget, but a one-rule, mostly one-time optimization that incumbents and consultants can copy, capped near $30M.

pool: 340B Drug Pricing Program covered-entity purchases (the spread and the rebate transition)
title: Cass for 340B: audit-and-pay hub for drug purchases, fees and remittances
one_liner: Freight audit-and-pay for drugs: an independent hub that audits every 340B invoice, credit-and-rebill, pharmacy fee and remittance against ceiling prices and contracts, pays the clean ones, and advances cash against contract-pharmacy remittances.
deciding_reason: Hospital-side contingency recovery already exists, the leak rate is unmeasured, the float needs a balance sheet, and $100M needs heroic share.

pool: 340B Drug Pricing Program covered-entity purchases (the spread and the rebate transition)
title: Switzerland: hospital-governed, manufacturer-funded 340B claims trust
one_liner: A claims trust owned by hospitals and health centers that holds the unit-level ledger behind a firewall and returns only pass/fail and payment; the rail the Senate bill calls an independent clearinghouse, built before the law and usable under all three political outcomes.
deciding_reason: Neutrality is a real insight, but the buyer picks the platform and the only big pot is a single federal contract under unpassed bills.

pool: 340B Drug Pricing Program covered-entity purchases (the spread and the rebate transition)
title: Open TPA: 340B administrator with no pharmacy attached
one_liner: Flat per-claim pricing, a portable ledger so a hospital can leave CVS's or Walgreens' administrator without losing its positions, and an independent pharmacy network.
deciding_reason: Flat-fee and independent TPAs already exist, the lock-in sits with chain pharmacies, and the realistic share is small.

pool: 340B Drug Pricing Program covered-entity purchases (the spread and the rebate transition)
title: JG-Day for Payers: 340B cut pass-through desk for non-conflicted Medicare Advantage plans
one_liner: Give MA plans that do not own a 340B pharmacy business a contract-and-claims desk that uses CMS's new JG/TB/XX modifiers to pass the 340B cut through hospital contracts and audit modifier accuracy, paid a share of savings.
deciding_reason: A modifier edit and contract language are features plans do themselves; the buyers are the plans with the strongest in-house teams.

pool: 340B Drug Pricing Program covered-entity purchases (the spread and the rebate transition)
title: Specialty Door: shared specialty pharmacy utility for health systems
one_liner: A shared, accredited, PBM-credentialed specialty pharmacy that health systems use as their own front door (their patients, their 340B account, flat fee per script), timed to the Medicare any-willing-pharmacy rules arriving 2027-2029.
deciding_reason: Shields already aggregates over a third of health systems with new Evernorth backing, so the shared-scale insight is the incumbent's pitch.

pool: 340B Drug Pricing Program covered-entity purchases (the spread and the rebate transition)
title: Pigeonhole: IRA MFP-versus-340B duplicate-discount floor for manufacturers
one_liner: Using only data manufacturers already hold (340B chargebacks by ship-to pharmacy and the Medicare Transaction Facilitator feed), prove for each pharmacy and month the minimum number of units that received both MFP and 340B, and recover them.
deciding_reason: Best-argued idea with a funded buyer, but few buyers, an incumbent just consolidated, and the recovery path is legally uncertain.

pool: Captives, group captives and fronting: corporate premium moving out of the commercial market
title: Clean Exit: sponsor-level cell captives built to be sold with the company
one_liner: A sponsored-captive platform for private-equity sponsors where every portfolio company gets a cell and every cell is born with its exit: buyer-ready accounting, a pre-priced loss portfolio transfer (LPT) at sale, and fund-level pooling above the cells.
deciding_reason: Real pain but the veto premise is unsupported, exit tools are already standard, sponsors adopt portfolio programs once or twice a decade, and short holds undercut captives.

pool: Captives, group captives and fronting: corporate premium moving out of the commercial market
title: The 12th Member: a cross-agency fill-rate machine for group captives
one_liner: A neutral network that assembles new group captives from pre-scored members spread across hundreds of independent agencies, because the scarce input is the twelfth qualified, similar member in the room.
deciding_reason: The gap is already filled by open heterogeneous captives and a dominant incumbent; $100M needs about a fifth of future market premium.

pool: Captives, group captives and fronting: corporate premium moving out of the commercial market
title: Zero-Collateral Cell Reinsurer: a pooled $250M reinsurer that qualifies for the U.S. no-collateral rule
one_liner: A Bermuda multi-cell reinsurer capitalised above $250M by hundreds of captives plus institutional money, so every group captive that is one of its cells cedes from U.S. fronts without regulatory collateral.
deciding_reason: Legal premise appears broken (RJ scope excludes captive classes), fronts keep contractual discretion, and no pilot is possible before $250M of capital.

pool: Captives, group captives and fronting: corporate premium moving out of the commercial market
title: The 97% Book: buy the agencies and managers that sponsor group captives
one_liner: A permanent-capital holding company that acquires the agencies, consultants and independent managers that sponsor and run casualty and MSL group captives, the one corner of commercial insurance with 97-98% retention and member-owned capital accounts that make leaving costly.
deciding_reason: Already being done by funded rivals; it is a capital-allocation trade, not a gap, and the arbitrage is priced by competing buyers.

pool: Captives, group captives and fronting: corporate premium moving out of the commercial market
title: Pareto TPA: paid on the 7% of claims that carry 40% of the cost
one_liner: A claims administrator for owner-managed casualty programs that puts its best adjusters, nurses and defence strategists on the top slice of claims by dollar exposure and is paid a share of verified savings against the captive actuary's pick.
deciding_reason: Savings-share fees are legally restricted in at least one major self-insured state and Paradigm already sells outcome-priced large-claim management; the niche stays small.

pool: Captives, group captives and fronting: corporate premium moving out of the commercial market
title: Retained-Risk Bureau: the NCCI of captives, self-insureds and large deductibles
one_liner: A member-governed data cooperative that pools loss triangles, claim outcomes and safety data from captives, TPAs and self-insured programs and sells development patterns and proof of selection to reinsurers, carriers and MGAs.
deciding_reason: Cold-start give-to-get pool with thin buyer wallet and existing manager and TPA-built benchmarks.

pool: Captives, group captives and fronting: corporate premium moving out of the commercial market
title: Broker Mutual: a member-owned liability RRG that underwrites every freight load
one_liner: A risk retention group owned by mid-size freight brokers and 3PLs that insures negligent-selection claims after Montgomery and prices each tendered load on the carrier, truck and driver behind it.
deciding_reason: Best shock in the pool but the premium pool is about 3x smaller than assumed, Marsh already supplies rated paper, and an unrated RRG carries verdict tail on thin capital.

pool: Captives, group captives and fronting: corporate premium moving out of the commercial market
title: The TPA Captive: stop-loss captives sponsored by the people who see the claims first
one_liner: Give independent third-party administrators their own medical stop-loss group captive in a box, so employers with 50-1,500 lives stop buying lasers and annual repricing from carriers who see the same claims six to twelve months later.
deciding_reason: Real pricing pain (Segal +12.7%) but crowded with consultants and carriers, no TPA appetite for insurance risk evidenced, and tightening reinsurance capacity.

pool: Utilities' and developers' outsourced transmission and distribution engineering and line-construction contracts
title: Ready-to-Build: the constraint-clearing layer for line crews
one_liner: Sell line contractors and utility construction departments a live 'ready backlog' in which every job is gated on the six things that actually idle a crew, and charge per crew-month.
upside_assumptions: (a) Price 2-3x the best analog, plausible only if pilots prove hard-dollar standby savings (~25% likely); (b) 15-20% of addressable crews, which Locusview showed is reachable but took ~11 years (~40%); (c) Itron, Maximo, SAP and FYLD do not bundle a readiness module (~25%). Joint odds are low; without (a) the ceiling is ~$40-50M.
deciding_reason: Real pain, but the only scaled analog (Locusview) is ~3x cheaper per crew, already on 4,000+ crews, and now owned by Itron; $100M needs 3x pricing or half the market.

pool: Utilities' and developers' outsourced transmission and distribution engineering and line-construction contracts
title: Zero-Redline: outcome-priced distribution work packages
one_liner: A vendor-neutral design pod that delivers construction-ready distribution work packages, priced per package accepted with zero redlines, using the incumbents' tools plus each utility's standards compiled into checks.
upside_assumptions: Tool-enabled first-pass acceptance above 95% on 100k+ packages a year (~30%); utilities accept nearshore pods under their standards and data rules (~50%); hourly firms and AI-native entrants do not copy outcome pricing (~35%).
deciding_reason: Outcome pricing is a real wedge nobody sells, but software owners (Enverus, Itron), entrenched design firms and funded AI-native entrants cap this services model near $60M.

pool: Utilities' and developers' outsourced transmission and distribution engineering and line-construction contracts
title: Spec Passport: shared product qualification, paid by the suppliers
one_liner: Test a distribution product once and let many utilities accept it: free to utility standards engineers, paid for by the manufacturers who want onto approved-materials lists.
upside_assumptions: 25+ IOUs cede engineer-of-record liability to a manufacturer-paid credential (~10%); 100+ manufacturers pay $200k+ a year (~15%). Both together are very unlikely.
deciding_reason: The co-op wedge is already served by a free federal acceptance list, IOUs will not cede liability, and the qualification-fee pool is invented; ceiling ~$30M.

pool: Utilities' and developers' outsourced transmission and distribution engineering and line-construction contracts
title: Capacity Upgrade Desk: limiting-element-first reconductoring, funded by the load
one_liner: Find the single span or terminal that actually limits each congested line, fix it, and reconductor only where it pays, with the data-center or industrial customer funding the work in exchange for deliverable capacity.
upside_assumptions: Becomes the default neutral scoping layer for developer-funded upgrades in 3+ RTOs (~15%); state PUCs approve a rider structure for capacity rights (~30%); fees stay near 12% against EPC pushback (~40%).
deciding_reason: Neutral advice and EPC economics cannot coexist, the fee path needs ~21% of all reconductored miles, and the upside is a ~$60M consultancy.

pool: Utilities' and developers' outsourced transmission and distribution engineering and line-construction contracts
title: Accredited Delivery Partner: customer-funded connections at the customer's speed
one_liner: Be the utility-accredited third party that designs, permits and builds customer-funded connections to the utility's standard, so customers who would pay to go faster can; a regulated utility structurally cannot sell that.
upside_assumptions: Five states formalize accreditation (~15%); wins 3-4% of a $2.5-3.5B pool against Quanta-owned contractors (~20%); 'energized by date or we pay' guarantee is insurable (~40%). Gross only; net ~$8M.
deciding_reason: A general contractor wedge: big jobs bypass the standard path, Quanta-owned contractors already do it, state patchwork limits scale, and net revenue is ~$8-18M even at $100M gross.

pool: Utilities' and developers' outsourced transmission and distribution engineering and line-construction contracts
title: Pooled Crews: a contract vehicle with reserved crews for co-ops and munis
one_liner: Pool about 2,800 small utilities' line construction, engineering and materials demand into a pre-competed multi-year vehicle with reserved crew-months, so small utilities stop being last in line behind Quanta's backlog.
upside_assumptions: Three or more G&T systems adopt the vehicle (~20%); contractors reserve crew-months for aggregated unpaid demand (~15%); RUS and lender rules accommodate it (~40%).
deciding_reason: Pooled purchasing, co-op-owned crews and generalist vehicles already exist; RUS rules force co-op-level contracts; $100M needs 14-33% of the pool and contractors will not hold crews for unpaid demand.

pool: Utilities' and developers' outsourced transmission and distribution engineering and line-construction contracts
title: Pre-Accepted Substations for non-hyperscaler load
one_liner: Sell developers of 20-300 MW campuses a customer-owned substation and gen-tie package designed in advance to their utility's standard, with equipment slots reserved, so interconnection takes 12-15 months instead of 24-36.
upside_assumptions: 4-6 sites a year at ~$25M from neoclouds with no track record to buy from (~15%); reserved transformer slots, which need $10M+ of deposits (~50%); Unlimited Industries, GE Vernova and Quanta do not take the same buyers first (~30%). Gross pass-through; net-equivalent ~$12-15M.
deciding_reason: Only pool that can carry $100M, but that is gross pass-through (~$12-15M net), the standards library is available on request, and OEM turnkey plus a funded a16z entrant are already selling it; median under $20M.

pool: Utilities' and developers' outsourced transmission and distribution engineering and line-construction contracts
title: Make-Ready Rail: the bulk pole-application exchange
one_liner: Be the single bulk-application, loading-analysis, estimating and make-ready rail between telecom attachers and about 2,000 pole-owning utilities, paid per pole by the attacher, so FCC shot clocks are met and fiber gets built.
upside_assumptions: Major pole owners accept one standard bulk package (~25%, since Alden already sits on the owner side); the FCC revokes state certifications or states copy the FCC rules (~25%); non-BEAD attacher volume is 6M+ poles a year and the rail wins 10% (~25%).
deciding_reason: Wrong regulator for the California wedge, co-op and municipal poles exempt from FCC clocks, and owner-side and engineering incumbents already serve both sides; even 100% of BEAD is ~$80M a year of fees.

pool: US heavy-duty (Class 6-8) truck repair, maintenance and parts aftermarket
title: Shop Ledger: cross-shop carrier-health network, paid in 24 hours
one_liner: A neutral credit network across independent heavy-duty shops that sees every shop's invoices to a carrier plus the carrier's ELD activity, so shops get paid in 24 hours and healthy carriers get net-45 terms.
upside_assumptions: (1) Fullbay and cbCharge stay passive while the network signs 2,000+ shops (low-moderate). (2) ELD plus cross-shop behavior beats cbCharge's existing ledger enough to price at 2% and hold losses under 1% (unproven; backtest not done). (3) Warehouse funding at under 8% in a freight recession (moderate). (4) Expansion into parts, tire and dealer trade credit triples the volume base (plausible but those sellers have credit departments). Even all four give about $70M, not $100M.
deciding_reason: cbCharge has done 24-hour pay with fleet credit risk since 1995 and already holds the cross-shop ledger; the ELD score is a feature incumbents can copy, and $100M exceeds Fullbay's whole installed base.

pool: US heavy-duty (Class 6-8) truck repair, maintenance and parts aftermarket
title: Overnight Yard Crews: Level-1 PM and tire crews with remote master techs
one_liner: Fix the technician shortage by changing the job: train hourly Level-1 crews in weeks to do checklist work (PM, inspections, tires, brakes, lights) in the fleet's own yard at night, with a Level-3 master tech on video for escalations.
upside_assumptions: (1) Level-1 hires with 4-8 weeks of training hit 70%+ billable utilization without quality failures (unproven). (2) A fleet-wide Level-3 inspector-of-record structure satisfies 49 CFR 396.19 and 396.25 so crews can sell inspections and brakes (plausible but narrows the labor model). (3) Acquisitions or an OEM campaign contract add volume (plausible). (4) Ryder and Love's do not copy the model (low). Reaches about $90M with 260-ish crews.
deciding_reason: Labor-capped services business in a space Ryder, Love's and a PE roll-up are consolidating; $100M needs 3x Ryder's mobile tech base and the inspection rules narrow the Level-1 scope.

pool: US heavy-duty (Class 6-8) truck repair, maintenance and parts aftermarket
title: Pay-by-the-Mile: major-repair credit repaid through the factor and the odometer
one_liner: Finance the $2,500-$40,000 engine, transmission and aftertreatment repairs owner-operators and small fleets cannot pay for, collect in cents per mile through the freight factor or settlement they already use, with the odometer as the schedule.
upside_assumptions: (1) A large factor signs a sweep agreement and subordinates or shares its UCC lien (low-moderate; factors earn the fee and can build the same product). (2) Losses stay under 3% on thin-file borrowers (low). (3) Funding at under 8% (moderate). (4) Origination volume reaches $300M+ at 14% yield (moderate). Even then revenue is about $45M.
deciding_reason: Crowded with four named financing products, unit economics negative on the idea's own numbers, and the upside stays under $50M.

pool: US heavy-duty (Class 6-8) truck repair, maintenance and parts aftermarket
title: Warranty Wrapper: the OEM-paid multi-brand network for non-dealer warranty and campaign work
one_liner: Be the contract vehicle between OEM warranty budgets and the independent shops, fleet in-house shops and mobile crews that can do warranty and recall work faster than dealers, carrying authorization, training, prior approval, parts return and claims compliance.
upside_assumptions: (1) Two or three OEMs sign multi-year provider programs (low; Daimler chose a single large partner, Love's). (2) OEMs accept paying a 10% intermediary fee instead of paying dealers (low). (3) Dealer franchise agreements and state dealer laws do not block it (unverified). (4) Samsara does not own the claim workflow (low). Reaches about $30M net.
deciding_reason: The $3.94B pool is two-thirds farm and construction equipment, Love's already does multi-OEM non-dealer warranty with claims filing, and telematics vendors are absorbing the claim workflow.

pool: US heavy-duty (Class 6-8) truck repair, maintenance and parts aftermarket
title: Uptime Plan: cost-per-mile maintenance for the fleet the lessors and OEMs ignore
one_liner: A fixed price per mile for PM, wear items and covered repairs at any shop in a network, for mixed-make trucks in fleets of 3-50, underwritten from ELD data and repair history and backed by an insurer.
upside_assumptions: (1) A distribution partner (ELD vendor, factor or insurer commercial book) delivers 1,500 trucks a year (moderate-low). (2) Loss ratio holds at or below 78% on small old fleets with independent-shop price variance (low-moderate). (3) Reinsurer and fronting capacity at acceptable cost (moderate). (4) State classification works out, including California's exemption for 30,000-lb-plus vehicles (confirmed) but not other states (mixed). Gross revenue only; net take at 22% is about $17M in the upside.
deciding_reason: Ryder, Penske, FleetNet and NTP already sell outsourced maintenance on customer-owned mixed-make trucks; the unique piece (small old fleets, ELD pricing) has an unsolved distribution and adverse-selection problem.

pool: US heavy-duty (Class 6-8) truck repair, maintenance and parts aftermarket
title: Public Fleet Bench: fixed-fee maintenance for fleets that cannot pay market wages
one_liner: Sell school districts, transit agencies, counties and refuse haulers a fixed per-vehicle maintenance contract delivered by market-wage crews inside their own garages, because their pay scales guarantee they cannot hire.
upside_assumptions: (1) Level-1 crews are hired at scale (shared with Yard Crews, unproven). (2) Procurement and union no-subcontract barriers are manageable in several states (unverified). (3) The entrant wins 50+ RFPs against First Student (low-moderate). (4) Refuse, transit and public-works fleets add vehicles (plausible). Gross revenue with thin margins; about $80M.
deciding_reason: A funded national incumbent (First Student) already sells maintenance-only to districts, contracts are about $1.3M each, and most of the revenue is parts pass-through.

pool: US heavy-duty (Class 6-8) truck repair, maintenance and parts aftermarket
title: Second Source: graded, warrantied used and reman power-train parts plus a core exchange
one_liner: Become the default 30-60%-below-new answer to the tariff: dismantle donor trucks, buy cores from shops with instant pay, test and grade every engine, transmission, turbo, ECM and injector set to a published standard, and sell with a 12-month warranty.
upside_assumptions: (1) Core and donor supply scales to 5,500 trucks a year (moderate). (2) A published grade card becomes trusted by shops (moderate-low; dealers and OEMs run closed core loops). (3) Tariff persistence keeps reman demand elevated (moderate). (4) Warranty claim rates stay under 5% on used units (unknown). Reaches about $70M.
deciding_reason: A mature, OEM-dominated category with salvage and independent rebuilders already present; plausible volume but thin margins, no technology moat, and the upside stays under $100M.

pool: US heavy-duty (Class 6-8) truck repair, maintenance and parts aftermarket
title: Aftertreatment Exchange: pooled, multi-brand DPF/DOC/SCR swap units
one_liner: A national pool of cleaned, flow-tested aftertreatment units shipped to any shop in 4 hours at a flat exchange price, so the truck leaves in hours instead of waiting two days for cleaning.
upside_assumptions: (1) Fleets pay a premium to avoid a day of downtime (moderate-low because same-day cleaning exists). (2) Multi-brand pooled inventory works across hundreds of DPF part numbers (hard). (3) Shops route through a third party instead of dealers or local cleaners (low). (4) Metals prices stay high enough to make failed-unit recovery pay (volatile). Reaches about $35M.
deciding_reason: OEM exchange at 800+ locations, dealer same-day cleaning, a licensed cleaning network and fleets' in-house shops already cover it; the swap barely beats a few hours of cleaning and the upside is about $35M.

pool: Medicaid home- and community-based services (personal care, home care agencies, fiscal intermediaries)
title: Clock-Out Capital: visit-level Medicaid finance priced on recoupment
one_liner: Buy each EVV-verified Medicaid visit the day it happens, pay the aide that night and the agency by morning, and price it on whether it will be clawed back, not on how old the invoice is.
upside_assumptions: (1) Visit-level recoupment pricing wins ~25% of externally financed Medicaid receivables: moderately plausible but unproven, since incumbents can copy a five-check screen. (2) Funding at 8-9% from credit funds with warehouse lines: plausible once loss data exists. (3) Cross-sell payroll rail and expand to all HCBS and several states: plausible. Even then $100M needs most of the market, which is not believable.
deciding_reason: Financed-balance pool is too small for a $667M book, incumbents already advance 85%, and true-sale factoring is barred; upside tops out near $55M.

pool: Medicaid home- and community-based services (personal care, home care agencies, fiscal intermediaries)
title: The exception-free fiscal intermediary
one_liner: Run statewide participant-directed payroll at about 30% under the incumbent's price by making the EVV record the timesheet and automating the exceptions that eat the call center.
upside_assumptions: (1) Acquire a small/mid FI to get past performance and references: plausible (60%). (2) Win two or three 15-40k-participant state RFPs in the 2027-2029 rebid wave: each maybe 20-25%. (3) NY reopens after the DOJ suit and a new operator wins a slice: speculative (~10-15%), no rebid or receiver ruling found. (4) Incumbents do not cut price: PE-backed GT and PPL will respond. Together this is a top-decile outcome, not a base case.
deciding_reason: Mandated state spend with a named signer, no free substitute, live precedent and rebid wave, and a believable ~85k-participant or NY-class path to $100M.

pick.title: Fiscal-intermediary consolidator with a payroll-certainty SLA
pick.one_liner: Buy a small or mid FI for past performance, re-platform it so EVV hours become payroll, and bid state FMS rebids on guaranteed first-payroll performance.
pick.sharpened_pitch: Run statewide participant-directed payroll as a consolidator, not a bid-from-zero startup. Step one is to acquire a small or mid fiscal intermediary with live state contracts and a clean record, because after New York every state director now scores past performance and day-one payroll risk above price. Step two is to re-platform it so EVV-approved hours flow straight into payroll, onboarding (I-9, W-4, background and exclusion checks) is a tracked pipeline measured in days, and exceptions are auto-resolved or routed with deadlines. Step three is to compete in the rolling wave of state FMS rebids (Kentucky is open now with a stated 2026-11-06 deadline, Ohio and others on five-year cycles) and to be the credible second operator if New York reopens after the June 2026 DOJ suit against PPL. Drop the blanket 30% under pricing: NY already pays $68.50 per member per month while Louisiana-type states pay $100-117. Sell a service-level guarantee instead: zero missed first payroll, onboarding in days, and a funded payroll backstop if the state pays late. Add MCO-delegated FMS as a second channel and cross-sell working capital later.
pick.payer_and_signer: State Medicaid director or developmental-disabilities director through competitive procurement, from the FMS administrative line with federal match; MCOs for delegated FMS.
pick.path_to_100m: About 85k participants at ~$100 blended PMPM ($1,200 a year), or half of a NY-class contract (250k x $68.50 x 12 = ~$205M a year). FMS-vendor pool is ~0.7-1.0M people (~$0.8-1.2B a year, my estimate), so $100M is ~8-12% of the vendor pool. Reference: GT Independence serves 60k+ participants and just took H.I.G. growth capital, implying the #2 player is roughly $60-90M. Median ~$20M from one acquisition plus one or two mid-size wins.
pick.competitors_and_edge: PPL (DW Healthcare/Linden-owned, NY sole FI), GT Independence (H.I.G.-backed), Acumen, Palco, Tempus, with HHAX at the EVV layer. Edge: fresher EVV-to-payroll architecture, an SLA story states can defend after New York, and optionality on a NY rebid; no free substitute exists.
pick.why_now: New York collapsed ~600 FIs into one and then was sued by DOJ (filed 2026-06-16); PPL settled an aide underpayment class action for $162M. States are consolidating and rebidding (WV 2024, NY 2025, OH and KY 2025-26), the self-directing population grew 23% from 2019 to 2023, and H.R.1 cost pressure favors cheaper administration.
pick.moat: Multi-year state contracts with switching costs (thousands of enrolled workers), scale economies in fixed software cost, process power in exception handling, and state past-performance references.
pick.biggest_open_risk: Winning contracts as a new or newly acquired operator against PE-backed incumbents that can cut price, in procurements that weight past performance heavily; a possible bundle by HHAX CarePay is a second threat.
pick.cheapest_next_test: Get the Kentucky RFP text and map the state fiscal-agent tracker for contract expiry dates; call one former state FMS program manager and two small FI owners (including a displaced NY FI) about acquisition or teaming terms. Zero build cost.

pool: Medicaid home- and community-based services (personal care, home care agencies, fiscal intermediaries)
title: Proof-of-Visit: the verification rail for home care
one_liner: Sell a signed assurance score and evidence pack for every home care visit (right person, right place, no impossible overlaps), the way identity vendors sell a check per login.
upside_assumptions: (1) One NY-class state accepts a 20% savings share: unlikely (~10%) given procurement and the NY-DOJ dispute. (2) HHAX/Sandata do not bundle equivalent scoring: unlikely, they already hold visit and payroll data. (3) Biometric or device-attestation add-on gets adopted by EVV vendors: unproven and friction-averse. Upside capped by those.
deciding_reason: EVV owners already hold both visit and payroll data, per-visit pricing is unsupported, and the savings-share route rests on one disputed NY number; upside near $45M.

pool: Medicaid home- and community-based services (personal care, home care agencies, fiscal intermediaries)
title: Personal-care administrator for fee-for-service states (the NEMT-broker model)
one_liner: Take what a state buys piece by piece (assessment, authorization, network, EVV, payroll, fraud) and sell it one reconciled paid hour, the way NEMT brokers sell a managed trip.
upside_assumptions: Needs 3-4 mid-size FFS states each paying ~1-2% of spend, winning against Maximus/Acentra/PCG bundles, while FFS carve-outs shrink as states move to managed care. Not believable for a new entrant.
deciding_reason: The 3-5% fee premise is contradicted by observed 0.5-2% state admin fees; even the upside is small.

pool: Medicaid home- and community-based services (personal care, home care agencies, fiscal intermediaries)
title: The neutral LTSS manager for plans that compete with Elevance
one_liner: The same at-risk HCBS management CareBridge sells, owned by no health plan, for the Medicaid plans that will not hand their sickest members to a rival.
upside_assumptions: (1) Two non-Elevance anchor plans (Centene, UHC, CVS/Aetna or Molina) commit 25k+ members each by year 4-6: plausible only if they co-invest as in 2022 (~15-25%). (2) Net economics hold at $1,300+/member-year with a firewalled neutral structure: moderate. (3) Savings are capturable because buyers are D-SNP-aligned plans holding Medicare and Medicaid: plausible if targeted. (4) Capital for at-risk contracts is raised from the plans: plausible. Top-decile, not median.
deciding_reason: Demonstrated demand and a $2.7B exit comp, plan budgets that already paid for this, a fresh competitor-ownership shock, and a believable top-decile path to ~$100M.

pick.from_title: The neutral LTSS manager for plans that compete with Elevance
pick.title: Neutral HCBS operating system for D-SNP-aligned Medicaid plans
pick.one_liner: A plan-owned-by-nobody HCBS manager with plan co-investors and a firewalled data model, replacing the independent CareBridge that Elevance bought.
pick.sharpened_pitch: Build the independent HCBS manager that Medicaid plans co-funded in 2022 and then lost to Elevance in December 2024. Sell to the VP of LTSS or Medicaid CMO at plans whose Medicare and Medicaid sides sit under one parent (FIDE-SNP and HIDE-SNP), because for dual-eligible members the acute savings from fewer missed shifts, ED visits and nursing-home stays accrue to the same parent that pays the contract. Product: real-time visit and authorization data across every EVV aggregator (not one owner's), same-day missed-shift response, continuity-based agency steering, fraud triage and a risk-adjusted shared-savings contract with a floor. Capital and governance: two or three non-Elevance plans co-invest in exchange for volume commitments, the CareBridge 2022 template, with a written data firewall and a governance seat per plan so neutrality is a contract term, not a slogan. Start with a 5,000-member pilot in one state, but price and fund it as the first contract toward 70-90k at-risk members, not a boutique. Add network, fraud and payroll-signal modules on the same data to lift net revenue per member.
pick.payer_and_signer: The plan: SVP/VP of LTSS or Medicaid chief medical officer, paid from medical-cost management and care-management budgets, out of savings against the plan's own HCBS and hospital trend.
pick.path_to_100m: CareBridge-implied net economics are about $1,100-1,500 per member-year (about 5% of ~$30k managed spend; my inference from a ~1x-revenue exit). $100M needs about 70-90k at-risk members, 60-80% of CareBridge's 2023 base of ~115k, or roughly 4% of managed-LTSS HCBS members if there are 1.5-2M (unverified). Median case is 15-20k members for ~$20M; $100M is top-decile.
pick.competitors_and_edge: CareBridge/Carelon (17 states plus DC, says it serves all customers), HHAeXchange payer tools (no risk-taking, 180+ MCOs claimed), plans' in-house LTSS teams and Optum. Edge: a contractually neutral owner with rival-plan co-investors, EVV-aggregator-agnostic data, and a D-SNP-aligned buyer focus so savings are capturable.
