pick.why_now: Elevance closed the CareBridge purchase on 2024-12-10; Anthem, Optum, CVS and Centene had co-invested in 2022, so three of those four now face a competitor-owned vendor. H.R.1 cuts of ~$911B over 2025-34 press plan margins and make a lower hospital and nursing-home trend on the sickest HCBS cohort more valuable. Renewal windows for existing CareBridge contracts are opening in 2026-2028.
pick.moat: Switching costs once a plan's HCBS data and workflows run on the system, process power in missed-shift response, and a neutrality guarantee an owned competitor cannot copy. Cornered resource only if plan co-investors commit volume.
pick.biggest_open_risk: Whether rival plans will move volume to a neutral vendor rather than keep CareBridge, build in-house or lean on Optum; secondary risks are capturing savings that accrue to Medicare and raising capital for at-risk contracts.
pick.cheapest_next_test: Three calls to LTSS leaders at Centene, UnitedHealthcare Community Plan and CVS/Aetna (plus one ex-CareBridge executive): are you renewing CareBridge after Dec 2024, would you co-invest or commit members to a firewalled neutral vendor, and on what contract form (PMPM or shared savings). Zero build cost.

pool: Medicaid home- and community-based services (personal care, home care agencies, fiscal intermediaries)
title: Risk and Mobility MGA for home care agencies
one_liner: Use visit, route and authorization data as the underwriting file for workers' comp, non-owned auto, liability and billing-error cover, and hand agencies the loss-control savings.
upside_assumptions: Needs carriers to cede pricing authority based on visit and drive-time data nobody has validated, brokers to move their books despite commission conflicts, and a 15%+ share of a niche class. Not believable.
deciding_reason: Premium pool is far smaller than assumed, so $100M needs a heroic share, and a national home-care MGA program already exists.

pool: Medicaid home- and community-based services (personal care, home care agencies, fiscal intermediaries)
title: Continuity Bench: pooled W-2 aides for the TPS and fill-rate gap
one_liner: A Medicaid-native pool of W-2 aides, work-authorization verified and guaranteed full-time hours, that agencies draw on when staff are lost or hours go unfilled.
upside_assumptions: Needs agencies to pay a spread they cannot afford, ShiftMed/Clipboard to stay out of Medicaid personal care, and states to allow subcontracted W-2 staff to bill under the agency (varies by state, unverified). Not believable.
deciding_reason: Price exceeds value ($4 spread on a $19 hour) and the bottleneck is labor supply and pay, not pooling; funded W-2 competitors exist.

pool: Medicaid home- and community-based services (personal care, home care agencies, fiscal intermediaries)
title: Partner-not-buy network for independent agencies
one_liner: Give independent home care agencies the back office, payer contract, insurance and capital of a chain without selling the company.
upside_assumptions: Needs owners to pay ~5% for services costing them ~3-4%, MCOs to sign one delegated contract at above-state-set rates, and trust among competing agencies, which the 2021 attempt failed to show. Not believable.
deciding_reason: No payer-contract uplift exists in state-set Medicaid rates and a 5% fee exceeds owners' margins; even the upside is small.

pool: US biofuel producers' purchases of fats, oils and grease feedstock
title: Grease Elevator
one_liner: Neutral, heated, assayed drop-off terminals where independent grease collectors and small renderers deliver any load size, get paid the same day, and have their oil consolidated into full tankers sold on term contracts with origin paperwork attached: a grain elevator for waste lipids.
upside_assumptions: (1) 25 terminals averaging 50M lb within six years: plausible only if small collectors truly lack alternatives, which is unverified. (2) Spread of 4c or more after handling: low-moderate plausibility, needs a real price premium for assay and origin paper from buyers that now get it from Veriflux and QAP providers. (3) Working-capital advances on electronic warehouse receipts add about $10M: moderate, needs a lender. (4) Renderers and Eco-Energy-type terminals do not respond: low.
deciding_reason: Real asset, but volume is capped near the independent pool, merchant spreads are 1-3c not 5c, and Eco-Energy, Neste and traders already operate the model. Top-decile net revenue is about $60M.

pool: US biofuel producers' purchases of fats, oils and grease feedstock
title: Bankable Supply
one_liner: A pooled-supply company that signs 3-7 year feedstock supply agreements (volume bands, index plus fixed fee, a carbon-intensity true-up, a delivery guarantee) with independent renewable-diesel, biodiesel, SAF and co-processing projects, and fills them back-to-back from hundreds of small collectors, renderers, ethanol plants and crushers.
upside_assumptions: (1) Lenders accept a new pooled supplier with about $150M of working capital as a creditworthy counterparty: low plausibility, since Vitol, Macquarie and Bunge are what they accept. (2) 10-12 agreements of 250M lb sign within six years: low-moderate. (3) A reinsurance layer for the delivery guarantee is available at a cost that leaves 1.5c net: moderate. (4) Traders do not copy the CI true-up clause: low.
deciding_reason: Balance-sheet traders and banks already provide supply paper to financed independents; a startup is not the credit lenders want, and the customer set is about 30-40 projects.

pool: US biofuel producers' purchases of fats, oils and grease feedstock
title: Cleared Lot
one_liner: The PSA of waste lipids: a private grade and sealed-sample certificate for every load of UCO, tallow and corn oil with a binding deduction schedule so gate-lab disputes disappear, an origin file, and an RIN/45Z eligibility warranty sold through an independent insurer.
upside_assumptions: (1) The certificate becomes a contract-cited standard on 45% of waste-lipid lots: low-moderate, large inspectors and Darling can ship one. (2) An insurer will write lot-level RIN/45Z eligibility cover: low-moderate; the only RIN coverage case I found went against the policyholder. (3) Price holds at $90 a lot: moderate. (4) Warranty premium of 0.5c/lb is accepted: unverified.
deciding_reason: Inspection, QAP defense and contract clauses already do most of the job; the warranty is the only new piece and its premium is the insurer's revenue. Top-decile net is about $35M.

pool: US biofuel producers' purchases of fats, oils and grease feedstock
title: Oil Yield Partner
one_liner: Zero-capex, pay-from-the-oil upgrades of corn-oil recovery at ethanol plants: we install and run the extraction system, guarantee the yield, and take a share of the extra oil for five years, after which the plant owns the equipment.
upside_assumptions: (1) Lenders (CoBank/AgStar type) consent to liens and revenue sharing: precedent exists (Green Plains 2011), but consent was form-specific; moderate. (2) Plants prefer paying about $12.7M over five years to buying a $6M skid: low-moderate, only for capex-capped or cash-poor plants. (3) DCO stays at 60c or more, which depends on RIN and 45Z policy: moderate. (4) OEMs do not add finance arms in an 18-24 month window: low-moderate. (5) The yield guarantee can be underwritten: moderate.
deciding_reason: Real yield gap, but revenue-share extraction has precedent, OEMs and enzymes compete, self-funding plants simply buy, and 40 plants is a heroic share of the addressable set.

pool: US biofuel producers' purchases of fats, oils and grease feedstock
title: Second Stream
one_liner: Put an automatic grease-removal unit at fryer-heavy restaurants and collect the skimmed grease on the same stop as the used cooking oil: the restaurant pays a flat fee that is less than it saves on pump-outs, and we sell the grease as feedstock.
upside_assumptions: (1) City FOG ordinances accept the units as interceptors in many metros: moderate. (2) Restaurants pay $1,200 a year on top of hardware: low-moderate, since pump-out savings are variable and they can buy the unit outright. (3) A UCO collector partner adds the stop at near-zero marginal cost: moderate. (4) Pumpers do not retaliate by bundling or underpricing pump-outs: low.
deciding_reason: The customer can buy the hardware, the grease is worth far less than assumed, and PE-backed pumpers and Restaurant Technologies own the stops. Top-decile about $45M.

pool: US biofuel producers' purchases of fats, oils and grease feedstock
title: Oil Check
one_liner: Pay soybean farmers for the oil they deliver: per-load oil, protein and moisture settlement at independent elevators and farmer-owned crushers, a variety-level pounds-of-oil-per-acre score for seed choice, and identity-preserved premium contracts funded by the crusher's extra margin.
upside_assumptions: (1) ADM, Bunge or Cargill adopt composition pricing and outsource settlement: very low, since flat pricing is their profit. (2) Farmer-owned crushers pay 4c a bushel for a program they already run themselves: low. (3) Seed licensing of oil-per-acre scores adds $10M: low-moderate, public trial data compete.
deciding_reason: The model already runs at farmer-owned crushers, the reachable crush is about a fifth of the market, and the big three profit from flat pricing. Even the upside is about $20M.

pool: US biofuel producers' purchases of fats, oils and grease feedstock
title: Co-Pro Desk
one_liner: Sell petroleum refiners hydrotreater-ready lipid feed, receiving skids, 14C sampling and RIN accounting as one service on a RIN-linked formula, so they can generate their own D4 RINs instead of buying them at $2.20.
upside_assumptions: (1) 10 or more merchant refiners adopt co-processing despite no 45Z: low. (2) RINs stay above $2 so D5 self-generation beats buying: moderate, but D5 not D4. (3) Hydrogen, catalyst and corrosion limits allow 3-5% on their units: moderate. (4) Ag lobby opposition and EPA stay quiet: low-moderate.
deciding_reason: Wrong RIN class, no 45Z, Phillips 66 walked away, integrated majors do it in-house, and the idea's own unit economics are thin. Upside is about $30M.

pool: US biofuel producers' purchases of fats, oils and grease feedstock
title: Premium Ledger
one_liner: Measure each lot's carbon intensity from plant-level actuals (rendering and crush-plant energy, transport mode, allocation, farm practices) and clear the premium between supplier and producer by formula, taking a fee on the premium and a share of the credit that default scores leave unclaimed.
upside_assumptions: (1) Treasury allows measured plant-level CI for waste lipids with real credit value: unverified, low. (2) Suppliers disclose primary data to a third-party ledger: low. (3) Producers share credit with suppliers by formula: low. (4) Soy and corn farm-level CI becomes the bulk of volume: moderate in market, but crowded with farm-data firms and crusher programs.
deciding_reason: Key input (FD-CIC) does not cover waste lipids, Veriflux already traces them, and the $114M path needs near-total share. The idea itself calls it closest to dead.

pool: Indonesia: free-meals programme (MBG) money flowing from BGN through ~27,000 community kitchens (SPPG) to ingredient suppliers
title: Siap Masak: certified cook-ready prep plants for 4-hour kitchens
one_liner: Move the riskiest, most labour-heavy step (raw chicken and vegetable handling) out of 27,820 volunteer-run kitchens into audited plants that deliver portion-weighed, chilled, cook-ready kits timed to the new 4-hour rule.
upside_assumptions: BGN would have to accept large certified processors as eligible sellers (against its Dec 2025 stance on big-company factory food and the micro/small/coop-only eligibility list, about 10% plausible); kitchens accept one processor for their two biggest lines despite the 15-supplier and anti-monopoly enforcement (about 30%); Japfa, CP and Danantara do not respond (about 40%). A cooperative-owned plant is policy-aligned but makes revenue the coop's and leaves a management fee.
deciding_reason: A centralised plant is exactly the structure BGN is policing: eligible sellers are micro, small and cooperative only, supplier concentration is sanctioned, and the incumbent integrators already hold the chicken lane.

pool: Indonesia: free-meals programme (MBG) money flowing from BGN through ~27,000 community kitchens (SPPG) to ingredient suppliers
title: Satu Faktur: kecamatan consolidation hubs in idle Kopdes cold stores
one_liner: Run the state-built Kopdes cold-store warehouse in each kecamatan as the one place that turns 15-40 eligible micro-suppliers into one purchase order, one invoice, one delivery and one payment per kitchen, with the cooperative as the legal seller of record.
upside_assumptions: Kemenkop or Agrinas designates a few private operators to run hubs at scale (about 1,000 hubs); the fee is accepted as an allowable at-cost line; the BGN portal leaves physical consolidation to hubs. Plausibility of each is low to middling; the first is the gate.
deciding_reason: Policy-aligned, but the operator layer is pre-empted by Agrinas, Bulog, Pos and Telkom, the BGN portal does the single-PO job, and the fee is capped.

pool: Indonesia: free-meals programme (MBG) money flowing from BGN through ~27,000 community kitchens (SPPG) to ingredient suppliers
title: Franchisor-in-a-box for the institutional operator groups
one_liner: Sell the HQ functions a franchisor would have (central lab, procurement master agreement, lender reporting, training) to the handful of institutional groups that run hundreds of kitchens under one chain of command.
upside_assumptions: Both Polri and Kadin plus at least one more group buy the full stack and abandon in-house builds (about 15%); a service fee and procurement margin are accepted as allowable (low); no reputational shock from KPK/ICW scrutiny (low).
deciding_reason: Four to six buyers, about 2,500 reachable kitchens, in-house HQ logistics, and a procurement-margin model that is the commission regulators are chasing.

pool: Indonesia: free-meals programme (MBG) money flowing from BGN through ~27,000 community kitchens (SPPG) to ingredient suppliers
title: Java-to-3T protein corridor (own the logistics where infrastructure is weak)
one_liner: Own the chilled lane that ships Java's egg and chicken surplus to the frontier kitchens where BGN says the same programme costs up to three times as much.
upside_assumptions: (1) BGN publishes a numeric cost index and rent incentive for remote kitchens (about 60%); (2) a local coop or BUMDes can be seller of record for Java-sourced goods and the portal admits it (about 50%); (3) Pelni, Kopdes and Bulog do not pre-empt the chilled lane (about 40%); (4) remote kitchens reach several thousand, not a few hundred, despite the CSR/foreign-funding search and the 5 Oct incentive cut (about 40%); (5) a Papua operating team executes. Joint probability is single digits, which is what top-decile means.
deciding_reason: The only idea on the programme's growth edge with a real logistics gap, but median is about $14M and the upside is about $90M, short of both bars, with the key rules still undefined.

pool: Indonesia: free-meals programme (MBG) money flowing from BGN through ~27,000 community kitchens (SPPG) to ingredient suppliers
title: Kitchen workforce employer-of-record: the liability BGN cannot take
one_liner: Become the legal employer, payroll and BPJS provider for the roughly 1.3M kitchen 'volunteers' so the yayasan chair stops carrying employer liability and the at-cost wage claim becomes audit-proof.
upside_assumptions: A court or labour inspector forces employee status and the first sanctioned yayasan triggers a rush (low to middling); BGN allows the EOR fee as an at-cost line (unverified, unlikely since it is a margin); 6,000 kitchens (22%) sign. Net upside about $30M; gross billings upside about $380M but that is not revenue quality.
deciding_reason: Net take is $4-8k per kitchen, the fee is not an at-cost line, BGN already pays the BPJS premium, and EWA and payroll fintechs exist.

pool: Indonesia: free-meals programme (MBG) money flowing from BGN through ~27,000 community kitchens (SPPG) to ingredient suppliers
title: Mitra resolution operator: the special servicer banks and BGN cannot be
one_liner: Take management contracts over stalled, suspended and non-compliant kitchens from their owners and their banks, fix them, get them reinstated and share the restored incentive (weakest of the eight, flagged).
upside_assumptions: BGN creates a steady-state management-contract category (not found, unlikely), banks refer thousands of loans, and a second wave of closures arrives; even then the pool is one-off and mostly equity-funded kitchens.
deciding_reason: Small bank-financed pool, closed kitchens unpaid, the flat incentive is gone, and the problem is a one-off wave, small even in the upside.

pool: Indonesia: free-meals programme (MBG) money flowing from BGN through ~27,000 community kitchens (SPPG) to ingredient suppliers
title: Telur Koperasi: farmer-cooperative egg grading, pasteurising and glut-buffer plant
one_liner: Build the processing plant that turns the state's forced egg demand into a stable business: grade, sanitise and pasteurise local eggs for kitchens, and freeze or dry the glut for industry.
upside_assumptions: BGN or Bapanas mandates pasteurised or processed eggs for Salmonella control (low), the state plant is delayed or contracts out (low), cooperatives qualify as seller of record and buy the processing premium (low).
deciding_reason: HAP caps any premium, the programme wants direct farmer-to-kitchen sales, the state is building its own egg-powder plant, and the industrial market is small.

pool: Indonesia: free-meals programme (MBG) money flowing from BGN through ~27,000 community kitchens (SPPG) to ingredient suppliers
title: Dapur Utilitas: IPAL, gas and water as a per-portion service

upside_assumptions: BGN or Danantara bundles utilities programme-wide with state financing (low), PGN pipeline and CNG reach many kitchens (limited to mapped zones), kitchens accept 5-7 year contracts despite the incentive reset and no-pay closures (low).
deciding_reason: Price exceeds value for IPAL, gas is a thin pass-through against state-owned suppliers, and the counterparty's income was just reset.

pool: US prison and jail health care (state corrections departments and counties paying contractors)
title: Custody Mutual: jail-health liability program priced on clinical process data
one_liner: An MGA-style insurance program for jails that prices and discounts coverage from a few clinical-process indicators in the medical vendor's record, and that covers the county when a bankrupt vendor's indemnity proves worthless.
upside_assumptions: (1) Vendors hand over EHR timestamps despite discovery risk: low plausibility. (2) Process indicators actually separate bad from average outcomes in 50 closed claims: unknown but cheap to test. (3) A fronting carrier and reinsurer back a first-of-kind program: plausible. (4) 15-20% share of insurable jail liability in 6 years via pools: low-to-moderate. Reaching $100M of revenue additionally requires converting to a risk-bearing carrier with 25-30% share: not credible.
deciding_reason: Insurable pool is about $0.3-0.4B; $100M GWP is 25-30% share and only about $15-20M of MGA revenue; the data and privilege premises are fragile.

pool: US prison and jail health care (state corrections departments and counties paying contractors)
title: Outside Care Plan: the DOC's own off-site health plan
one_liner: A risk-bearing benefit manager that takes all off-site care (hospital, ED, specialty, dialysis, oncology) for a state DOC or large jail system at a fixed per-member-per-month price, with referral-timeline guarantees, Medicaid match capture and case management for the sickest 1-3%.
upside_assumptions: (1) 2-3 states restructure a vendor or in-house arrangement to carve hospital payments out to a third-party risk-bearer: no 2026 precedent (every shock produced a vendor swap), low plausibility. (2) Hospitals accept Medicare-plus rates for 15-day payment and 5-10 year volume: plausible. (3) Insurer or health-plan licensure and stop-loss are workable in target states: unknown, unverified. (4) Georgia-style unpaid-provider fallout makes a 'payer of last resort' valuable to DOCs: plausible but not yet a procurement trend.
deciding_reason: Real budget line and pain, but states already hold carve-outs, Medicaid rates and TPAs, 2026 buyers replaced vendors instead of restructuring, and risk-bearing needs licensure and capital for a 5-8% margin.

pool: US prison and jail health care (state corrections departments and counties paying contractors)
title: Clinical Corps: pre-cleared nurse and tele-psychiatry pool
one_liner: A W-2 pool of nurses and tele-psychiatry clinicians with standing security clearance and correctional training for a state's facilities, dispatched in 24-72 hours and billed per verified hour with a fill-or-credit guarantee, replacing registry and agency nursing.
upside_assumptions: (1) Clearances and training are portable across 15-20 states: low plausibility, each state has its own background and key-control rules. (2) States let contractors pay above civil-service scales: plausible. (3) Win the California registry or its tele-psychiatry gap: the RFP is already bid, so low for this cycle. (4) Margin survives once rivals copy the credential in 6-12 months (the idea's own estimate): low.
deciding_reason: Corrections staffing already exists and is bid competitively; the idea itself rates the moat weak and copyable in 6-12 months.

pool: US prison and jail health care (state corrections departments and counties paying contractors)
title: Piggyback Prime: the first cooperative contract for jail medical services
one_liner: Win a cooperative-purchasing master agreement (or a large state contract with a political-subdivision piggyback clause) for jail medical services so any county can join in days, with uniform quality standards, a pooled insurance/indemnity backstop, and regional operators or public hospitals delivering care.
upside_assumptions: (1) A cooperative accepts a professional-services solicitation for clinical care with indemnity: unproven, none found. (2) Rival operators subcontract to the prime: low plausibility. (3) Sheriffs give up local procurement control: low. (4) Emergency buyers choose the pre-papered vehicle over the best-capacity vendor: plausible but unproven.
deciding_reason: A prime that holds the contract and the liability is just a new thin-margin Wellpath; $8-12M net on $100M gross by its own math, and operators will not subcontract to a rival.

pool: US prison and jail health care (state corrections departments and counties paying contractors)
title: Day 91: reentry care organization that starts inside the walls
one_liner: A reentry care organization that works inside facilities for the 90 days before release (paid by Medicaid under 1115 waivers), then holds a per-member contract with Medicaid plans for the first year after release, using a nurse, prescriber and community-health-worker team.
upside_assumptions: (1) Plans sub-capitate 12-month total cost of care for released members to a specialist: not yet seen in reentry, low-to-moderate. (2) 4-5 states keep funding the benefit through 2031: plausible (CMS approved 3 more on 2026-09-23) but Michigan withdrew for lack of appropriation. (3) Release-date data feed stays proprietary: weak, the waivers build it in. (4) Outcome data (ED, overdose) is strong enough to move plans: unproven.
deciding_reason: Real Medicaid-paid benefit, but FQHCs, CBOs, plans and vendors already deliver it, the release-date pipe is built into the waivers, and the payer and federal funding can walk.

pool: US prison and jail health care (state corrections departments and counties paying contractors)
title: Cure Carve-Out: high-cost drugs out of the per-diem

upside_assumptions: Needs states to mandate pass-through and the federal subscription bill to fail, while the operator keeps a fee on HIV and MOUD volumes too. Each is plausible alone; together they still cap near $25M.
deciding_reason: A finite, mostly pass-through $0.9B one-time pool with a 6-10% fee that a pending federal subscription bill would bypass.

pool: US prison and jail health care (state corrections departments and counties paying contractors)
title: Day 21: forensic capacity for court-ordered competency restoration
one_liner: Secure psychiatric capacity that can come online in 6-12 months (jail-based restoration units and modular/converted licensed units), paid per bed-day by the state at 30-45% below a state hospital bed, with an outpatient track for low-risk defendants.
upside_assumptions: (1) Fifth Circuit upholds Ward v. Muth (permanent injunction 2026-07-07, 21 days, four years): uncertain, the state is appealing and a 2012 21-day order was paused. (2) HHSC meets it partly by contracting rather than only building, which its $3.7M-per-bed build cost and 747 private beds/day support: plausible. (3) Win 300-400 Texas full-service beds plus 150-200 in Washington/Oklahoma/other states over 5-6 years: plausible for top-decile execution. pick.from_title: Day 21: forensic capacity for court-ordered competency restoration
pick.title: Day 21: multi-state operator of full-service forensic restoration beds
pick.one_liner: An operator that adds licensed secure forensic beds in 6-12 months, paid per available bed-day by state forensic agencies under court deadlines, starting with Texas.
pick.sharpened_pitch: A multi-state operator of full-service secure competency-restoration beds, sold on 5-year availability-based contracts to state forensic agencies, delivered in leased and modular licensed units next to existing campuses, with an owned clinical staffing pool and an outpatient restoration track for low-risk defendants. Do not make jail-hosted treatment-only slots the core: Liberty's San Bernardino contract works out to about $170 per bed-day (county supplies the bed) and Harris County's program about $261, while full-service beds price at $412-$800 and Wellpath Recovery Solutions earns about $388 per patient-day. $100M needs about 600 full-service beds at $450. Texas is the anchor: the wait list was 1,626 in June 2026, HHSC adds only 175 net new beds by 2027 and told lawmakers it will still be short, and a state-built bed costs about $3.7M against about $164k a year for a contracted one. Then replicate under the same kind of pressure in Washington, Oklahoma and Colorado. Use jail-based units only as a door opener with counties that are already suing. The edge is speed, outcome data (days to competency, restoration rate) and a staffed, licensed footprint, not a technology moat.
pick.payer_and_signer: Payer: Texas HHSC's private inpatient competency-restoration bed line (about 747 beds a day already contracted), plus equivalent forensic lines in Washington DSHS, Oklahoma ODMHSAS and Colorado CDHS. Signer: HHSC deputy executive commissioner for state hospitals and procurement; the legislature appropriates (next regular session starts January 2027), and the federal court monitors benchmarks.
pick.path_to_100m: 600 beds x $450 x 365 = $98.6M. Example mix by year 6: Texas 350 beds, Washington 150, Oklahoma/Colorado/next-wave state 100. Texas alone is a 1,000+ bed gap I estimate at $160M+ a year; the national unmet need is 3,000-4,000 beds per the pool file (unsourced), so $100M is roughly 15-20% share, at the edge of heroic. Requires 5-year take-or-pay or availability payments to finance leased units. Revenue per full-service bed is about $164k a year; exit multiples are low (Wellpath RS sold at about 0.9x revenue).
pick.competitors_and_edge: Wellpath Recovery Solutions ($425M revenue, 3,000 patients, 70 facilities, creditor-owned), Liberty Healthcare, GEO Group, and likely UHS and Acadia (unverified); HHSC's current private-bed vendors are not named in public sources. Edge: deployable in 6-12 months versus years for state construction ($2.5B for about 680 beds), a price below HHSC's own cost per bed ($412 at Harris's state-hospital comparison, $697 at North Texas State Hospital in 2016), and a clean restoration-outcome record. Edge is thin and copyable by incumbents with buildings.
pick.why_now: Ward v. Muth permanent injunction on 2026-07-07 requires admission within 21 days with four years to comply; HHSC says beds will still fall short; Washington fined about $100M in 2026; Oklahoma began paying $100-$500 a day per waiting person in Oct 2025; Colorado has paid $55M in capped fines through a decree that ends 2027-12-01; Wellpath RS is now creditor-owned, loosening an incumbent.
pick.moat: Thin: licensed and permitted beds, site and lease agreements, 3-5 year contracts, a credentialed staff pool and a restoration-outcome record. A rival with owned buildings can copy it; the defence is speed to first contract and track record.
pick.biggest_open_risk: The Fifth Circuit narrows or reverses Ward v. Muth (the state has asked it to pause benchmarks, argues the Constitution never required the remedy, and an earlier 2012 21-day order was paused), removing the urgency that moves Texas from building to buying.
pick.cheapest_next_test: File a Texas Public Information Act request to HHSC for every private inpatient competency-restoration contract (vendor, per diem, beds, term, occupancy) and the SB 528 cost-comparison report; read the benchmark order and any Fifth Circuit stay ruling on the docket; get three modular or leased-unit quotes and staffing plans for a 60-bed unit; call the Dallas and Bexar sheriffs and HHSC contract management.

pool: Airlines' and lessors' spend on commercial aviation MRO and aftermarket parts
title: Slot Book: block-booked engine shop capacity for mid-tier operators
one_liner: Sign take-or-pay capacity blocks at independent engine shops and resell guaranteed-window shop visits to the operators too small to command a slot.
upside_assumptions: Needs: (1) shops sign binding take-or-pay capacity with guaranteed induction windows (the cited StandardAero release does not show this and its terms say it may reject any order; implausible); (2) OEM licenses allow resale or subcontracting of slots (unverified, new-gen engines sit in closed networks); (3) scarcity persists past 2030 while StandardAero, FTAI and others add lines (contested); (4) the broker holds ~12% of mid-tier visits at a 4% take (heroic). Even if all hold, parts shortages, not slots, drive the 180-day turnaround.
deciding_reason: Premise contradicted: no binding capacity product is evidenced, parts rather than slots gate turnaround, and even the pitch's own math needs 26-32% share; upside is about $35M.

title: The Repair Library: approved-repair IP for engine piece parts
one_liner: Own a library of FAA/EASA-approved repair schemes for engine piece parts, with field evidence behind each, and run automated repair cells that use it.
upside_assumptions: (1) Three or four hot-section CFM56 schemes win DER approval and shop adoption (moderately plausible given Chromalloy precedent); (2) $60-100M of capital for cells, which venture has not funded in this niche (plausible but slow); (3) a lessor writes approved schemes into workscope clauses (speculative, only a 90-day goal in the pitch); (4) shops share post-repair CT and flow data with a neutral party to build the moat (unlikely); (5) LEAP and GTF repair licensing opens (CFM says it will consider requests). Together these are below top-decile odds, and the upside still tops out under $100M.
deciding_reason: Real pain but scaled incumbents (Chromalloy 50+ DER repairs on the same parts, HEICO) and heavy capital; median about $10M, upside about $80M.

pool: Airlines' and lessors' spend on commercial aviation MRO and aftermarket parts
title: Fleet Buying Group: a Vizient for aircraft maintenance with PMA offtake pools
one_liner: A vendor-paid buying group that pools mid-tier maintenance volume and uses it to fund PMA offtake for the part numbers nobody develops.
upside_assumptions: Needs OEMs and distributors to pay rebates to a brand-new buyer collective (low plausibility while AAR and SkySelect ship pooling), 60+ members with pooled RFPs, and PMA developers committing to offtake letters (non-binding today). Rule-of-reason antitrust exposure after FTC and DOJ withdrew collaboration guidelines in Dec 2024.
deciding_reason: AAR Airvoyant and SkySelect are shipping the pitch's year-2 product, the only aviation GPO precedent is dead, and OEM sole-source pricing limits pooled leverage; upside about $35M.

title: Graded Parts: authentication, escrow and indemnity for non-OEM parts
one_liner: An independent grade, escrowed settlement and an indemnity for used and non-OEM aircraft parts so a buyer can prove a part is what its paperwork says.
upside_assumptions: Needs lenders, insurers and the airline coalition to mandate this grade as the standard (the pitch itself says that is the only path; low plausibility while OEM-backed digital certificates and DUST are being rolled out), an admitted insurer willing to underwrite consequential AOG loss (no product found), and sellers accepting a buyer-paid fee.
deciding_reason: Authentication layer is occupied and funded; indemnity layer has no evidenced insurer or loss data; realistic fee base is a few percent of a small USM pool.

one_liner: Forecast a shop visit's missing parts 60-120 days ahead, assemble a documented kit, and induct the engine only when the kit is complete.
upside_assumptions: Net revenue (gross profit) basis; gross billings median ~$35M and upside ~$150M. Needs: privileged teardown and USM supply against FTAI, AAR, AerSale and CFM Materials (low plausibility); $100M+ of inventory financing (plausible); shops accepting induction gating that cuts their utilization metric (the pitch concedes this); and a findings-data forecast edge that is an unverified insider hypothesis. Revenue passes $100M easily, gross profit does not.
deciding_reason: FTAI already runs this as a profitable module factory and sells to third parties; the entrant has the forecast but not the parts. Gross profit upside is about $22M.

pool: Airlines' and lessors' spend on commercial aviation MRO and aftermarket parts
title: Shop-Floor Ledger: evidence capture the MRO ERPs cannot do
one_liner: Capture shop-floor work (voice, photos, tool data) as it happens, draft the paperwork, and produce a tamper-evident evidence package lessors can rely on.
upside_assumptions: ~30,000 seats at a lower effective price, lessors and insurers accept the evidence package for reserve claims (speculative, unverified), and no ERP vendor bundles a native version (they sell to the same shops). Adoption inside regulated shops is slow.
deciding_reason: A $100M outcome would exceed Ramco's whole revenue; the space is funded and consolidating under IFS and AVIATAR; matches the generic AI copilot cliche. Upside about $20M.

title: Engine Lifeline: flexible-term spare-engine cover pool for institutional owners
one_liner: A neutral pool manager that serves 60-180 day cover needs from institutional owners' engines and airlines' idle spares under one standardized swap protocol.
upside_assumptions: Fee-basis net revenue. Needs: (1) $3-3.5B of third-party engine AUM within 7 years, with a $300-500M anchor LP (plausible, GFH just did this for Bridgepoint); (2) engine supply by secondary purchase because OEM spares go to CFM's leasing arm and SES (plausible but expensive); (3) rents stay high to 2030 (contested; SMBC Aero Engine Lease's CEO warned in Feb 2026 that rents will collapse if spare ratios normalize, and ELFC warns of premature part-outs); (4) the standardized swap protocol really cuts the $150-300k per-swap cost (unverified insider hypothesis); (5) no warranty or TRUEngine friction from installing third-party engines (unverified). On a principal-lessor basis revenue passes $100M with ~$0.9B of owned engines, but that is a financing business with no edge over Willis or Blackstone-backed rivals, so it is not counted.
deciding_reason: Cleanest payer and fee pool in the pool, but short-term cover and third-party engine capital already exist at scale and the why-now is the crowding signal; median about $12M, upside about $75M.

one_liner: A roster of pre-vetted certifying staff with portable company authorizations, sold to hangars and line stations short of signatures.
upside_assumptions: Net revenue (gross profit) basis; gross billings median ~$25M and upside ~$120M. Needs ~1,000 placed FTE via two or three large MRO accounts (plausible for a strong tech-enabled roster), hosts accepting a portable record in place of their own authorization process (unlikely, since the FAA authorizes per station), and working capital for payroll. Revenue clears the bar but at staffing margins and against an incumbent with a matching platform.
deciding_reason: Aviation staffing is already done at scale; revenue can pass $100M but net economics are staffing-grade with no moat; upside net revenue about $25M.

pool: US consumer auto-loan interest and fees, with the subprime servicing, collections and repossession layer under stress
title: Last Mile: a locate-first, net-recovery operator for the default chain
one_liner: A forwarder paid on dollars recovered per defaulted dollar instead of per truck roll: it finds the car before the file is assigned, offers cooperating borrowers a scheduled hand-back, and routes each recovered unit to its best sale channel.
upside_assumptions: (1) Randomized pilot beats the incumbent forwarder and the lender consolidates recovery spend into one invoice: needs 3-5 anchor lenders at 15-25k repossessions each, about 10% chance. (2) Net-proceeds pricing stays a differentiator: weak, copyable once proven, so the moat must be the per-unit outcome dataset and managed-resolution workflow. (3) Outcome pricing does not trigger wrongful-repossession or UDAAP problems: manageable if pay is on net proceeds net of complaints. (4) Plate-data supply stays available: likely, DRN sells to many buyers.
deciding_reason: Only idea with an existing budget line, easy bake-off switching and a $100M gross path from 3-4 anchor lenders; but incumbents sell every component except net-proceeds pricing, so upside is borderline and the median is soft.

pick.title: Last Mile: outcome-priced recovery operator for non-captive auto lenders
pick.one_liner: A single-invoice, net-proceeds-priced recovery operator that runs locate, voluntary hand-back, forwarding and remarketing for non-captive auto lenders, proven by randomized holdouts and an account-level outcome dataset.
pick.sharpened_pitch: Do not sell 'we locate cars'; plate-sighting data is sold lender-direct by DRN, and Primeritus, Servicing Solutions and Resolvion already sell locate, forwarding and remarketing. Sell accountability for dollars recovered per defaulted account. One accountable operator replaces the lender's separate forwarder, transport, storage, auction-coordination and title vendors with one invoice and one outcome metric. Price: a base fee below today's forwarding bill plus a share of net proceeds above a baseline set by a randomized holdout on the lender's own accounts, with the share reduced by wrongful-repossession and complaint events so the contract cannot reward aggressive repo. The product is the account-level decision (pre-locate, managed voluntary hand-back, dealer-assisted pre-repo sale where the lender has pre-authorized it, repossess, or release) and the route-to-sale choice. Fix the metrics: sell on net dollars per defaulted account and on fewer repeat assignments (only 54% of accounts are assigned once), plus more voluntary hand-backs (10-19% of completions) and redemptions (22-34%), not on the 29% unit ratio. Target the 20-25 non-captive lenders with 8-30k repossessions a year; three to four anchors at 15-25k each is about 60-70k units, or $100M of gross billing at $1,450-1,700 all-in a unit. Wedge via bake-offs, since lenders already split assignments across forwarders. Exit path: the outcome dataset becomes a recovery-pricing engine and an ABS-investor reporting product.
pick.payer_and_signer: SVP Collections/Recovery signs, CFO co-signs; paid from the existing recovery line (forwarder fees, transport, storage, auction and title costs) at about $1,450 all-in per recovered unit today.
pick.path_to_100m: Gross billing basis: one invoice at about $1,450-1,700 per unit x 60-70k units a year = $100M, i.e. 3-4 anchor lenders at 15-25k repossessions each, about 3% of the 1.8-2.1M remarketable units. Net basis ($650 a unit) needs 154k units, which is heroic; present revenue on a gross basis and margin separately. Reachable pool of about $2.6-4.3B of annual recovery cost (1.8-2.95M units x $1,450).
pick.competitors_and_edge: Primeritus, Servicing Solutions, Resolvion, RDN (assignment network), DRN (lender-direct locate), AANGO, Loanbridge.AI. Edge: net-proceeds pricing and single-invoice accountability that activity-paid forwarders cannot offer without cannibalising their own per-assignment revenue, plus a randomized proof per lender. Not an edge: locate data, which is a bought input.
pick.why_now: Repossessions at multi-year highs, non-prime recoveries weak, forwarders consolidating to 66% of completions with higher consumer fees flagged by the CFPB, Senate Banking attention on repossessions, ABS investors asking for recovery reporting, and digital remarketing channels available to plug into.
pick.moat: Weak at first (pricing is copyable). Durable only if the per-unit outcome dataset and managed-resolution workflow create a recovery-pricing engine and switching costs once embedded in a lender's servicing flow; scale economies in dispatch density.
pick.biggest_open_risk: Incumbent forwarders copy the DRN-fed pre-locate and match outcome pricing once a pilot proves the lift, leaving a services business competing on price. Second: the 3-point recovery lift on which the economics rest is unproven and confounded by used-car price swings.
pick.cheapest_next_test: A 2-3 week data-only test: get 12 months of de-identified assignment history (assignment date, days past due, forwarder, outcome, fees, sale channel and proceeds) from 3-5 mid-size lenders or an ex-forwarder ops head, then measure (a) the share of assignments with zero recovery and the fees spent on them, (b) the share of accounts assigned 2+ times, (c) net proceeds by sale channel. If avoidable waste is at least $400 per recovered unit, the $650 net economics hold and a randomized 1,000-account pilot is worth buying.

title: Downshift: a lender-approved short-payoff and trade-down exchange
one_liner: Before the repossession, a delinquent borrower is matched with a dealer that buys the car near retail value and puts them in a cheaper one, with the lender pre-approving the short payoff: the auto version of a mortgage short sale.
upside_assumptions: Needs several lenders to adopt a pre-authorized short-payoff window as standard policy (ABS consent, 1099-C and credit-reporting treatment solved; moderate plausibility, slow), and dealers to pay above wholesale funded by finance yield (plausible for BHPH, regulatory optics poor). deciding_reason: Most non-obvious idea and a real loss-mitigation insight, but the lender gain depends on dealers overpaying wholesale and adoption is slow; median is far below $20M.

upside_assumptions: (1) $500M+ of warehouse or forward-flow capital at under 8% cost, plausible but needs a track record. one_liner: The title company for insurance repair money: a licensed, bonded escrow that holds and releases claim proceeds against milestones and signs an indemnity to the servicer and carrier.

deciding_reason: The fee-on-whole-settlement math is internally inconsistent with the $1-4k uplift and is restricted or barred in several states; contractors supplement for free; median is far below $20M.

deciding_reason: The clearance standard does not exist until 2027-2029, the 13,000 LA files are likely outside the new law, and the payer is the conflicted insurer; national path rests on other states copying California.

pick.title: Hold-forever Handwerk platform with owned origination (new name needed)
pick.one_liner: A permanent-capital buyer of owner-led Handwerk and technical-service firms below PE's size floor, built as regional hubs with tuck-ins, an owned pre-sale funnel and a Meister-equity ladder.
pick.sharpened_pitch: Buy owner-led German Handwerk and technical-service firms (electrical testing, fire protection, heating and water service, lift maintenance) that PE platforms skip, and never sell them. Five changes from the gate. (1) Buy the contract book, not revenue: target firms with at least half of revenue from recurring statutory inspection or service work, and price against that book. (2) Hub-and-spoke: six to eight hubs of 15-60 staff (EUR 2-4M revenue) in Bavaria and NRW, then tuck in micro firms and the customer books of closing firms around each hub, so deal count stays manageable and routes get denser. (3) Own origination: chamber and Steuerberater referral is shared with HWP, Builtech and Konzmann, so add a pre-sale programme for owners two to three years out with a right of first offer, plus a catch net for the roughly 27,000 Handwerk closures a year. (4) Price the gap honestly: owners expect a median 60% of revenue (Handwerk about 87%), so offer 0.4-0.6x with half deferred against contract retention, keep the old Meister as Betriebsleiter for two to three years, and give a Geselle a Meister-equity ladder. (5) Fund with EUR 15M permanent seed and EUR 45-80M total consideration over five years, using seller notes and Buergschaftsbank cover. Target 60 firms x EUR 1.5M, about $103M revenue at 6-9% margin by year six or seven. Rename: Meisterwerk is a funded Berlin software startup.
pick.payer_and_signer: Customers pay: building owners, property managers and small industrial sites, from maintenance and statutory-inspection budgets. Signers on each deal: the seller-owner (Inhaber). Capital signer: the CIO of a permanent-capital LP (Versorgungswerk or family office).
pick.path_to_100m: 60 firms x EUR 1.5M = EUR 90M (about $103M). Pace roughly 2, 5, 8, 10, 12, 12, 12 deals over seven years. Consideration EUR 45-80M (0.5-0.87x revenue, half deferred), above the original EUR 22-45M. About 27,000 Handwerk closures and about 25,000 handovers a year mean twelve deals is a fraction of a percent of reachable sellers. EBIT at 6-9% would be $6-9M, so this is revenue scale, not software-like value.
pick.competitors_and_edge: Konzmann (21 firms, EUR 180M revenue, KLAR Partners), HWP (30-40 units, about 1,250 staff, GRIP), Builtech (51 firms, 2,000+ staff, merging with VDK) and Purpose Evergreen Capital (minority capital). Edge: they buy firms of about 20 staff and EUR 2M revenue and up and have changed hands within five or six years, so a hold-forever buyer of smaller firms with a Meister pipeline is a real counter-position; the edge is modest.
pick.why_now: KfW Jan 2026: planned closures exceed successions for the first time. In Handwerk about 54,000 firms expect to close within two years against 49,000 handing over, owners are on average 54 and those handing over about 59, and 33% of firms plan a handover within five years (HWK Dortmund). PE platforms get flipped, which makes a no-flip promise credible to sellers.
pick.moat: Thin: scale economies in back office, procurement and compliance scheduling; a Meister pipeline as a modest cornered resource; counter-positioning against PE flips. Mostly execution and cost of capital.
pick.biggest_open_risk: Adverse selection and churn: owners expect about 1.5-2x what a hold-forever buyer pays, so the platform may only get weaker firms or sellers with no alternative, and contract books and Meister may leave after the owner exits. At 6-9% margin one bad cohort of deals can erase equity.
pick.cheapest_next_test: In 6-8 weeks, through HWK Nachfolgemoderatoren get anonymised customer ledgers from 6-8 target firms and measure recurring share and three-year retention; sign three non-binding term sheets at 0.6x revenue or less with half deferred; hold five talks with Versorgungswerk or family-office CIOs on a EUR 15M seed. Stop if recurring revenue is under 40% or sellers insist on over 0.8x in cash.

one_liner: Sell nuclear plants finished, signed, Appendix B-compliant engineering deliverables at a fixed price per deliverable, produced by an AI pipeline that sits inside a qualified quality program, instead of selling another AI tool or more hourly engineers.
upside_assumptions: (a) Buy or white-label an ASL-listed boutique in year 1: plausible, PE is actively buying nuclear engineering. pick.from_title: Signed-Off: the QA-accountable AI engineering house
pick.title: Signed-Off: fixed-price, AI-native nuclear engineering house (acquire the audit, automate the work)
pick.one_liner: Buy or white-label an approved-supplier-listed nuclear engineering boutique, rebuild its workflows AI-first under an NQA-1 software QA program, and sell finished, signed Appendix B deliverables at a fixed price with a rework guarantee.
pick.sharpened_pitch: Do not lead with the claim that AI output is unusable until a qualified organization owns it. No rule says that, and Nuclearn, Everstar and Westinghouse already sell AI to licensee engineers who verify and own the result. Lead with capacity, speed and a price guarantee in a market where capital spending is rising, about 30 uprates, three restarts and 20+ renewals queue, and the engineer pool is thin. Step 1: acquire or white-label a 30-100 person boutique already on customers' approved supplier lists, skipping the 12-24 month audit queue that blocks greenfield entrants. Step 2: rebuild its bounded, high-volume deliverables (50.59 screenings and evaluations, calculation revisions, engineering change packages) AI-first, version-locked under NQA-1 Subpart 2.7, with nuclear-qualified engineers independently verifying and signing every output. Step 3: price per deliverable class at a discount to hourly, with rework guaranteed, and sell to single-site operators and restarts first. Step 4: add developer-facing licensing (docketing completeness, RAI response, absorbing idea 8) and fleet uprate engineering (idea 7's engineering slice). Data asset: customer-accepted calculation and evaluation templates per plant design. Path: $20-25M boutique in years 1-2, about $55M by year 4 across 8-10 owners, $100M+ by year 6 with about a quarter from developers. Edge over Enercon and Sargent & Lundy is AI-native unit economics, not QA exclusivity.
pick.payer_and_signer: Contracted engineering and supplemental-staff lines in owner O&M plus project engineering in the capital budget. Signer: Director of Design Engineering or VP Engineering; Supply Chain adds the firm to the approved supplier list and the QA director accepts the software QA program. Developers: VP Licensing.
pick.path_to_100m: Outsourced nuclear engineering is a multi-$B budget (Enercon alone about $200M engineering revenue per an older figure; reported $1.25B equity deal April 2026; S&L ENR #1), so $100M is roughly 4-5% of a plausible $2-3B pool (the pool's $1.3-1.4B figure is an unverified assumption). $100M at about $250k per billable engineer is 250-400 engineers, which AI leverage of 30-40% must reduce. Mix: about 8-10 owners at $4-6M each plus 6-8 developers and restarts at $3-5M each plus uprate engineering.
pick.competitors_and_edge: AI software: Nuclearn ($10.5M Series A, 65+ reactors), Everstar/Gordian (DOE test), Atomic Canyon ($7M seed), Westinghouse bertha. Services: Sargent & Lundy, Enercon/Pond (2,700 professionals, PE-backed), Jensen Hughes, Framatome. Edge: fixed-price deliverables with an engineer's signature and a rework guarantee, built on AI-native workflows; incumbents bill hours, tool vendors do not carry accountability.
pick.why_now: Capital spending rose sharply in 2025 (reported +24%), uprate and restart pipeline backed by hyperscaler contracts, NRC clocks under EO 14300 raise licensing volume, DOE/INL test showed 4-6 weeks of drafting done in a day, and PE is paying up for nuclear engineering capacity.
pick.moat: Switching costs and process power: supplier-list status, per-owner acceptance of the software QA program, and a growing library of verified templates per plant design. Weak early; strengthens with signed-deliverable history.
pick.biggest_open_risk: AI may not remove 40% or more of hours on safety-related deliverables at independent-verification quality (Nuclearn's CEO told the NRC complex analysis is non-trivial). If leverage is under 20%, fixed-price undercutting loses money and the firm becomes a fourth-tier hourly shop; Enercon can also copy the model with fresh PE capital.
pick.cheapest_next_test: Paid pilot of about 20 50.59 screenings and 10 calculation revisions with 1-2 single-site operators, plant engineer signing, measuring hours versus baseline and rework rate, while interviewing 10 design-engineering directors and QA managers on what they would need to accept the software QA program and which boutiques are acquirable.

pick.title: Outreach Partner Labs
pick.one_liner: An independent operator co-owns a new outreach lab company with a health system and runs every commercial function (sales, couriers, patient service centers, billing, payer enrollment), leaving the hospital its core lab, brand and a real equity stake.
pick.sharpened_pitch: Give health systems the option Quest and Labcorp cannot: keep control. Form a co-owned outreach LLC with its own CLIA, NPI and TIN (the PAML, Frisbie and Corewell templates). The hospital core lab keeps 80-85% of testing. The operator buys 50-51% with growth capital, so the hospital gets cash up front plus retained upside, and runs sales, couriers, patient service centers, billing, payer enrollment and client services under a cost-plus management agreement. That fixes the original idea's flaw: an 8% fee cannot fund the operations. Where the operator controls the LLC, revenue is the LLC's outreach revenue, so one $45M system is nearly half of a $100M business instead of a $3.6M fee. Where it only manages, revenue is cost plus a 6-10% fee. Once three or more systems share a metro or state, route routine overflow and send-outs to a regional hub (this absorbs Third Lab, fed by hospital volume instead of distressed independents). Sell the CFO on retained contribution margin (23-40% on fixed costs inpatient volume already pays for) and on what a nationals takeout strips out, and on control. Start with 2-3 mid-size systems under Medicaid and ACA-subsidy pressure that are unwilling to sell, then add one system with $100M+ of outreach. Build compliance in from day one (EKRA, AKS, per-entity payer contracts).
pick.payer_and_signer: The health system. Signer: system CFO, with the outreach VP or lab service-line leader. Budget line: the outreach P&L and capital plan; mandate: the 2027 CLFS cut (15% on about 775 tests, more in 2028-29), H.R.1 Medicaid cuts and the Quest/Labcorp offers as a price benchmark.
pick.path_to_100m: Pool is about $20B across 600+ systems (Quest 2025 investor day). Two controlled JVs of about $45M each is $90M of consolidated revenue; plus 8 managed systems averaging $35M outreach at 9% adds about $25M; total about $115M. Equity need is about 1.0-1.3x revenue for the stake, so $50-90M at 50-51% ownership (inference from Quest's $183-230M per large program and older 1.3x revenue benchmarks). Equivalent all-fee version: $1.2B of managed revenue at 8-9%, which is about 6% of the pool.
pick.competitors_and_edge: Quest (Co-Lab about $800M, Corewell 51/49 JV, $613M of outreach buys in 2024), Labcorp (13 hospital or regional deals in 2025, CHS $194M), Sonic USA (0% organic growth), Mayo/ARUP (advisory and connectivity, not operators), consultants such as Chi Solutions. PAML proved the model (about $300M revenue, nine JVs) and then was absorbed by Labcorp in 2017, so no independent operator exists today. Edge: independence, no hub pull on the hospital's testing, and control left with the system, which Quest's 51/49 structure does not offer.
pick.why_now: 2027 CLFS cut and more in 2028-29; H.R.1 Medicaid cuts and end of ACA subsidies squeeze hospital margins; Quest and Labcorp are buying roughly $1B a year of outreach revenue, so CFOs are being solicited and want alternatives; Sonic is stalled and PAML is gone, leaving the independent slot empty.
pick.moat: Cornered resource (multi-year operating agreements and payer enrollments in each metro); scale economies in couriers, patient service centers and billing; switching costs once the entity is the system's outreach vehicle; counter-positioning against Quest and Labcorp, who must pull volume to their own hubs.
pick.biggest_open_risk: Hospitals that want cash take Quest and Labcorp offers, and those that want to stay can run outreach themselves with ARUP, Mayo or Chi; PAML's end state was acquisition. Also raising $50-90M of equity without a track record, and EKRA/AKS exposure on any percent-of-revenue or equity-linked compensation.
pick.cheapest_next_test: Build an outreach contribution model for 25 systems from CMS and PAMA data (about a week of work); hold 5 CFO or outreach-VP conversations asking what would make them choose this over Quest's 51/49 JV; get one healthcare PE or infrastructure sponsor to say in writing whether it would fund $75M of equity; buy a short EKRA/AKS opinion on the fee and equity structure.
