pool: Clinical laboratory testing (independent, hospital-outreach and reference labs)
title: Lab OS for Small Labs
one_liner: A subscription that gives a physician group, urgent-care chain, dialysis or skilled-nursing operator or specialty clinic a compliant moderate- or high-complexity lab: remote director and technical supervisor, proficiency-testing and QC management, LIS, and a billing hook.
upside_assumptions: The proposed rule is finalized as written (moderate); multi-site operators consolidate labs onto one vendor (low); the five-lab director limit is relaxed (not proposed); lab owners keep labs despite the 2027 cut (low).
deciding_reason: Director services already sell for under $30k a year per lab, the five-lab cap forces headcount, and the multi-site customer base is tiny; upside about $20M.

pool: Cyber and liability premiums being carved out for generative-AI risk (cyber, tech E&O, D&O, GL)
title: Seam Map
one_liner: A fee-only service and data product that reconciles every policy's actual wording, the company's real AI deployments, and the insurance and indemnity clauses in its customer contracts, then turns the gaps into carve-back asks backed by wordings carriers already granted peers.
upside_assumptions: (a) Exclusion wave is broad and sticky (~50%); (b) peer-wording corpus becomes a real cornered resource, which needs brokers or counsel to share wordings and conflicts with fee-only stance (~15%); (c) it grows into a fee-only placement shop for residual gaps, i.e. a brokerage competing with funded entrants (~25%). 1,000 recurring customers x $25k + $15M placement/benchmark = $40M. $100M needs the full 2,500 x $40k, which I do not believe.
deciding_reason: Real pain and real budget, but the $40k recurring price is unsupported, Risklytics already sells the core, and free broker and counsel analysis cap the market.

pool: Cyber and liability premiums being carved out for generative-AI risk (cyber, tech E&O, D&O, GL)
title: Warranty File
one_liner: Turn the signed AI and cyber application into an evidence-backed, time-stamped file, and get carriers to agree by endorsement not to rescind on verified answers: a contractual incontestability clause for commercial cyber, tech E&O and affirmative AI cover.
upside_assumptions: (a) 2-3 large carriers/MGAs sign the verified-answers endorsement and market it (~25%); (b) the File becomes the accepted AI supplement across carriers rather than AIUC-1 or bespoke forms (~20%); (c) GRC vendors do not simply add a carrier export (~25%). Joint probability low; $100M needs all three plus the heroic 35% share.
deciding_reason: Sharpest insight in the pool (claims die by rescission), but the evidence layer is already built, insured-side price exceeds value, and no carrier has agreed to waive rescission.

pool: Cyber and liability premiums being carved out for generative-AI risk (cyber, tech E&O, D&O, GL)
title: The Mutual
one_liner: A Bermuda-domiciled, member-owned excess liability mutual for independent frontier AI developers and the largest AI deployers, writing the $50M-$1B layers commercial markets will not, with training-data copyright carved out as uninsurable legal-regime risk.
upside_assumptions: (a) 3+ top labs choose a shared mutual over their own captives (~25%); (b) reinsurers and ILS supply $1B+ of layers over correlated single-model risk despite CSA calling it the uninsurable frontier (~30%); (c) litigation pushes towers to ~$2B per top lab at 8-10% rate on line (~35%); (d) this team, not AIUC, is the manager (~15%). 3 labs x $160M + deployers $300M = ~$780M x 10-12% = $78-94M. Whole chain under 5% and still below $100M.
deciding_reason: Biggest pool, but only 3-5 whale buyers who can self-insure, and the best-funded would-be builder (AIUC) wrote the proposal; manager fee, not gross premium, is the revenue.

pool: Cyber and liability premiums being carved out for generative-AI risk (cyber, tech E&O, D&O, GL)
title: Gate Meter
one_liner: Usage-based AI liability cover sold as a toggle on the model gateway or cloud marketplace: premium is a few basis points of the metered AI bill, priced from runtime telemetry the gateway already sees (tool scopes, spend caps, guardrail hits, human-override rates, model versions), never from content.
upside_assumptions: (a) AI premium pool is 2-3x Deloitte (~30%); (b) a hyperscaler or top-two gateway makes this the default attach, though that partner can swap MGAs (~15%); (c) telemetry pricing demonstrably beats questionnaires on loss ratio, needing 3+ years of claims (~35%). $100M possible only if all three land.
deciding_reason: Good pattern transfer from usage-based auto, but it is a pricing method rather than a moat, replicable by funded rivals, and the gateway channel is the weakest link.

pool: Cyber and liability premiums being carved out for generative-AI risk (cyber, tech E&O, D&O, GL)
title: Waive List
one_liner: A per-policy generative-AI footprint score plus an exclusion rules engine that lets a carrier waive CG 40 47 (or attach only CG 40 48, or a sublimit) for the ~60-70% of its book with little AI in the causal chain, and tells the reinsurer why.
upside_assumptions: (a) A filed rating variable that regulators accept (~20%); (b) treaty pressure forces reinsurers to demand the score (~20%); (c) incumbent data vendors do not bolt on a copy (~25%). All three plus ~60% share of the top 50 groups gets ~$45M, not $100M. Why-now also decays once affirmative AI cover becomes standard (2028-29).
deciding_reason: Small even in the upside, treaty premise unverified, and carriers' existing data vendors and plain application questions are the obvious substitutes.

pool: Cyber and liability premiums being carved out for generative-AI risk (cyber, tech E&O, D&O, GL)
title: Mirror Policy
one_liner: An exclusion-triggered difference-in-conditions (DIC) policy sitting beside a company's GL and umbrella program: it pays what the primary would have paid but for the gen-AI exclusion, priced as a percentage of the primary premium so the primary underwriter's pricing does the heavy lifting.
upside_assumptions: (a) ISO exclusions attach broadly to GL at 2027-28 renewals (~40%); (b) customer contracts force a buy-back (~50%); (c) reinsurers give casualty quota share with an AI cap despite no loss data (~35%). With 20-25% attach on ~$9B AI-exposed premium at 8% load, premium is $150-200M, MGA take ~$40-60M. $100M requires becoming an all-exclusion wrapper, a different thesis.
deciding_reason: Genuine unserved BI/PD gap, but the author's own math caps AI-only below $100M, primaries can sell back, and the wrap-everything stretch is a different, more crowded business.

pool: Cyber and liability premiums being carved out for generative-AI risk (cyber, tech E&O, D&O, GL)
title: Causation Desk
one_liner: A pre-agreed neutral panel that decides within 30 days whether a loss 'arose out of' generative AI, written into policies as an expert-determination clause like the appraisal clause in property policies.
upside_assumptions: An AAA-like neutral wins a handful of form-level adoptions: ~1,000 determinations x $18k = ~$18M. Needs the same scale of carrier adoption the pitch calls fragile, and carriers that prefer quiet denial to a published ruling on a form filed ~2,369 times are not natural buyers.
deciding_reason: Central legal analogy fails and the buyer prefers silence; at best a $10-20M expert-services practice.

pool: Cyber and liability premiums being carved out for generative-AI risk (cyber, tech E&O, D&O, GL)
title: Trigger
one_liner: An independent model-provider incident index and calculation agent, built on continuous probing of frontier-model behaviour, that serves as the trigger for parametric covers, industry-loss warranties and cat bonds on systemic AI events.
upside_assumptions: Parametrix-style economics extended to AI: a few $50-100M deals a year at 1-2% plus a ~$10M monitoring line. Requires investors to take correlated single-provider risk that CSA calls uninsurable, with no loss history.
deciding_reason: Occupied by Parametrix, and sized against a cat-bond market about 100x too small for the $5B referenced limit.

pool: US manufactured-home sales and chattel (personal-property) finance
title: Lot-Lender
one_liner: A chattel lender that lends only inside land-lease communities that sign a three-party agreement, so the park's lot-rent ledger becomes the credit file and the collection channel.
upside_assumptions: (1) 60-day lot-rent history predicts default materially better than FICO: unproven, perhaps 25% likely. (2) $150M equity and an $850M warehouse available: plausible, since Saluda, Pretium, Apollo and Forum money is flowing. (3) Exclusive agreements covering 100+ communities from operators who today also work with Zippy and 21st Mortgage: about 40% plausible. (4) Funding cost close to Clayton's: not plausible, so the edge must come from losses and approval rates.
deciding_reason: Park-lender contracts and a lender community channel already exist (21st Mortgage, Zippy), capital is flooding in (Pretium/Cascade, Saluda/Zippy), and the one new claim, that rent ledgers beat FICO, is untested.

pool: US manufactured-home sales and chattel (personal-property) finance
title: Open Lot
one_liner: A multi-brand retail chain built by buying independent dealers, with every lender competing for each buyer, in-house set crews, and the finance and insurance economics kept inside the chain.
upside_assumptions: (1) 25+ dealers bought at 0.3x sales or less while shipments are down 7.3% YTD: plausible in a downturn. (2) Multi-brand wholesale terms from plants that prefer their own stores: uncertain. (3) F&I reserve retained under state law: varies by state. (4) Four-lender waterfall raises approvals: weak, since independents already use several lenders. Revenue upside is plausible, profit upside is not.
deciding_reason: Revenue is easy but the moat is not: manufacturers with captive plants, lenders and cash are already buying the same independents, and independents already shop lenders. A distribution roll-up with thin margins.

pool: US manufactured-home sales and chattel (personal-property) finance
title: Park Shield
one_liner: A manufactured-home insurance program underwritten community by community, enrolled through the lease and paid in the monthly rent draft, so the insurer is paid first and the park enforces the mitigation that makes the risk insurable.
upside_assumptions: Both large REIT owners plus several regionals sign a default-enrollment addendum (about 60,000 policies at $1,100 = $65M premium), a fronting carrier and reinsurer agree to community-specific rating, and regulators accept mitigation credits. The REIT assumption is the weak link: they have in-house risk managers and are already being courted by MSI.
deciding_reason: MSI, backed by Baldwin Group, launched park-lease embedded insurance 18 days ago, Triad and others already sell it, and MGA commission cannot reach $100M of revenue.

pool: US manufactured-home sales and chattel (personal-property) finance
title: Park Utility Co
one_liner: A water and sewer utility for manufactured-home communities that buys or operates the failing private systems under the parks, rebuilds them with state and federal money plus rate-based financing, and bills a utility charge instead of a lot-rent spike.
upside_assumptions: A national program appears (PRICE appropriated at $225M a year, authorized to 2033 by Sec. 304 of P.L. 119-101 but proposed for elimination in FY2027) AND the firm wins a third of all park infrastructure grants AND moves into rate-based ownership with an infrastructure fund. The first condition is currently going the wrong way.
deciding_reason: The payer is one-time grants that are shrinking, a utility charge is a rent increase by another name, and even a third of visible grant money is about $50M.

pool: US manufactured-home sales and chattel (personal-property) finance
title: Covenant Parks
one_liner: An owner-operator that buys manufactured-home communities under a recorded covenant (capped rent growth, pre-granted resident right to buy, resident equity glide path), financed with agency tenant-protection loans.
upside_assumptions: (1) An anchor pension or insurer commits $200M+ at roughly 7-8% levered returns: unproven but the buyer pool exists, about 40% plausible. (2) Sellers aged 65+ in right-of-first-refusal states accept a covenant bid within about 5% of market for a clean closing: untested, 50% plausible. (3) Agency debt prices the covenant at least as well as tenant protections: likely. (4) 22 parks a year of sourcing: Havenpark-style roll-ups have done it with PE capital: plausible. Combined perhaps 15% for the upside.
deciding_reason: Real gap with no scaled for-profit covenant owner found, counter-positioned against REIT rent growth, tailwinds intensifying, and the $100M path survives at corrected numbers. Price-to-return is the open risk.

pick.title: Covenant Parks
pick.one_liner: A for-profit owner-operator of small and mid-size land-lease communities that records a rent-growth covenant and a resident buy option at closing, financed by agency tenant-protection debt and pension or insurer equity.
pick.sharpened_pitch: Covenant Parks is the first scaled for-profit owner-operator of small and mid-size land-lease communities that records a rent covenant at closing: increases capped at the lesser of CPI or 4% for 10 years, with documented capital-cost pass-through reviewed by a residents' association, plus a pre-agreed formula price and 90-day path for residents to buy, structured as an option that recycles our capital rather than an obligation. Delaware's CPI-linked cap produced large increases in 2022, so the ceiling is fixed. It is sold to three audiences. Sellers aged 65+ in right-of-first-refusal states (New York since Oct 2023, Maine since Sep 2025) get a clean, litigation-proof closing. Agency lenders get tenant-protection compliance built in; Fannie financed 19,808 pads with those protections in 2024. Pension and insurer capital gets stable lot-rent cash flow, no rent-gouging label, and a hedge against rent regulation. The $100M path is not shrunk: at $7,000 a site-year it needs about 14,300 sites (about 143 communities, 0.33% of 4.3M homesites), roughly $835M of assets and $290M of equity over 6-7 years, about 22 parks a year. The original pitch's $9.0-9.4k a site understated the sites needed by a third. Seller trust and the capital pool are the moat, not a limit on scale.
pick.payer_and_signer: Residents pay lot rent every month (existing budget line, about $7,000 a site-year in small parks). Signers: the selling owner or broker (right-of-first-refusal states), the investment committee of a pension, insurer or impact fund, and a Fannie or Freddie MHC lender for the debt.
pick.path_to_100m: $100M / $7,000 = about 14,300 sites = about 143 communities of 100 sites = 0.33% of 4.3M homesites. At Northmarq's Q1 2026 median of $58,400 a space that is about $835M of assets, about $290M of equity at 65% LTV, about 22 parks (about $125M) a year over 6-7 years. Median case $25M: about $75-80M of equity and 3,500 sites. Correction to the pitch: $9.0-9.4k a site is REIT-level rent (Sun $766 a month, ELS $956); small independent parks run $350-500 a month.
pick.competitors_and_edge: ROC USA (nonprofit, resident-led only, capital-constrained: $47M pool, $38.1M PRICE); NY MHAP (3% cap, subsidized debt for mission buyers); Minnesota grant covenants (5% cap, grants only); Fannie tenant protections (no cap); REITs and funds (Sun, ELS, UMH, Havenpark, Apollo $850M, OZ Impact) underwrite 5-6% rent growth and cannot promise caps. No for-profit covenant platform at scale found. Edge is counter-positioning plus seller trust in right-of-first-refusal states.
pick.why_now: Right-of-first-refusal laws in New York (Oct 2023) and Maine (Sep 2025, first use in Jay in 2026), a Pennsylvania 4% CPI-tied cap bill and a federal tenant bill pending, 2025 transaction volume up 47% (Berkadia), REIT rent growth of 5.2-5.6% fueling backlash, and agencies already pricing tenant protections.
pick.moat: Counter-positioning (REITs cannot match a cap without cutting guided rent growth), cornered resource (seller and resident trust in right-of-first-refusal states), and pre-compliance if states cap rents. Thin until sellers are shown to accept a covenant bid.
pick.biggest_open_risk: Price-to-return: a buyer capped near 4% bids against REITs and funds underwriting 5-6% growth at about a 6% cap rate, and impact capital that accepts below-market returns already goes to ROC USA near 1%. Whether a pension and insurer pool accepts about 7-8% levered returns at $290M scale is unproven.
pick.cheapest_next_test: Within 30 days: underwrite five live New York and Maine listings with and without the cap and compute the bid gap to market; get written answers from a Fannie or Freddie MHC lender on covenant pricing and from three pension or insurer allocators on a 7-8% target at $50M+ tickets; ask 20 sellers aged 65+ via brokers whether a covenant bid within 5% of market with a clean closing wins. Success: three LOIs and one allocator term sheet. Cost under $30k.

pool: US manufactured-home sales and chattel (personal-property) finance
title: Deposit Bridge
one_liner: A credit-union service organization that gives member credit unions a turnkey chattel program (origination, underwriting standard, servicing, repossession and title in every state) and a participation market, so deposit funding finally reaches manufactured-home loans.
upside_assumptions: Hundreds of credit unions each clear ALCO and board approval, commit capital to the CUSO, and shift chattel from half a percent to a large share of originations within about eight years. Credit unions are slow and have little chattel appetite today, so this is implausible.
deciding_reason: Credit unions already have a top-five chattel lender and Triad markets to them; the $6B managed book is unsourced and heroic. Even a $3B book yields about $55M.

pool: US manufactured-home sales and chattel (personal-property) finance
title: Title I Reborn
one_liner: A Ginnie Mae manufactured-home MBS issuer that aggregates FHA Title I chattel loans from credit unions, banks and non-Berkshire lenders, giving the roughly half of the market Berkshire does not fund a government-guaranteed funding path now, and a GSE exit later if the pilots happen.
upside_assumptions: Would need Congress or HUD to remove the 10% portfolio cap and pay full-loss claims, FHA premiums low enough to price below 8.5%, and non-Berkshire lenders to switch en masse. The enacted P.L. 119-101 Title I changes (higher limits, 30-year max term, lease flexibility) do not appear to touch the cap in the bill text I read, so none of this is in motion.
deciding_reason: Premise is false on primary data: Ginnie manufactured-housing MBS is only $92M and shrinking, and Title I cover is capped at 10% of a lender's portfolio, so it does not convert chattel into a Treasury-linked asset.

pool: US manufactured-home sales and chattel (personal-property) finance
title: Keyring
one_liner: A fund-backed landlord that buys new HUD-code homes at fleet prices, places them on vacant pads in other people's communities under a three-party agreement, and offers a rent-to-own path to residents the lenders denied.
upside_assumptions: (1) About 6,500 homes ($620M of assets) financed with 70-75% debt in a market without agency debt for scattered-site fleets: uncertain. (2) Fleet pricing meaningfully below Census retail prices ($88-91k single-section): plausible with underused plants. (3) Residents denied chattel credit can carry $1,000 plus lot rent: doubtful. (4) Parks agree to remit home rent: possible but adds counterparty risk.
deciding_reason: Works inside REIT parks; outside them it adds park-remittance risk, rent-to-own law exposure and a thin spread, and 21st Mortgage already funds infill for park owners.

pool: Private-school-choice money: state ESAs, vouchers, tax-credit scholarships, plus the federal tax-credit scholarship starting 2027
title: National ESA provider network (Forage + CAQH + Headway for ESA vendors)
one_liner: A payer-agnostic provider credential, one-invoice billing to every ESA/scholarship wallet, and two-day payout for the tutors, therapists, pod leaders and curriculum sellers who get paid from choice dollars in every state.
upside_assumptions: (1) Two or more large states accept the network credential as a pre-check: low-to-moderate, no ESA precedent (closest analog is the FSMB Uniform Application for physicians, which works because boards agreed). (2) A large share of about 40,000 providers pay $60 a month: moderate. (3) A fast-pay premium sells even though platforms pay in 2-10 days: low.
deciding_reason: Payers own vendor lists by statute, payout is already 2-10 days, and the realistic ceiling is about $40M even if states cooperate.

pool: Private-school-choice money: state ESAs, vouchers, tax-credit scholarships, plus the federal tax-credit scholarship starting 2027
title: School payments and capital OS (Toast for private schools and microschools)
one_liner: Multi-payer tuition acceptance with automatic reconciliation, next-day payout, and working-capital advances repaid by sweeping scheduled ESA/SGO payments through a wallet partner.
upside_assumptions: (1) A wallet platform grants payment-direction or sweep rights: low-to-moderate, platforms sell to states and may refuse. (2) A $300M+ cost-of-funds facility at around 8% appears: moderate. (3) 4,000-6,000 schools adopt a non-FACTS payment stack: low, FACTS owns the school relationship. (4) FACTS/Nelnet does not copy it despite having the schools and balance sheet: low.
deciding_reason: Real pain but half the cash is front-loaded, no assignable receivable, and FACTS/Nelnet owns the schools and a balance sheet. Upside depends on platforms' cooperation.

pool: Private-school-choice money: state ESAs, vouchers, tax-credit scholarships, plus the federal tax-credit scholarship starting 2027
title: K-12 education wallet and custody (HealthEquity for scholarship dollars)
one_liner: A bank-partnered wallet for the 600-700 new SGOs: they move scholarship dollars into it on day one (counted as 'spent' for the 90% test), it holds them until families spend, pays vendors directly, and shares the yield.
upside_assumptions: (1) Federal-credit giving reaches $11-26B, 2-5x Arizona's mature per-capita rate: low-to-moderate. (2) One wallet wins about 30% against ClassWallet, FACTS, ACE and Odyssey: low-to-moderate. (3) Final rule keeps transfer-equals-spent treatment: moderate (comments close 1 Dec, hearing 15 Dec). (4) SGO boards accept the wallet keeping a defined share of float, despite the earnings-must-be-spent rule: moderate-to-low. (5) Sponsor bank and KYB for 600-700 small nonprofits can be built self-serve: moderate.
deciding_reason: Best premise and ceiling, but median is about $13M and $100M needs Treasury-scale giving, about 30% share and contested yield retention together.

pool: Private-school-choice money: state ESAs, vouchers, tax-credit scholarships, plus the federal tax-credit scholarship starting 2027
title: SGO host (Fidelity Charitable for scholarships)
one_liner: A registered multi-state SGO that hosts branded affiliate funds for dioceses, school associations and networks that want their own donors but cannot run 25F compliance.
upside_assumptions: (1) Branded affiliate funds get a clean legal opinion and Treasury blessing: moderate. (2) A neutral host beats ACE's donor base and brand: low. (3) Large dioceses and associations cede brand and donor files to a third party: low. (4) $1.25B hosted: low.
deciding_reason: Already done: ACE's EmpowerEd is a free white-label host for the same affiliates with a 25-year donor base. Upside under $40M.

pool: Private-school-choice money: state ESAs, vouchers, tax-credit scholarships, plus the federal tax-credit scholarship starting 2027
title: Neutral eligibility and anti-duplication clearinghouse (National Student Clearinghouse for K-12 scholarships)
one_liner: A consent-based ledger of who was awarded what for which expense across SGOs, state ESAs and vouchers, plus a reusable eligibility credential verified once.
upside_assumptions: (1) Treasury treats a shared registry as a 'reasonable procedure' or states mandate it: low. (2) Competing platforms share award data: low, they are rivals and wallets already satisfy the safe harbor. (3) 30 states each pay about $1M for analytics: low, Arizona's Treasurer says fraud monitoring is not her office's job. (4) Treasury-scale recipients (5M): low-to-moderate.
deciding_reason: The rule's wallet safe harbor bundles duplicate control, the recipient base is small, and payers have no budget line; NSC's analog took 30 years.

pool: Private-school-choice money: state ESAs, vouchers, tax-credit scholarships, plus the federal tax-credit scholarship starting 2027
title: Family-facing funding stack and net-price front door (Common App for choice dollars)
one_liner: One free application and net-price screen that shows a family every ESA, voucher, SGO scholarship and school aid it qualifies for, school by school, and submits once; paid per funded student by SGOs and per enrolled student by schools.
upside_assumptions: (1) SGOs outsource applicant intake and income verification to a third party they do not control: low. (2) Applicant supply binds after the 90% test starts, so SGOs pay for leads: moderate. (3) Schools pay $300 per enrolled student at scale versus FACTS and Niche: moderate. (4) 55% of funded students route through it: low.
deciding_reason: A funnel, not a business: FACTS Grant & Aid, FACTS Compass and ACE already route families, SGOs get applicants from schools and parishes, and the idea concedes it feeds ideas 3 and 5.

pool: Private-school-choice money: state ESAs, vouchers, tax-credit scholarships, plus the federal tax-credit scholarship starting 2027
title: Permitted-seat platform (E-occupancy landlord and turnkey seats)
one_liner: Convert closing school buildings and church education wings into permitted 100-seat schools once, then sell turnkey seats to microschool operators on long leases backed by the ESA and SGO payment stream.
upside_assumptions: (1) Texas funds the waitlist and keeps funding through 2030: moderate. (2) Operators sign long leases at about $2,900 a seat, 28% of the award: moderate-to-low for 20-student microschools. (3) $0.7-1.6B of real-estate capital raised at a 6-7% cap: low-to-moderate. (4) Permitting process power is real and not easily copied by Primer or churches: low.
deciding_reason: Real capacity shortage but revenue is rent on about $1.6B of real estate, Primer already sells such buildings, and demand depends on one state's budget.

pool: Private-school-choice money: state ESAs, vouchers, tax-credit scholarships, plus the federal tax-credit scholarship starting 2027
title: Credit concierge (free planning tool for tax professionals and payroll, paid by SGOs)
one_liner: Make a $1,700 gift to a scholarship organization cost the donor nothing by planning it with their CPA or payroll team: capacity, state-credit stacking, W-4 offset and payroll deduction.
upside_assumptions: (1) Federal-credit giving reaches $5B or more: moderate in 2030. (2) A free CPA tool changes where donors give, not just whether: low, giving follows parish, school and denomination affinity. (3) SGOs accept 5-6% fees when ACE's partner share is 3%: low. (4) 30% intermediation: low. (5) Payroll plus W-4 Step 3 cash-neutral pattern is tolerated by Treasury and employers: low (unendorsed, unsourced).
deciding_reason: Channel is already addressed by ACE's advisor partner programme at 3%, donors give by affinity not accountant choice, and 6% is too heavy for a 10% overhead.

pool: US banks' and credit unions' spend on core, digital-banking and processing vendors (Fiserv, FIS, Jack Henry)
title: Parity
one_liner: A fixed-price, date-certain conversion assurance and migration engine that rebuilds how an institution actually runs (from configs, exam findings, tickets, call recordings, staff walk-throughs), proves account-by-account parity before cutover, and keeps every source-to-target mapping as a reusable library.
upside_assumptions: (a) boards and examiners come to expect independent parity proof (no rule requires it; low-moderate); (b) vendors give data-dictionary access despite lock-in incentives (moderate); (c) $250-350k price holds above $1B in assets (moderate); (d) ~30% of ~300 sizable events a year (low-moderate); (e) challenger cores license it per live bank rather than build (low, since Thought Machine and 10x already partner or build); (f) insurer-funded warranty gets agreed (unproven). The idea itself says $100M needs Sunset, which is dead.
deciding_reason: Real but small: conversion budgets cap per-event fees at about 10% of all-in cost, vendors and challengers are building AI migration themselves, and the Sunset volume it depends on is dead. Upside about $60M.

pool: US banks' and credit unions' spend on core, digital-banking and processing vendors (Fiserv, FIS, Jack Henry)
title: Tenancy
one_liner: Run the whole back office of several hundred small credit unions on one multi-tenant stack with shared specialists, so each keeps its own board, brand and charter and pays per member per month instead of per institution plus six salaries.
upside_assumptions: (a) 100-120 CUs at ~$550k by year 7 (low-moderate; CU*Answers took decades); (b) AI workflows keep a 40-50% cost edge over in-house staff (moderate); (c) examiners accept a shared BSA seat (uncertain; board names the officer); (d) boards decide in under 18 months (low); (e) $30-60M for a multi-tenant stack from anchor CUs or venture (moderate).
deciding_reason: Best-structured idea and demand is proven, but the proof is incumbents: CU*Answers and Aux/CU Service Network already do it, and $100M means out-scaling a 50-year-old CUSO in six years. Upside about $65M.

pool: US banks' and credit unions' spend on core, digital-banking and processing vendors (Fiserv, FIS, Jack Henry)
title: Quorum
one_liner: A free price-and-peer engine for bank and CU executives (what did a $2B bank on DNA actually pay and get?) built from banks' own invoices and contract abstracts, paid for by vendors who buy disclosed, qualified shortlist slots, with committed-volume group buying as phase two.
upside_assumptions: Needs most competitive decisions routed through the platform (low), vendors paying 6% of first-year contract value instead of per-lead prices (low), and group buying reaching 100+ FIs per vendor block (moderate but unproven). All three would have to hold.
deciding_reason: Author concedes likely dead standalone; consultants and Paladin already own the pricing data and sell to the bank side; vendor-paid lead budgets are small. Small even in the upside.

pool: US banks' and credit unions' spend on core, digital-banking and processing vendors (Fiserv, FIS, Jack Henry)
title: Sunset
one_liner: Outcome-priced migration as a service for the incumbents themselves: a fixed price per account moved from a platform the vendor wants to retire onto its strategic platform, with a no-churn guarantee, so Fiserv, FIS or Jack Henry can finally prune the second and third cores they carry.
upside_assumptions: Needs a vendor to announce a dated sunset and outsource it (low, vendor says the opposite), a successful retention guarantee (moderate), and a second vendor as a customer (low; FIS and Jack Henry have announced no sunset).
deciding_reason: The vendor tried this sunset, lost clients, and publicly renounced it; one buyer; no announced retirement anywhere. The premise that makes it big is false.

pool: US banks' and credit unions' spend on core, digital-banking and processing vendors (Fiserv, FIS, Jack Henry)
title: Books of Record
one_liner: A vendor-neutral, always-on copy of the bank's ledger and customer records, built from the core's own journals and owned by the bank. It gives 24/7 balance truth and stand-in processing for instant payments, then feeds data and AI, then becomes the control that lets any new core take accounts in cohorts.
upside_assumptions: Cores expose journals or events and contracts allow it (unproven, vendors charge for extracts); instant-payment volume grows 10x so stand-in matters (moderate, 2-3 years); regulators treat a neutral replica as part of exit plans (moderate); banks trust a startup as ledger of record (low); challengers pay per live bank (moderate).
deciding_reason: Crowded sidecar category with funded players, small current instant-payment volume, and the expansion step is just becoming a core. Upside about $45M.

pool: US banks' and credit unions' spend on core, digital-banking and processing vendors (Fiserv, FIS, Jack Henry)
title: Day One
one_liner: Move each customer's financial graph (bill-pay payees and schedules, direct deposits, card-on-file tokens, external-account links, alerts, Zelle/P2P enrolment) before conversion day, so there is no re-enrolment cliff and first-month attrition collapses.
upside_assumptions: Invisible-connection breakage is the main cause of attrition (author's inference, untested; plausible); old and new vendors cooperate with data capture (moderate); the digital-banking vendors do not bundle it themselves (low-moderate, Alkami and Q2 already partner); a primary-account switching rail adds $36M against funded switchers (low).
deciding_reason: Attrition pain is real but the connections leg is sold by funded switchers inside the digital vendors, and sizable M&A events number about 100 a year. Best as a module of a larger offer; upside about $40M.

pool: US banks' and credit unions' spend on core, digital-banking and processing vendors (Fiserv, FIS, Jack Henry)
title: Switchboard
one_liner: Open-book, cost-plus debit and card processing for banks and CUs under $10B, with pre-certified multi-network routing so no community institution depends on one network owner, plus an optional cooperative-equity layer for FIs that want to own the plumbing.
upside_assumptions: Win ~500 FIs at renewal cycles of 5-7 years (low-moderate); open-book margin of ~$0.035 holds against price cuts by Fiserv, FIS and cooperatives (low-moderate); a seller and capital for an Accel-sized routing layer (low, since sale is doubtful); Visa/Mastercard certification and BIN sponsorship done on time (moderate).
deciding_reason: Cleanest payer and a credible audit wedge, but the cooperative layer and cost-based pricing already exist (Velera, SHAZAM), consultants sell the audit, and the net margin is assumed. Upside about $60M.

pool: US banks' and credit unions' spend on core, digital-banking and processing vendors (Fiserv, FIS, Jack Henry)
title: Bureau
one_liner: Buy the independent bank and CU processors, and the pieces Fiserv wants to shed, whose 7-10-year contracts and high retention are the asset; consolidate them on one AI-run stack; run them at the incumbents' margin.
upside_assumptions: A sponsor commits ~$500M after a track record (low for a first-time team); sellers available at 4-5x revenue and outbid Centerbridge/Bridgeport/Veritas (low-moderate); client banks consent to change of control without churn (moderate); an AI-run single stack cuts cost to serve enough to earn returns (unproven, depends on the weak Parity engine).
deciding_reason: A financing play in a space deep-pocketed PE already works; multiples are double the pitch; the edge is capital, not product. Not a venture a founder can start.

pool: US graduate-school borrowing displaced from Grad PLUS (private lending gap)
title: Gap Ledger
one_liner: A cap-gap ledger for graduate deans that shows each admitted student's remaining federal headroom and the exact buydown dollars needed to keep them, then lets the school buy one fixed per-loan fee for a program-wide fixed rate from a competing lender panel.
upside_assumptions: 500 programs at $40k software (implausible against free lender tools, Workday and in-house RFPs) plus the full $12M desk number (needs schools to buy ~$2B of buydowns; low plausibility) = ~$35M. Reaching $100M needs the Factory's book, which is a different business.
deciding_reason: A feature with free substitutes (lender calculators, Workday cap logic, Juno, in-house RFPs), and the entire school buydown fee pool is smaller than the revenue target. The $100M is another idea's balance sheet.

pool: US graduate-school borrowing displaced from Grad PLUS (private lending gap)
title: Seasoning Factory
one_liner: A bank-partnered, on-balance-sheet buyer of outcome-based graduate loans from many small originators on one tape standard, funded by insurer term notes and a first-loss slice, that builds the performance record ABS investors say they need.
upside_assumptions: (1) Raise ~$100M+ first-loss capital for an unproven conduit (low to moderate). (2) Sign 8-10 originators who would otherwise sell to KKR or Nelnet and keep brand and servicing (low to moderate). (3) Insurers take ~$0.9B of 10-15 year notes (moderate). (4) Outcome-based loans perform; Ascent's own ABS shows higher-than-expected losses (unknown). Gross interest of $150M is reachable; net is the honest number.
deciding_reason: Best of pool and a genuine capital-and-data gap, but no verified edge over Nelnet, KKR and Ascent's own ABS, and net revenue upside (~$55M) is about half the bar. First-loss capital is a precondition, not an outcome.

pool: US graduate-school borrowing displaced from Grad PLUS (private lending gap)
title: Offer-Backed
one_liner: In-school graduate loans for clinicians underwritten on a hospital's no-clawback hiring commitment, repaid first from the paycheck and priced off the hospital's credit, paid for out of the contingent-labor budget the hospital would otherwise give to staffing agencies.
upside_assumptions: (1) Courts leave the professional-degree stay lifted, restoring the PT and nursing gap (uncertain, ED vows to defend). (2) Hospitals pay a $5k per-hire fee for in-school financing, competing with Clasp (moderate; cheap vs recruiter fees). (3) A lender actually prices off a no-recourse pledge (low; no source found). (4) 3,000-8,000 financed hires a year (low; far above Clasp's observable traction).
deciding_reason: Carrot-only employer design is a real insight, but the lending half rests on an unsupported credit claim, the employer half belongs to funded incumbent Clasp, and volumes are unsourced.

pool: US graduate-school borrowing displaced from Grad PLUS (private lending gap)
title: Operator Rail
one_liner: Sell graduate financing to the few operators that run most cap-exposed online and health-professions programs, fund it as a per-start conversion fee from their marketing budgets, and become the lender of record behind their programs.
upside_assumptions: Win 3-4 anchor operator contracts despite Adtalem having already contracted Sallie Mae (low), with enough above-cap graduate starts (unproven) and a capital partner that bears the tail (moderate). Even then fee revenue is tens of millions at most.
deciding_reason: The anchor operator already announced a Sallie Mae loan-cap partnership with a capital syndicate, and the above-cap graduate starts needed for $100M cannot be shown.

pool: US graduate-school borrowing displaced from Grad PLUS (private lending gap)
title: Program Score Exchange
one_liner: A neutral exchange where lenders contribute loan performance tapes and schools contribute consented alumni earnings, and ABS investors, rating agencies, schools and lenders buy program-level scores no single lender can publish; the 'FICO for programs' NBER says is missing.
upside_assumptions: Most active lenders pool tapes with competitors (low, legally exposed), rating agencies pay six-figure to seven-figure data fees (low), and a quarter or more of 1,500 schools buy at $30k despite free federal data (low).
deciding_reason: Too few payers, free federal substitutes, and a revenue sum that assumes near-universal adoption and unusually high data fees.

pool: US graduate-school borrowing displaced from Grad PLUS (private lending gap)
title: Employer-Cohort Cap-Fit
one_liner: Graduate programs priced at or under the $20,500 federal annual limit so no private debt is needed, recruited through hospital and district employers instead of paid marketing, with the university granting the degree and the platform running curriculum, clinical placement and cohorts for a fee.
upside_assumptions: Land 30+ employer-cohort programs at ~400 students each (low; competes with WGU and Guild at the same price), keep a 17% services fee that survives incentive-compensation scrutiny (moderate), and employers keep sending cohorts (moderate).
deciding_reason: The cap-fit price already exists at scale (WGU with hospital partners), the OPM model is the one that is failing, and $100M needs 100+ programs.

pool: US graduate-school borrowing displaced from Grad PLUS (private lending gap)
title: Earnings Replica
one_liner: For each graduate program, an alumni-consented replica of ED's earnings test built from tax transcripts and payroll data 12-18 months before ED's own determination, with student warnings and program-restructuring support.
upside_assumptions: ~500 schools buy at $50k to avoid losing Direct Loans (low; only ~6% of programs are at risk) and consented alumni data reaches statistical validity (low; self-selected samples, response rates unproven).
deciding_reason: ED already published the program-level estimates free, the consent-based sample is statistically weak and IVES-constrained, and only ~6% of programs are exposed.

pool: US graduate-school borrowing displaced from Grad PLUS (private lending gap)
title: Verified-Pay Part-Timer
one_liner: Graduate loans for working adults employed in their field, underwritten on verified payroll and repaid first through a voluntary direct-deposit split, with in-school interest paid from salary so balances do not capitalize.
upside_assumptions: Win ~20% of displaced part-time borrowers (heroic; over the 20% share flag), keep losses near 1.5% on unsecured graduate debt (unproven), and borrowers leave the payroll split on (low; revocable). Capital for a $1B book is a precondition.
deciding_reason: Capital-heavy unsecured lending with unsourced volume, no moat (payroll APIs are sold to all lenders), and net upside around $25M.

pool: England social landlords' repairs and maintenance spend (housing associations, Awaab's Law era)
title: One Knock: the annual home check that replaces six statutory visits and fixes what it finds
one_liner: A two-ticket technician team does the gas check, electrical test, alarm test, a 29-hazard screen and small fixes in one 75-minute visit a year, so the landlord pays for one access attempt and starts no legal clock it cannot meet.
upside_assumptions: 15-20 mid-size landlords' combined lots won on price against Sureserve/Mears (low-moderate plausibility); dual-ticket staff retained (moderate); 25-30% lower visit count proven (same claim Sureserve already makes); fix revenue materialises (unproven).
deciding_reason: The one-visit bundle is already sold by Sureserve and tendered as combined lots; EICR cycle mismatch and a nearly spent catch-up wave leave thin differentiation.

pool: England social landlords' repairs and maintenance spend (housing associations, Awaab's Law era)
title: Hot-Spot Contract: capitated root-cause care for the worst 5-8% of homes
one_liner: Take a fixed annual fee per home for every repair, disrepair claim and root-cause fix on a landlord's highest-cost homes, guarantee the fix for five years, and keep the savings.
upside_assumptions: Top 5% homes carry at least 25% of repair spend (likely, unproven); 15-20 landlords hand over 1,500-2,500 homes each within six years (low plausibility without three reference pilots); reinsurer prices the tail on a shared dataset after 12-24 months (plausible); framework call-offs avoid 12-18 month tenders (plausible).
deciding_reason: Only idea where no one was found taking capitated risk on the costliest homes; budget lines exist, skew is plausible, and a data/reinsurance asset gives a scale route; kill test still open.

pick.from_title: Hot-Spot Contract: capitated root-cause care for the worst 5-8% of homes
pick.title: Hot-Spot Contract: capitated root-cause care for the costliest homes
pick.one_liner: Take a fixed annual fee per home for every repair, disrepair-defence cost share and root-cause fix on a landlord's costliest 5-8% of homes, buy stop-loss cover on the tail, and keep the savings.
pick.sharpened_pitch: Sell it as a capitated service contract, not an insurance-style guarantee. For the costliest 5-8% of a landlord's homes (ranked by three-year trailing cost of repairs, disrepair and compensation), the contractor takes every repair, a share of disrepair defence cost and the root-cause works (ventilation, roof, leak, heating controls) for a fixed fee of about 80% of trailing cost. The 'five-year guarantee' is simply the capitation running five years; the contractor buys its own stop-loss reinsurance, which keeps it outside the FSMA insurance perimeter. The landlord stays the duty holder for Awaab clocks, so the contractor runs them under delegation and claims-defence savings are shared, not guaranteed. Enter through a framework call-off or a below-threshold pilot, because registered providers are generally contracting authorities under the Procurement Act 2023 and a standalone multi-year tender takes 12-18 months. Make the cross-landlord loss dataset (job-level cost, cause, recurrence) the scaling asset: after 12-24 months it prices building risk better than any single landlord can, which supports reinsurance and later a carrier-fronted product. Use two payer lines: repairs spend plus the disrepair legal budget, with root-cause works capitalised. Do not narrow to damp only; the cohort is defined by cost, whatever the cause.
pick.payer_and_signer: Finance Director and Director of Assets sign; funded from responsive repairs plus disrepair, compensation and legal budgets, with root-cause works capitalised. CEO and board approve the multi-year contract.
pick.path_to_100m: 35,000 homes x GBP2,200 capitated fee = GBP77M (about $100M). That is about 16% of a 220,000-home cohort (5% of 4.4M homes), 0.8% of all stock, roughly 15-20 landlords at 1,500-2,500 homes each, or about three Mears-Thurrock-sized annual contract values (GBP24M a year each; Thurrock home count unverified). If skew follows the old 80/20 record, cohort cost per home is above the GBP2,800 assumed and fewer homes are needed. Net margin 12-18% plus shared savings.
pick.competitors_and_edge: Mobysoft RepairSense and Switchee sell analytics/sensors and take no risk; primes (Mears, Osborne, Wates) sell whole-stock price-per-property or total-asset contracts, not a worst-homes carve-out with repeat-repair accountability. Edge: outcome pay on the cohort where patching is most profitable for incumbents, plus a cross-landlord loss dataset and reinsurance relationships no one else holds.
pick.why_now: Awaab's Law phase 2 goes live 30 Nov 2026 and makes repeat failures a s.10A breach with County Court damages; fixed recoverable costs stay off disrepair until at least Oct 2028; Ombudsman findings cite temporary fixes and poor diagnosis; landlords' interest-cover covenants favour capitalised fixes over revenue patches.
pick.moat: Cornered data asset (job-level cost, cause and recurrence across landlords that prices building risk), reinsurance relationships, 5-year contracts with switching costs, and counter-positioning against visit-based pay. Honest limit: none exists until three or more cohorts have 12-24 months of data.
pick.biggest_open_risk: The skew premise is unproven at cost level (only an old KPMG 80/20 via Oxford and Leicester repeat-repair counts), landlords may refuse job-level data or a carve-out from existing total-asset contracts, and a five-year uncapped guarantee could be treated as insurance if not structured as a service contract.
pick.cheapest_next_test: In 6-8 weeks at analyst cost only: obtain three years of job-level repair and disrepair cost data from three landlords (direct, or FOI to councils with in-house records) and measure the share of spend carried by the top 5% of homes. Stop if the top 5% carry under 15% in two of three, or if no landlord will release job-level data. Then ask two landlords whether their current repairs contract permits a cohort carve-out.

pool: England social landlords' repairs and maintenance spend (housing associations, Awaab's Law era)
title: Clock Desk: pay per closed Awaab case, not per hour
one_liner: A vetted assessor network and a case desk run the entire statutory clock (intake, 10-day investigation, 3-day summary, 5-day make-safe, 12-week works, early settlement of any claim) for a fixed price per closed case, with a pooled fund behind the deadlines.
upside_assumptions: Phases 2 and 3 widen clocked hazards (certain but already priced into current volumes); private renting added (no date; consultation opened 9 Oct 2026 per search summary, unverified); landlords outsource whole cases rather than buy software or frameworks (low plausibility).
deciding_reason: Case count is 3-5x too high on real data, the idea's own path is heroic share, and frameworks, law-firm tools and in-house teams already occupy the space.

pool: England social landlords' repairs and maintenance spend (housing associations, Awaab's Law era)
title: Home Safety Technician Guild: the scarce input behind every other idea
one_liner: A landlord- and levy-backed guild trains career changers into dual-ticket home-safety technicians (gas plus electrical plus hazard screening) and bills hours under take-or-pay offtake from landlords and primes with funded backlogs.
upside_assumptions: Landlords sign take-or-pay hour offtake (not how the sector buys; low plausibility); levy transfers fund training (capped at 50% and rules changed 1 Aug 2026); shortage persists and no one poaches (moderate).
deciding_reason: Already done by employers and academies, no scale asset beyond headcount, and the idea itself concedes a weak moat that dies if the shortage eases.

pool: England social landlords' repairs and maintenance spend (housing associations, Awaab's Law era)
title: Void Clock: the one party paid for the days between tenants
one_liner: A fixed price per void, a 35-day target against today's 74, and a payment that moves with the days, with the provider owning the whole chain: certificates, asbestos, works, clear, clean, inspection, keys and lettings handover.
upside_assumptions: Win about 14 landlords at 1,400 voids each (moderate-low); prove step-level days savings versus prime bundles (moderate); landlords restructure to a voids-only lot (moderate; voids-only frameworks exist); avoid being copied by primes who already bundle voids (low).
deciding_reason: Real budget line and signer, but bundled fixed-rate voids and void KPIs already exist, the days gap is smaller on the right baseline, and most revenue is pass-through works with no moat beyond process.

pool: England social landlords' repairs and maintenance spend (housing associations, Awaab's Law era)
title: Decant Reserve: idle void days and block-leased units as the supply landlords and councils cannot trade
one_liner: A licensed, furnished stock of void-gap homes and leased apartments that landlords call on for Awaab decants and councils call on as temporary accommodation overflow, priced under nightly-paid hotels.
upside_assumptions: A large share of void days is lettable but unlet (unsourced, 10-25% guess); nominations, VAT, insurance and licence status blocks are solved (low plausibility); councils keep paying nightly rates rather than moving to leases (contradicted by Brent/Oxford/Westminster).
deciding_reason: In-pool market is tiny and already served by own-void licences; the $100M path needs temporary accommodation, where institutional capital and long leases are crowding out nightly-paid void-gap supply.

pool: England social landlords' repairs and maintenance spend (housing associations, Awaab's Law era)
title: Falls on a Clock: standard adaptations delivered inside the Awaab deadline
one_liner: From 30 Nov 2026 a handrail, stair, bath or level-access failure for an older tenant is a clocked hazard (make-safe in 5 working days, fuller works within 12 weeks); a phone-based trusted-assessor protocol and standard kits replace an occupational-therapy queue that runs to 8 months.
upside_assumptions: Councils hand DFG minor-works streams to a new provider (low plausibility; council-controlled, 5-7 year contracts); trusted-assessor protocol adopted by OT services (moderate); landlords treat adaptations as a clocked hazard (low).
deciding_reason: Small in-pool, the DFG bridge is council-controlled and thin-margin, and the one proof point (Millbrook) is mis-cited.

pool: England social landlords' repairs and maintenance spend (housing associations, Awaab's Law era)
title: Whole-Home Once: one disturbance per home instead of five component programmes
one_liner: A factory-made interior service core (kitchen and bath, ventilation, electrics, heating controls, alarms, handrails) fitted in 5 working days with the tenant in place, sold at a fixed price per home archetype and capitalised.
upside_assumptions: 8 archetypes cover most of a landlord's stock (unproven); occupied-home install in 5 days works at scale (unproven); working capital and bonding for a factory are raised (hard); sector offsite track record (Ilke, L&G Modular failed, from memory) is overcome (low plausibility).
deciding_reason: Real budget and a plausible visit-count insight, but offsite whole-home delivery has scaled slowly everywhere, the upside needs 5x Europe's annual pace, and execution/working-capital risk is severe.

pool: India: interest and fees households and small businesses pay on gold-backed loans (banks, NBFCs, informal)
title: Girvi Formalizer
one_liner: Buy the books, vaults and people of retiring pawnbrokers in Tier-3 towns, re-paper their customers into one RBI-regulated NBFC at roughly half the informal rate, and run each shop as an employee-staffed branch with an XRF reader and a shared ledger.
upside_assumptions: (1) A recurring supply of willing sellers: unproven, no seller-count data. (2) Ticket books pass diligence (realised loss under 0.5%, redemption over 85%): untested and the pitch's own kill switch. (3) $50M+ equity raised within three years: plausible only if (2) holds. (4) Bank lines at 10-11%: plausible. (5) No licensed-pawnbroker rate cap blocking the borrower saving: unverified. Reaching $100M needs ~1,000 conversions, which is not credible top-decile for a startup.
deciding_reason: Biggest pool and no direct competitor, but the savings premise is unproven for rate-capped licensed pawnbrokers, the gold-book buyer field is crowded, and a competent upside is about $60M gross interest income.

pool: India: interest and fees households and small businesses pay on gold-backed loans (banks, NBFCs, informal)
title: Bullion-Bid
one_liner: A lender-neutral national bid layer that sells pledged gold when a loan goes bad, before or inside the Directions' auction, and lets stressed borrowers sell part of their gold to renew a loan instead of losing all of it.
upside_assumptions: (1) A genuine stress year with ~3% of stock reaching notice: contradicted by falling stage III and gold only ~18% below peak. (2) 20-40% of the flow despite lenders keeping auctions in-house: low plausibility. (3) Lenders pay for uplift above a rule-set 90% reserve floor: moderate. (4) Scrap-marketplace extension earns ~0.8% on ~5% of the $30-37B flow (~$14M): plausible but small.
deciding_reason: Auction flow tracks NPAs, which are falling; e-auction vendors and lender portals already exist; the pitch's own $100M needs 40% of a stress-year flow. Small even in the upside.

pool: India: interest and fees households and small businesses pay on gold-backed loans (banks, NBFCs, informal)
title: Karat Ledger
one_liner: An independent verification and record layer for pledged gold: instrument-backed assay evidence at the counter, surprise re-assay for the lender's own audit team, a shared appraiser track record, and a live collateral ledger that holds each pledge's LTV through its tenor (Persona/Socure-style per-event rail created by a liability-shifting mandate).
upside_assumptions: (1) Large lenders outsource evidence they now produce in-house: low plausibility. (2) System of record for ~25% of pledges plus per-loan fees (~$25M + ~$25M): needs LMS vendors not to bundle it. (3) Cross-lender appraiser data pooling clears DPDP Act and competition law: uncertain. (4) An insurer fronts a warranty that is real but small (~$10M): plausible.
deciding_reason: Real mandate and real appraiser fraud, but large lenders run in-house audit, LMS vendors already hold collateral records and XRF is cheap; the warranty line is inflated 10-50x. Tops out near $60M; the pool itself calls it a wedge.

pool: India: interest and fees households and small businesses pay on gold-backed loans (banks, NBFCs, informal)
title: Gold Float
one_liner: A revolving credit line on UPI secured by gold already in a lender's vault, charging interest only on days money is used and sweeping UPI inflows to repay it (Fuliza-style auto-overdraft plus control of the repayment channel).
upside_assumptions: (1) RBI extends UPI credit lines to NBFCs: no evidence, and The Ken reports RBI wants to curb NBFC revolving credit. (2) RBI tolerates revolving consumption lines against gold despite the 12-month bullet cap: unconfirmed. (3) Banks outsource a core product when Axis built its own: low plausibility. (4) 5% of the bank base drawn: optimistic.
deciding_reason: Axis built it in-house through its own Freecharge subsidiary; UPI credit lines are banks and SFBs only; revolving consumption lines conflict with the 12-month bullet cap. Small even in the upside.

pool: India: interest and fees households and small businesses pay on gold-backed loans (banks, NBFCs, informal)
title: Switch Desk
one_liner: A lender-neutral desk that moves gold borrowers from 20-48% lenders to 9-12% banks at the moment their loan matures, paid by the bank per completed switch plus a share of the borrower's first-year saving.
upside_assumptions: (1) Borrowers pay a 10% success fee: low plausibility, the pool flags it. (2) Banks pay 0.5-0.75% of principal for gold sourcing: unverified. (3) Banks stay capacity-constrained: they are already growing 105% a year without a desk. (4) NBFC pricing stays high: new entrants are pushing it down. (5) Maturity-timed triggers from bureau or Account Aggregator data under DPDP consent: feasible.
deciding_reason: Real price gap and a real maturity-date hook, but lenders already run balance transfers, the gap is smaller than pitched, fees are DSA-sized, and the honest upside is below $100M.

pool: India: interest and fees households and small businesses pay on gold-backed loans (banks, NBFCs, informal)
title: Co-Lend Exchange
one_liner: A neutral trust layer that lets banks fund gold loans originated and vaulted by NBFCs: independent collateral attestation, a shared ledger, the payment waterfall and LTV monitoring in one place.
upside_assumptions: (1) Several banks and NBFCs adopt one neutral ledger: low plausibility since NBFCs deal bilaterally and Muthoot prefers its own balance sheet. (2) 35 bps fee holds: unverified. (3) Gold co-lending volume grows ~35% a year (ICRA) and routes through the platform: optimistic.
deciding_reason: Author concedes it is dead stand-alone; bilateral gold co-lending and Yubi Co.Lend occupy it; 80:20 is the old model; $100M needs 45% of the NBFC book. Small even in the upside.

pool: India: interest and fees households and small businesses pay on gold-backed loans (banks, NBFCs, informal)
title: Renewal Wall Cure Desk
one_liner: An outcome-priced desk that gets lenders' borrowers through the renewal LTV test with the cheapest cure (pay-down, part-sale, transfer) instead of an auction, aimed at the dated cohort of peak-priced loans maturing in early 2027.
upside_assumptions: (1) Gold falls again by 15%+ before Jan-Apr 2027 renewals: possible but not the base case. (2) Lenders outsource cure work they do in-house and an NBFC earns interest on delay, so incentive is wrong: low plausibility. (3) 2% of stock needs a cure and 25% is handled: optimistic. (4) A third-party lender funds pay-downs without evergreening risk: workable.
deciding_reason: False premise: lower-of-30-day-average valuation means the one-day 29 Jan spike barely entered valuations, so the renewal shortfall is about 0-10%, not 12-23%; stress is not visible and the why-now window is short.

pool: India: interest and fees households and small businesses pay on gold-backed loans (banks, NBFCs, informal)
title: Gold Bay
one_liner: Pre-certified secure rooms in jewellery bazaars, leased to a lender as its own branch with the lender's employees inside, bundled with monitoring, assay kit, software and custody insurance and priced per year.
upside_assumptions: (1) Entrants need speed and cannot fit out themselves: contradicted by fast branch openings and acquisitions. (2) Lenders pay a premium for a pre-certified room: unproven, no cost data. (3) 30% share of the entrant wave: optimistic. (4) A leased exclusive bay qualifies as the lender's own branch: the author's make-or-break unknown; an ordinary lease already does.
deciding_reason: Strong-room fit-out is a commodity; entrants buy branches instead of building; the INR 9 lakh price is unsupported and $100M needs about 100% of the entrant wave.

pool: US enterprises' spend on offshore-delivered IT services (application development and maintenance, testing, infrastructure from Indian IT majors and captives)
title: The Meter: client-owned proof of what offshore vendors actually delivered
one_liner: A vendor-neutral system, owned by the client, that reads logs the client already holds (logins, tickets, commits, AI-gateway calls, invoices) to prove what offshore engineers delivered, clause by clause, and is paid mostly out of the savings it proves.
upside_assumptions: (1) Procurement names the Meter as neutral calculation agent in AI gain-share contracts: plausible but unproven, about 30%. (2) Clients grant read-only IdP/ITSM/commit telemetry: plausible for banks with a rebid pending. (3) Verified savings of 4-6%: unverified, no independent leakage study. (4) Fee levels above the ISG benchmark hold: doubtful. Together they support about $70M, not $100M.
deciding_reason: Governance, invoice validation and vendor-output measurement are already sold by ISG, Avasant, ServiceNow, CAST and BlueOptima at about 0.7% of spend; the novel telemetry join is real but is best an evidence layer, not a standalone $100M company.

pool: US enterprises' spend on offshore-delivered IT services (application development and maintenance, testing, infrastructure from Indian IT majors and captives)
title: Penny-Exact: independent proof that the AI-translated system behaves identically

title: The Middle: a sponsor-level AI-native maintenance utility for PE portfolios
one_liner: A private-equity sponsor signs one framework agreement and every portfolio company gets fixed-unit-price AI-native application maintenance and development from a shared pod, below the big Indian firms' minimum ticket and clean to carve out at exit.
upside_assumptions: (1) Six or more sponsors sign enforceable frameworks: heroic, about 10%. (2) Unit prices 40% below tier-2 hold as AI deflation continues: price pressure is real. (3) Clean-carve-out positioning sells without a safety record: unproven. (4) Ode and OpenAI DeployCo stay in transformation and do not move to run-and-maintain: uncertain.

title: Clawback: an IT-services contract recovery factory with claims financing
one_liner: A recovery-audit factory for IT-services contracts: find money vendors owe under rate cards, escalator caps, volume tiers, service-credit clauses and AI pass-through terms nobody enforces, take 20-30% of what comes back, and advance cash against signed credit memos.
upside_assumptions: (1) Measured recovery of 3% or more in the first ten audits: unproven, the idea's own test. (2) IT-specific rules library defeats generic auditors: thin, easily copied. (3) Vendors settle old claims inside renegotiations: plausible. (4) Credit facility advances at low loss: workable. Even stacked this stays under $100M.

title: Run-Base Shrinker: an energy-services company for the application estate
one_liner: We cut the run bill your offshore vendor is paid to maintain (repeat incidents, zombie applications, dead custom code), fund the engineering ourselves, and keep 30-50% of verified savings for three years.

(4) A lender finances the 36-month receivable tail: plausible. (5) About 12-15 new clients a year after year 2: demanding but not heroic.
deciding_reason: Only idea that reverses the buyer's incentive (paid from audited ledger savings, self-funding, vendor-neutral) with a named payer and a path to 6% of a $1.7B shared-savings pool; main risks are testable cheaply.

pick.one_liner: We fund the engineering that removes run cost from your application estate (zombie applications, dead custom code, licence and infrastructure right-sizing, then repeat incidents) and are paid 30-35% of audited reductions for 36 months.
pick.sharpened_pitch: An independent, vendor-neutral company that removes run cost from the application estate and is paid only from audited reductions in the client's ledger. We fund the engineering and take 30-35% of verified run-cost reduction for 36 months. Levers are sequenced by who controls the savings. First, client-controlled lines: zombie-application retirement, dead custom code removal before conversion, and licence, infrastructure and third-party support right-sizing, which cut real invoices without the offshore vendor's consent. Second, vendor-labor lines: AI root-cause repeat-incident elimination on unit-priced or soon-to-renew contracts, or with a co-negotiated baseline reset. The baseline is the contract's guaranteed AI pass-through, so we earn only beyond what the vendor already owes, which pre-empts the 'you are taking credit for AI deflation' objection. We publish an IT run-cost measurement-and-verification protocol (the analogue of the protocol energy-services companies use) co-signed by a Big 4 audit partner, with client-owned telemetry (identity, ticketing, commit logs) as evidence; that absorbs the Meter idea as the evidence layer. We sell through PE operating partners and CFOs under cost-take-out mandates who have no transformation budget, and finance the 36-month receivable tail with a specialty lender. Path: 79 clients at $1.26M a year, or about 110 at $0.9M, which is 6% of a roughly $1.7B shared-savings pool.
pick.payer_and_signer: CIO (run-cost budget owner) and CFO sign; Internal Audit signs the savings method; a PE operating partner or board cost-take-out mandate is the forcing function. The fee is paid out of the run-cost line being reduced, so no new budget is needed.
pick.path_to_100m: $30M offshore run base x 12% reduction over 3 years x 35% share = $1.26M per client-year, so 79 clients (about 5% of roughly 1,500 enterprises with $20M+ outsourced application spend; the 1,500 count and 12% reduction are estimates). Alternate: $22M base x 12% x 35% = $0.9M, so about 110 clients. Pool view: about $40B US run-related offshore spend x 12% x 35% = $1.68B, so $100M is 6%. Order of magnitude supported by Nasscom India IT services of about $149B.
pick.competitors_and_edge: Rimini Street ($421.5M revenue, flat; consulting-led root-cause work, not paid from savings), AMS vendors' self-funded transformation pitches (conflicted: they lose volume), ISG and Avasant governance (invoice validation, no engineering), app-retirement software (OpenText InfoArchive) and AI-native maintenance startups (AppFactor, LogicStar, DataAgent, Tessera: sell a cheaper replacement for the same volume). Edge: independence plus payment only from audited net reduction in the client's ledger, and a protocol Internal Audit can sign.
pick.why_now: ISG says providers are pricing deals on assumed AI savings that neither side can verify; clients want 25-30% cuts and the Cognizant CFO forecasts 25% of contracts renegotiated a year; AI makes root-cause fixes and code deletion cheap enough to fund on spec; SAP ECC mainstream maintenance ends Dec 31 2027 (extended maintenance to 2030).
pick.moat: Counter-positioning (the AMS vendor cannot copy it without cannibalizing its own revenue); a cross-client root-cause and retirement library; an auditor-accepted measurement protocol (process power); a 36-month contract tail; receivable financing as a balance-sheet edge.
pick.biggest_open_risk: Private-sector CFOs may refuse third-party shared savings (about 70% of commercial and industrial ESCO work is design-build, not performance contracting) and baseline disputes or vendor obstruction under FTE and volume-band contracts can erase measured savings.
pick.cheapest_next_test: Within 30-60 days, take historical ticket and CMDB exports from 3 unit-priced or soon-to-renew contracts under NDA and produce a repeat-ticket heatmap and zombie-application list with dollar values. Kill if addressable reduction is under 6% in the first three accounts, Internal Audit will not accept the method memo, or CFOs refuse any share above 20%.

pool: US enterprises' spend on offshore-delivered IT services (application development and maintenance, testing, infrastructure from Indian IT majors and captives)
title: Evergreen Release Utility: flat-price release remediation, Guidewire first

(4) Expansion to Salesforce, ServiceNow and Workday beats Copado, Provar, Opkey, Tricentis: crowded.
deciding_reason: Already contested by integrator factories, Guidewire-specific AI test tools and a $60M-funded Tessera; spend base looks inflated against $2.2M average ARR; upside tops out near $65M.

title: The Foundry: wholesale AI-native delivery for the incumbents
one_liner: Sell accountable, per-unit, AI-native delivery to the IT-services firms themselves, so they can meet 25-30% price cuts with variable cost instead of a pyramid they cannot restructure.
upside_assumptions: (1) A mid-tier anchor signs a multi-year unit contract: possible, no sign of one. (2) Client consent and data-residency clauses allow subcontracted AI delivery: unverified. (3) Foundry out-executes Cognition and Factory forward-deployed help that incumbents get already: doubtful. (4) Senior displaced engineers stay as pod partners: plausible.
deciding_reason: Counter-positioning logic is clever but incumbents are buying tools and embedded engineers directly; a single-anchor wholesale model tops out near $70M and sits on a delivery head's P&L.

title: Hot Spare: shadow-sourcing as a service
one_liner: Pay a second, AI-native provider to shadow-run 5-10% of your live application tickets so your exit plan is tested, your price is benchmarked, and a challenger already has a foothold on the day you rebid.
upside_assumptions: (1) Supervisors accept shadow-run as exit testing: not required by DORA, unverified. (2) Clients accept a duplicate-cost premium of 5-10% of the contract: doubtful. (3) Challenger vendors stay unpaid-pilot-starved and pay for access: plausible. (4) Two-sided network forms: slow. Upside stays well below $100M.
deciding_reason: The regulation requires tested exit plans, not a paid shadow vendor, so a cheap tabletop satisfies it; the buyer pays twice for the shadowed work and dual sourcing already exists; small even in the upside.

title: Dock Crews with a Turn-Time Guarantee
one_liner: Sell distribution-center docks a guaranteed 30-minute truck turn, delivered by trained loading crews that cost under half the standard-fare price of the same minutes and give the driver his capped hours back.
upside_assumptions: (1) Shippers buy per-turn SLAs instead of hourly labour: plausible, unproven. (2) Ukeoi structure survives labour-bureau scrutiny at hundreds of sites: moderate. (3) About 3,100 FTE recruited in a market where labour shortage is the root cause: hard. (4) The dock pain persists though it fell 38% in a year: weak. (5) A data or standard asset emerges so it is not just staffing: unproven. Even then gross profit is about $10M at $70M revenue.
deciding_reason: Real payer and price signal, but loading minutes are collapsing without a crew business, Timee and 3PLs already sell the hours, and revenue is staffing-margin pass-through (about 15% gross).

pool: Japan shippers' spend on contracted road freight (multi-tier trucking subcontract chain)
title: Open-Book Tier-1: Floor Plus Ten Percent, Carriers Free, Paid in Three Days
one_liner: A registered forwarder that contracts directly with shippers as the single legal tier-1, posts its margin at the statutory 10% fee, and pays the actual carrier within 3 days, so the layered 5-10% per-tier markup disappears and the two-tier rule and register are satisfied by design.
upside_assumptions: Top decile means about $310M of gross freight (about 15x Hacobell's 2021 volume) at an 8% posted fee. Requires: shippers collapse tiers voluntarily (the two-tier duty is effort-only until a hard rule; plausible by 2028), Hacobell/Seino do not match an open-book fee (they can, by burning cash), and the float is financeable (fine at scale). The posted-fee positioning is copyable in a week.
deciding_reason: The owner-backed leader did this for six years and is small; the open-book fee is a copyable pricing tactic; the $100M fee path needs about 60x the best precedent at roughly 4% contribution.

title: The Anchor Roll-Up: Buy the Permits the Cost Floor Will Strand
one_liner: Acquire 50-60 successor-less regional carriers as permit renewal, the cost floor and the register duties hit all at once, merge them into a few 80-plus-truck 'anchor' operators that can be tier-1 on their own, and lift margin by collapsing tiers and re-pricing to the legal floor.
upside_assumptions: 57 deals in 6-7 years (about 9% of annual sellers per the pitch's own 1% sale-rate guess; plausible but execution-heavy); integration without driver attrition (hard: drivers walk after a sale); EBIT lifts from 1% to about 5% via tier collapse on 20-30% of volume (no evidence); lenders fund 1%-margin businesses (regional banks yes, at modest leverage). Even the upside is about $5M EBIT.
deciding_reason: Revenue is bought, not earned: at a 1.0% sector margin the median case earns almost nothing, permits are not scarce, strategics already buy, and the cost floor lifts all carriers equally.

title: The Unit-Load Loop: RFID Rental Pallets for the Decade the Government Mandates T11

upside_assumptions: Needs a closed-loop sale to one industry (instant noodles, produce hubs) to prove a loss-rate guarantee, then lease financing for millions of pallets, then incumbents failing to add tags (they already are). The top case is a third pool one-third the size of UPR at a roughly 2% operating margin. None of these is plausible without assuming the incumbents stand still.
deciding_reason: Already done by both incumbents; UPR, the number-2 pool, is the $100M business at a 1.8% operating margin; entry costs about $160M of capex for a capital-heavy utility return.

title: The Carrier's Advocate: Contingency Recovery of Price, Waiting and Handling Charges
one_liner: A contingency firm that builds the evidence file, sends the legally required price-consultation requests and keeps 20% of the verified uplift: the one product every shipper-paid platform in this pool is structurally unable to sell.
upside_assumptions: Needs carriers to pay for something prefectures give away; needs a law-firm structure that blesses contingency; needs the 2028 formula not to make the product redundant; needs retention after the 24-month window. Each is implausible; together the upside is a boutique.
deciding_reason: Free and subsidised substitutes already exist, contingent negotiation collides with Attorneys Act art. 72, the fee is one-off for 24 months, and the 2028 cost floor will do the job by formula.

title: The Neutral Clean Room for Competing Shippers' Joint Trucks
one_liner: A trusted third party that holds lane-level shipment data from competing shippers, finds shared loads, books the trucks and settles the savings 70/30, with antitrust-safe aggregation.
upside_assumptions: Needs the free incumbent to stall, shippers to prefer a paid neutral over a METI-backed free one, and match rates to rise by an order of magnitude. Needs savings to be audited and shared 70/30 with the shipper's own CLO. Each is implausible against a free alternative.
deciding_reason: Premise false: METI-backed traevo noWa already runs anonymous shipper-to-shipper matching for free, and the Hokkaido pilot shows only 4.7% of registered routes seek a match.

title: The Capacity Reservation Exchange for Shippers Who Cannot Afford a Failed Tender
one_liner: A reservation book where carriers sell committed truck-days on defined lanes for a retainer and shippers buy assured capacity with a substitution guarantee, priced from the platform's own tender-acceptance data.
upside_assumptions: (1) Shortage deepens as forecast and CLOs have legal duty to plan capacity: moderate. (2) CLOs book retainers as a budget line: unproven, the key test. (3) Carriers accept retainers rather than direct long-term deals with big shippers: plausible at 0.6-1% margins. (4) You build tender-acceptance data before Hacobell or a 3PL copies the product: weak. (5) You can carry substitution risk on a balance sheet without it becoming an insurance product: unresolved. Top-decile is about a third of the pitch's $100M, i.e. about 0.9% of the pool.
deciding_reason: Largest real pain of the eight but willingness to pay is untested, there is no moat, the product puts capacity risk on your balance sheet, and Hacobell or a 3PL can copy it once demand is proven.

one_liner: A neutral relay operator that standardises hand-offs between competing carriers: one shipper contract, leg-by-leg carriage terms, liability at the swap point and instant fare splitting, built on existing DCs and truck stations so the shipper-facing chain stays legal.
upside_assumptions: Needs the largest carriers to open their relay networks to a neutral clearing layer (plausible only if a standard is mandated), the state to name your contract template as the standard (it is more likely to write its own), 10% of long-haul runs (heroic), and MLIT to treat relay legs as outside the two-tier effort duty (unverified). Top-decile revenue is a small fraction of the pitch.
deciding_reason: The largest carriers already run multi-party relays, the state is building hubs and pushing cooperatives as matchers, and the $100M path needs about 10% of a guessed 24M runs.

Targets are about 300 family-owned independents under $15M of revenue, where succession gaps, the PFAS and automation capex question and the Cintas/UniFirst repricing push owners toward a sale. Edge: three ex-regional presidents or plant GMs signed before the raise, an equity pool for route service reps, and a written 24-month price lock plus month-to-month option for acquired customers, aimed at first-year leakage on bought books. After deal 3, close duplicate small plants into one hub-and-spoke wet-processing plant per metro, so the Foundry idea becomes internal consolidation and any PFAS pretreatment is concentrated in one place. First close is capped at $60-80M of equity so the platform exists before any remedy appears; a remedy package or Vestis route book is upside, not the plan.

Entry 0.8-1.2x revenue (5-8x EBITDA) = $80-120M EV, $50-70M equity at 50% leverage.
