All copyable by a funded platform, so the edge is speed of trust with family sellers and retention results.

pick.cheapest_next_test: Call 20 independents under $15M with owners aged 60+ from the TRSA directory and ask what multiple and terms would make them sell to an operator-led buyer with route-rep equity; get three IOIs or NDAs in 60 days, and ask two M&A advisers for actual closed 2025-26 revenue multiples.

upside_assumptions: Needs (1) a binding PFAS limit on laundries via POTW permits or a rule: none found and EPA's agenda skips laundries; (2) the SKU-fingerprint hypothesis (5-10%) to hold, but the study found PFAS in almost all garment types; (3) laundries to outsource treatment rather than buy vendor skids. Low plausibility on all three.
deciding_reason: No laundry PFAS limit found, laundries a small PFAS source, apparel bans shrink the stream, and the capex quote is one consultant's number.

title: Counterweight: revenue-cycle management for body-shop chains
one_liner: An R1-style outsourcer for multi-shop repairers that fights insurers' automated estimate-stripping with OEM-backed documentation, learns what each carrier pays for, and takes a share of the money it recovers.
upside_assumptions: (1) Win at least one Big-5 MSO despite in-house central review (about 25% plausible). (2) The 2.5% incremental-recovery rate holds across carriers (unverified; some support from shop surveys, but CCC says over 60% of estimates already carry supplements). (3) Scope widens to payment posting, parts credits and deductible collection at a blended 1-1.5% take (plausible only if MSOs hand over the back office). (4) Insurers do not adapt rules against documented supplements (moderately plausible). Even then the ceiling is about $55M; $100M needs over half of all MSO revenue.
deciding_reason: Real pain and budget, but take is capped by recoverable dollars, the MSO tier is about $23B, and the biggest buyers insource; ceiling about $55M.

title: Severity Pool: volume-pooling purchasing group for tier-2/3 auto carriers
one_liner: A pool of regional carriers and MGAs that guarantees MSOs a share of claim volume in return for big-carrier repair terms, taking an admin fee plus a slice of verified savings and carrying the severity guarantee.
upside_assumptions: A 25% share of tier 2/3 volume across repair, rental, salvage and glass legs at about $113 a claim; MSOs honouring pooled tiers; no top-10 carrier needed. Plausibility of 25% in 6 years is low, and the result is still about $40M.
deciding_reason: Tier 2/3 is 24% of the market, so $100M exceeds 100% of the corrected repair-leg base ($79M); network setup is already cheap.

title: Cycle Close: outcome-priced total-loss finishing desk
one_liner: An outsourced total-loss desk paid per closed TL file with a days-to-payment guarantee: it owns the leg from 'owner accepted valuation' to 'lien paid, title/POA in hand, salvage released', which is where the weeks go.
upside_assumptions: Wins about 30% of tier 2/3 files at $175 (about $44M) and half of one top-10 carrier's files (about $20-30M). Requires a carrier to accept per-file pricing with a day-count credit, and a $175 price to beat offshore BPO. Moderately implausible.
deciding_reason: Lien and title software is crowded and funded; the corrected base is $147M at 100%; a services desk faces offshore BPO and carrier in-house units.

title: Same-Day: delivery-hour parts network with total-cost sourcing and tariff price-lock
one_liner: A collision-parts network that promises a delivery hour per part from pooled dismantler, distributor and dealer stock, picks the source on total repair cost (price plus rental days plus comeback risk), locks quotes for 48 hours against tariff swings, and funds shops net-45 against the insurer-approved estimate.
upside_assumptions: A 5-8% share of parts GMV with a 5.5% blended take, net-45 financing that works (no data), and LKQ/PartsTrader not matching a delivery promise. Low plausibility; the 5.5% take is above what a courier-heavy network earns.
deciding_reason: Overstated premise, entrenched neutral-looking incumbents (LKQ, dealers, MSO warehouses) and delivery economics below courier cost.

title: Open Yard: asset-light salvage sales from the tow yard where the car already sits
one_liner: A salvage network that lists a totaled car the day it is declared, from the tow yard or shop where it already sits, and ships it once, straight to the buyer, so the insurer skips the second tow, yard intake and dwell time.
upside_assumptions: (1) Insurers move 5-8% of units to a third network (plausible: a major insurer scaled IAA across 30 states in about 90 days). (2) Buyers multi-home and net proceeds match Copart (uncertain; bidder depth comes with volume). (3) Take holds near $250-300 as Copart/IAA cut fees (doubtful). (4) Copart plus ACV does not bundle dealer demand against you (uncertain). Top-decile is about $70M.
deciding_reason: Big pool and insurers move volume quickly, but Salvato already runs the model and Copart just bought ACV; buyer depth is the moat.

title: Dent Plan: prepaid repair membership priced off shop slack, not insurance risk
one_liner: A prepaid repair membership sold through collision chains, dealers and credit unions to drivers who dropped or never had collision cover: a monthly fee buys a yearly repair credit at fixed menu prices at network shops.
upside_assumptions: A compliant structure that still sells (membership plus cost-plus per-service fee), 200,000+ members from MSO lists, credit unions and direct marketing, and low adverse selection. Gross only; net about $15M. Low plausibility.
deciding_reason: As designed it is likely insurance; the fix removes the product; revenue is gross and distribution to owners of older cars is weak.

title: Proof Plate: neutral ADAS repair plan and completion record
one_liner: A vendor-neutral layer that fixes the list of OEM-required scans and calibrations on the estimate before repair, so insurer approval and shop duty are one document, then issues a tamper-evident completion record the shop can produce in court and the insurer can pay against without review; sublet calibration work routes through the same record.
upside_assumptions: (1) Insurers accept a neutral record as pre-approval (Allstate already reimburses Opus reports, so partly plausible). (2) Garage-liability underwriters credit premiums for verified records (untested). (3) Dispatch share of sublet calibration reaches 25-40% against asTech, Opus and vertical integrators (doubtful). (4) State laws widen beyond glass (pending MD and IL only).
deciding_reason: The plan layer already exists at $3 a report with an insurer reimbursing it; the legal mandate is glass-only; dispatch upside is capped.

title: Ground Truth: independent audit and sold-price data for total-loss valuations and claims AI
one_liner: An audit and data service that recalculates each total loss and AI damage decision under the state's rules using actual sold prices, flags the drift that cost Progressive $15-48M a case, and gives the carrier a file it can hand to a regulator or a judge.
upside_assumptions: NAIC adopts the AI examination tool in November 2026 (a target, not a scheduled vote) and carriers buy exam-readiness files at $250-750k; courts keep certifying fixed-adjustment classes (Sixth Circuit en banc resolved its split in Aug 2026, direction unconfirmed). Even then the pool is about $55M; reference-data expansion is a head-on incumbent fight.
deciding_reason: Self-assessed ceiling $40-60M; sold-price data is licensed from the vendors it would audit; the escape route is a head-on fight with Cox and J.D. Power.

title: Intercompany Reconciler
one_liner: Software plus a licensed filer that sets, documents and reconciles the intercompany price on every related-party import, so customs duty, income tax and the year-end transfer-pricing true-up stop contradicting each other.
upside_assumptions: (1) ~500 large groups buy at ~$150k ACV for SaaS plus managed ACE filing (moderate-low: tax and trade teams rarely buy together). (2) A clean answer to the 1059A/482 conflict and to parent-country audits (moderate). (3) Licensed broker partner and trade-counsel opinion on circumstances of sale (high). (4) Beat Optravis, ONESOURCE and Descartes to the ERP-to-ACE link (low-moderate). (5) CBP does not tighten W548314 (moderate-high).
deciding_reason: Real gap and legal premise hold, but Optravis already sells TP software with customs logic, advisers publish the playbook, and the 2% savings carrying the $100M path is unsupported; honest ceiling is a SaaS-plus-services niche.

pool: US importers' customs-duty payments on industrial inputs and the duty-mitigation services market
title: Rights Ledger
one_liner: A standard rights notice and shared ledger that lets a distributor that paid duty on imported goods pass the drawback right down the sales chain to the customer who exports the same goods, with insurance for the importer's liability.
upside_assumptions: (1) New Section 301 (10-12.5% on 60 economies, eff. 24 Jul 2026) stays in force and is drawback-eligible (secondary sources say yes, CSMS reportedly silent; pending court challenge: moderate). (2) Export drawback becomes mainstream like a VAT refund, lifting claims from ~$1-4B toward ~$6B (low-moderate). (3) Distributors join for a revenue share despite gaining little (moderate-low). (4) Platform takes ~20% of the resulting ~$700M fee pool before Flexport, UPS and Livingston copy the notice (low).
deciding_reason: Legal premise is sound and no cross-company ledger exists, but the base is conflated, the distributor gains nothing, per-client drawback vendors are many, and the upside depends on a court-challenged Section 301 duty.

pool: US importers' customs-duty payments on industrial inputs and the duty-mitigation services market
title: Origin Rail
one_liner: A certified third-party attestation per shipment of where goods were last substantially transformed, where the metal was smelted and the metal weight fraction, paid per shipment by the importer and by a yearly verified profile bought by the foreign factory (age-verification and e-invoicing rails, transferred to customs).
upside_assumptions: (1) CBP adopts supply-chain-visibility rules (ANPRM) that make foreign-factory records mandatory (moderate). (2) Importers force suppliers to buy verification the way retailers force social audits (moderate). (3) A cheap tiered evidence product beats incumbents' audit pricing (low). (4) Privilege structure survives FCA counsel scrutiny (moderate). (5) Altana does not move into attestation (low).
deciding_reason: Mandated demand (FCA wave, CF-28 volume) is real, but a $20 attestation is not defensible evidence, audits cost far more, and Altana already holds the CBP-facing provenance rail.

title: Licence Bank
one_liner: Buy licensed customs brokerages for their licences, licensed supervisors and importer powers of attorney, run them on one AI filing stack priced per clean entry with a correction warranty, and rent the licensed chassis to the software vendors that CBP ruling H350722 now locks out.
upside_assumptions: (1) Team raises $50-100M equity plus acquisition debt (moderate; Alba shows it is financeable, but it is an incumbent). (2) Buys 30-40 firms in 6-7 years and retains customers (low-moderate). (3) AI raises margins faster than competitors' SaaS-equipped brokers (low). (4) Chassis sales to vendors add real revenue (low; H350722 may instead push vendors to partner with any broker). (5) Outcome pricing with warranty is insurable (moderate).
deciding_reason: Closest to a mechanical $100M path, but it is a financing story: revenue is bought, PE and three AI-stack entrants already occupy both halves, and the claimed licence scarcity does not cap competitors.

title: Second Filer
one_liner: An independent, licensed post-entry auditor that works only for a share of recovered duty and delivers CBP-ready workpapers, aimed at large importers whose Big Four auditors are barred from contingent fees.
upside_assumptions: (1) True overpayment rate is 2-3x the pitch (duty-stacking errors; low-moderate). (2) Wins the audit-client segment where Big Four are barred (moderate, but Leyton, Tarifflo and others already take it). (3) Prevention subscription lands at $100k for 300 firms (low). (4) Underpayment findings handled under privilege without scaring clients (moderate).
deciding_reason: The core differentiator is false: licensed, independent, contingent recovery firms already exist, and the recoverable window is ~1-1.5 years of entries, not five; $100M would be about a quarter of the whole fee pool.

title: Peer Ledger
one_liner: An importer-controlled, firewalled pool of how real importers classify, value and document the same parts, giving each member an outlier score before CBP or a whistleblower finds it, and giving sureties, lenders, insurers and big buyers a compliance-risk score on consent.
upside_assumptions: (1) A trade association sponsors and 3,000+ members join (low-moderate). (2) Antitrust counsel clears pooling of declared values among competitors (low). (3) Sureties and lenders pay $100k+ for scores (low; few buyers). (4) Importers accept discoverability of a shared reasonable-care file (low).
deciding_reason: Antitrust, discovery and trust problems with pooling competitors' declared values, inflated buyer counts (surety feeds are tens of buyers), and free substitutes; even the pitch's own path needs 27% of importers.

pool: US importers' customs-duty payments on industrial inputs and the duty-mitigation services market
title: Weight Line
one_liner: A bill-of-materials-to-weight engine and evidence file that tells importers of Section 232 derivatives which SKUs sit within reach of the 15% metal-weight line (below it the duty is zero, above it 25-50% of full value) or the 10% US-metal lane, and does the redesign, supplier change and documentation to cross it.
upside_assumptions: (1) CBP requires BOM-weight evidence on every exemption claim and samples hard (moderate; one blog says sampled review through 2026-27). (2) 600+ importers pay $60k+ for the evidence file (low-moderate). (3) Annex lists and the 15% line stay stable for 5+ years (low; 232 rules changed several times in a year). (4) Large share of annex goods sit within a few points of the line (low).
deciding_reason: The cliff is real but thin: it excludes chapters 72-76, matters only to SKUs near 15%, redesign is one-time, and 232 rules keep changing; even upside is a niche.

title: Pass-Through
one_liner: A buyer-side recovery-audit firm for tariff surcharges: it finds every explicit surcharge on a customer's supplier invoices, matches it to the supplier's refund and contract clause, recovers the buyer's share of IEEPA refunds on contingency, then audits every future Section 232 and 301 surcharge against the duty actually owed.
upside_assumptions: (1) A large share of $166B reached B2B buyers as itemised surcharges (low; pitch range 5-20%, unsourced). (2) Suppliers settle at 35% rather than pass through voluntarily (low-moderate). (3) New refund events recur (Section 122 or 301 struck down) and the same machine reruns (low-moderate). (4) Non-lawyer demand process clears unauthorized-practice limits via a partner law firm (moderate).
deciding_reason: The one-time pool is mostly already refunded to suppliers, accounting firms and law firms already sell it, big carriers pass refunds through voluntarily, and the author concedes a 2-3 year spike.
